How the UAE-Israel-Morocco threat pushed Algiers to send troops to Niger Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:09 Rival gas projects with Morocco and growing Emirati influence in the Sahel drive Algeria’s move to break with its non-intervention doctrine Nigerien President Abdourahamane Tiani and Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune at a meeting on 16 February 2026 in Algiers (Algerian Presidency) Off An Algerian military convoy arrived in Niger last Friday, marking the country's first deployment of forces abroad since 1973, when it supported Egypt in its war against the Israeli occupation of the Sinai peninsula. The deployment marks a major departure from Algeria’s longstanding policy of principled non-intervention. It follows Algiers’ decision to send four fighter jets to Niger on 30 August to thwart an attempted coup against President Abdourahamane Tiani. Although the North African state opposed the 2023 coup that brought Tiani to power, Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune now appears willing to offer the beleaguered leader a much-needed lifeline. Tiani requested the deployment. Speaking on Sunday, Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti said the troops would protect economic infrastructure and oil facilities belonging to Algerian companies. Algeria is “not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger”, Boulghiti added. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Retired senior Algerian diplomat Amar Belani offered a clue to Algiers’ thinking in an article published in October. Belani described growing instability in the Sahel , including Niger, as part of a “destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates , Morocco , Israel and certain French proxies”. Continuing instability in Niger would “directly threaten Algerian interests” and hinder the Nigeria-Niger-Algeria trans-Saharan gas pipeline project, he added. Security imperative Zine Ghebouli, a visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told Middle East Eye that the situation in the region “is imposing new security imperatives on Algiers and the necessity to secure its strategic interests, particularly in the energy sector”. This evolving regional situation includes an increasingly strong presence of the United Arab Emirates , with which Algeria severed diplomatic relations in September after “exhausting all means to preserve bilateral relations”. 'Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive' - Zine Ghebouli, visiting fellow, ECFR The Algerian foreign ministry said it had repeatedly warned Abu Dhabi over its “hostile actions”, devoting significant effort to “drawing the attention of the Emirati side and warning it of the grave consequences that may result from its regrettable and unjustified behaviour”. “Despite these numerous warnings, the United Arab Emirates has persisted in these actions, which have reached a point where they can no longer be considered acceptable or tolerable within the framework of relations between two sovereign states, or remain unanswered,” the statement added. “The fact that Algiers took the plunge to break relations proves that Emirati manoeuvering was deemed by Algerian authorities as explosive and irreconcilable,” Ghebouli said. The UAE’s regional interventions and partnership with Israel have drawn growing opposition from governments across the region. Sudan broke ties with Abu Dhabi over its documented funding and fuelling of the country’s bloody civil war. Somalia, Libya and Yemen have also accused Abu Dhabi of threatening their territorial integrity through its support for rival armed groups and separatist forces. Analysis: How Algeria came to treat the UAE as a national security threat Read More » “For Algiers, Abu Dhabi’s diplomatic, financial and military support to several actors in the region from Libya to Sudan and the Sahel serves divisions,” Ghebouli said. “Algeria has accused the UAE of being responsible for bloodshed across the region and views the Emirati role as destructive. Also, the Emirati lobbying and pressures on regional actors to expand the Abraham Accords was another point of discord,” he added, referring to the normalisation deals with Israel and Arab states, including Morocco. In recent years, the UAE has intensively cultivated relationships with the Sahel’s military regimes through high-level diplomacy, gold trading and investment. In May 2025, Emirati minister Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan met the leaders of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger to discuss cooperation in economic development, energy and other sectors. Mali’s government explicitly included security among the subjects discussed. “The Sahel has long been considered as an extension of Algerian national security and Algiers now is actively acting based on that,” said Ghebouli. “Current geopolitical shifts and all that entails in regards to rivalry with and interventions of foreign actors mean that new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s redlines,” he added. Competing energy corridors Eastern Libya’s de facto ruler, Khalifa Haftar, presents another concern. The UAE backs Haftar, who commands the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF). His military expansion towards the corridors connecting Libya and Niger has heightened Algerian concerns about Emirati influence along its southern flank. 'By securing Niger, Algeria is protecting its own answer to the Morocco-UAE axis' - Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, senior political scientist at Irsem “Algeria has had a poor relationship with the Haftar family for several years, and the mutiny in Niger in the last days of August illustrated it,” Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst affiliated with the Royal United Services Institute, told MEE. Haftar’s son Saddam supports Mahamoud Sallah, a Nigerien opponent of Tiani. “Saddam Haftar and the Algerian state are on opposing sides,” Harchaoui said of Niger. “That being said, observers mustn’t assume that Algeria is intervening in Libya. Its current effort is to deploy troops on Nigerien soil, so its mission relates to what happens inside Niger: maintaining security within a framework that will become clearer over the coming days and weeks,” he added. Turkey’s rapprochement with Haftar in October could help Algeria consolidate its foothold in the Sahel. Ankara and Algiers maintain close diplomatic relations and share interests in Libya and Sudan, potentially giving Algeria a back channel to Haftar. Rabat is also making overtures to the Haftar family, according to reports. Lieutenant General Khaled Haftar, another of Khalifa Haftar’s sons and chief of the general staff of the eastern Libyan forces, paid an official visit to Morocco last month. The Sahel, a new front in the rivalry between Algeria and Morocco Read More » Separately, energy and economic interests also underpin Algeria’s approach to Niger. Algeria’s national energy company Sonatrach, the Nigerien government and the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation are jointly developing a 4,000-km pipeline to carry Nigerian gas through Niger and Algeria and onwards to Europe. “The troops are meant to protect energy installations, notably Sonatrach’s oil projects and the corridor of the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline”, said Dr Fatiha Dazi-Heni, a senior political scientist specialising in the Arabian Peninsula at Irsem in Paris and Sciences Po Lille. Morocco is promoting a rival pipeline along an Atlantic route, drawing on the same Nigerian gas reserves to supply the same European markets. Crucially, the UAE has agreed to support the Nigeria-Morocco pipeline financially and technically. “Niger is the one country the overland route cannot bypass. Rabat and Abu Dhabi clearly have an interest in the Atlantic route prevailing, and Israel indirectly through its partnership with Morocco,” Dazi-Heni told MEE. “Algeria’s traditionally cautious strategic culture” now reflects “the new strategic constraints it faces”, she added. ‘Complicit’: World Medical Association criticised for rejecting calls to suspend Israel Submitted by Amara Sophia Elahi on Wed, 11/04/2026 - 08:11 The WMA maintains Israel's membership despite allegations of Israeli doctors' involvement in torture and complicity in the Gaza genocide Medics from the IMA Out! campaign protest outside the World Medical Association General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, on 10 October 2026 (IMA Out!) Off The World Medical Association (WMA) is facing strong criticism for refusing to suspend the Israeli Medical Association (IMA), despite documented allegations of complicity by Israeli doctors in the torture of Palestinian detainees and abuses committed in Gaza . A petition signed by 6,500 medical personnel from the IMA Out! campaign, a coalition of health advocacy groups, was presented to the WMA General Assembly in Rotterdam, the Netherlands, last month, calling on the international body to expel the IMA. Hundreds of doctors also took part in protests as the General Assembly was convening, with some carrying a shroud bearing the names of 18,000 Palestinian children who have been killed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Doctors argue that the IMA has failed to uphold core standards relating to medical ethics, and that they are complicit in serious violations of human rights against Palestinians, including failing to penalise Israeli doctors who may have overseen the torture of Palestinian detainees and the deaths of Palestinian healthcare workers in Israeli prisons. The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), a group seeking justice for war crimes, crimes against humanity and human rights violations committed by Israel against Palestinians, also filed a complaint last month to the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging it to investigate whether Israeli doctors, as well as the IMA and officials from Israel’s ministries of health and defence, have been involved in the torturing of Palestinians. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); It is the first time that a WMA member has been referred to the ICC. Dr Jonathan Fluxman, a retired British GP of Jewish heritage and organising member of the IMA Out! campaign, attended the protests in Rotterdam. “Both the WMA and IMA are refusing to investigate multiple reports by numerous human rights agencies that were sent directly to them relating to the torture and murder of healthcare workers,” he told Middle East Eye. “This goes back 30 years - the WMA has been burying reports about Israeli torture. “They are behaving in the same way as the US and British governments, by allowing Israel to get away with a genocide. In my view, the WMA is complicit in the IMA’s involvement in this.” ‘Carte blanche’ to Israel Dr Fluxman believes that the WMA should immediately initiate an investigation into the potential involvement of IMA members in the torture, abuse and deaths of Palestinian detainees. “This is about defending medical principles and the application of them,” he said. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics, and we understand that a number of national medical associations remain very concerned about the situation.” ‘It raises very serious questions about the WMA’s role as the international guardian of medical ethics’ - Dr Jonathan Fluxman, retired British GP The WMA was established in 1947 to uphold medical ethics following the Second World War, after doctors from Nazi Germany were found to have participated in war crimes. One hundred and eighteen countries are currently represented within the international body. Each member country must adhere to WMA codes of practice, including its 1975 Declaration of Tokyo, which states that doctors must not participate in torture and have a duty to call it out. The last time an association was suspended was in 1976, when South Africa was blocked from attending two general assemblies due to doctors being complicit in torture during the apartheid. The first attempt to hold the IMA accountable for the alleged participation of Israeli doctors in the abuse of Palestinian detainees came in 2009, when 725 physicians from 43 countries presented findings by human rights groups to the WMA, which that year was holding its general assembly in Tel Aviv. At the time, the president of the IMA, Yoram Blachar, was also president of the WMA - he rejected allegations that Israeli medics were complicit in torture, describing them as defamatory. In 2016, 71 UK-based doctors again urged the WMA to suspend the IMA, but it refused. The Israeli association represents over 90 percent of doctors in Israel. Its current president, Zion Hagay, chairs the WMA’s socio-medical affairs committee, while its chief executive officer advocate, Leah Wapner, serves in several advisory roles, including on the WMA’s finance and planning, socio-medical affairs, and medical ethics committees. Dr Fluxman believes that the international body is protecting the IMA. “What has 30 years of inclusion and dialogue led to? Things have got worse, and the IMA has been given carte blanche to do whatever it wants,” he said. Around 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed by Israel since October 2023. South African push to expel IMA The call for the IMA to be suspended from the WMA was led by the South African Medical Association (Sama) last year. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sama’s motion failed to secure the majority that was needed to get the WMA to consider expelling the Israeli group. Dr Mvuyisi Mzukwa, the chairman of Sama, told MEE his group had decided to take its own approach against the IMA. “We were the first medical association to formally cut ties with the IMA,” he said. In fact, it has frequently sought to challenge criticism of Israel’s actions by international medical associations. Palestinian bodies released by Israel came from infamous Sde Teiman detention centre Read More » At this year’s WMA General Assembly, the IMA installed banners outside the convention, calling on medical associations not to boycott them and asking them to remember the 7 October 2023 attacks. In November 2023, IMA’s president, Professor Hagay, refused to call for a ceasefire and justified Israeli military strikes on hospitals in Gaza, arguing that Hamas fighters needed to be “rooted out of terror bases”. That month, 81 Israeli doctors signed a letter supporting the bombing of hospitals, something which the IMA refused to condemn, contravening WMA principles on the protection of healthcare settings and health workers. Furthermore, Dr Liav Goldstein, a senior member of the IMA’s ethics bureau and chief medical officer of the Israeli Prison Service, has approved the starvation diet imposed on thousands of Palestinian prisoners after 7 October by the national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir. The IMA’s attempts to safeguard the reputation of the Israeli state were also laid bare when in May 2024, Hagay wrote to the Israeli Prison Service about the death in prison of Dr Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was head of the orthopaedic department at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City. After a highly critical British Medical Journal article about the circumstances surrounding Dr Al-Bursh's death, Professor Hagay wrote: “We would appreciate any information that could help us refute this claim, which, needless to say, causes significant harm to Israel’s standing and image worldwide.” Torture camp Whistleblowers from Sde Teiman, an Israeli military base in the Negev desert that was converted into a detention camp at the start of the Gaza genocide, have documented the systemic abuse and torture of Palestinian detainees there, including the denial of medical treatment by Israeli medics. Accounts describe prisoners being held naked, shackled and forced to wear nappies instead of being allowed to use a toilet. Some have also had to undergo amputations, often without anaesthesia. 'The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table' - Dyab Abou Jahjah, Hund Rajab Association The centre has been used to detain thousands of Palestinians from Gaza, the majority of whom are civilians, including healthcare and humanitarian workers, who are being held under the so-called “unlawful combatants” law, which has been used to strip detainees of basic legal protections and enable their detention without charge or trial. Several individuals have died while being held there. IMA ethics board director Yossi Walfisch dismissed accusations of ill-treatment and said prisoners at the camp were receiving “appropriate medical care”. Dr Al-Bursh was held at Sde Teiman before being taken to Ofer Prison, where he died. While in prison he was brutally beaten, tortured and repeatedly raped, according to testimonies of released Palestinian prisoners who had met him. The Hind Rajab Foundation said evidence shows that medical participation in torture and abuse at the camp was structural. Dyab Abou Jahjah, director general at HRF, said: “Israeli physicians abandoned their neutrality when they agreed to treat patients in chains and erase what was done to them. “The WMA must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table.” If IMA members are found to be complicit in this, it would violate the WMA’s code of practice, values and guidelines, as well as international humanitarian law, Abou Jahjah said. The WMA told MEE: “Inclusion sits at the core of the WMA's identity. Patients remain our focus, alongside the protection of health personnel, including physicians, wherever they serve. “Our members, including the Israeli Medical Association, regularly call out injustices and violations of medical neutrality even when their own governments are involved.” MEE also contacted IMA but received no response by the time of publication. Aipac and the Michigan Senate race: How the Israel lobby became toxic "A lobby is like a night flower: it thrives in the dark and dies in the sun.” So said Steve Rosen , former foreign policy director of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) in a memo to a fellow staffer. Rosen would later be fired amid a major scandal involving espionage in passing classified US information to Israel . Rosen was correct about the danger to a lobbying organisation that publicity poses. But in December 2021, Aipac decided to test that theory by creating two political action committees (Pacs) that enabled it to take part directly in political campaigns. The results were mixed, and Aipac recently announced that it was closing one of the Pacs it had set up. Aipac had been an advocacy organisation, promoting Israel’s interests, but it did not fund campaigns directly, nor did it endorse or fund political candidates. In many ways, that made it more effective. It could do things like issue a congressional report card which rated every member of Congress’s support of Israel. Then other groups that were actual Pacs could use those reports to decide which candidates they should be contributing to. ‘Israel cannot afford to ignore’: Israeli press reels from Democratic sweep The Israeli press is taking stock of last night’s Democratic sweep of Congress, sounding the alarm over the consequences for Israel. A Haaretz analysis this morning said Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over pro-Israel candidate Mike Rogers demonstrated “that even strident opposition to Israel is no barrier to winning competitive federal races.” “El-Sayed won despite AIPAC spending more than $30 million to defeat him in the Democratic primary and another reported $9 million on behalf of Rogers in the general election,” it added. The Jerusalem Post warned: “The implications of the US midterm elections for Israel could extend far beyond the loss of Republican control of Congress. The defeat comes amid broader shifts within the Democratic Party regarding Israel, the war with Iran, and the strategic relationship between Jerusalem and Washington.” “One of the clearest takeaways from the election campaign is the political price the war with Iran has exacted on the Republican Party”, the analysis said, referring to the war Israel pushed the US into on 28 February. “The expansion of the camp critical of Israel, and its growing access to positions of influence, represents a shift that Israel cannot afford to ignore,” it added.

Gaza volunteer surgeon Adam Hamawy wins US House seat in New Jersey Democrat Adam Hamawy, who treated Palestinians in Gaza during Israel’s genocide, has defeated Republican Gregg Mele to represent New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District. The 57-year-old former US Army combat surgeon campaigned against military assistance to Israel and other countries committing human rights violations. He has also condemned the war on Iran as “illegal and immoral”. In a May interview he accused Washington of “catering to special interests of the defense contractors and war mongers and with organizations like [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] AIPAC and Israel’s special interests.” Hamawy joined missions to Gaza in 2024 and 2025 through the Palestinian American Medical Association, with coordination from the World Health Organization.

Iran’s Khamenei says US election results will not end hostility towards Tehran Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei says Washington will continue its confrontation with Tehran despite the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories. Aber Kawas becomes first Palestinian American elected to New York State Legislature Aber Kawas has won her bid for the New York State Senate District 12 seat, taking a 75 percent share of the votes with 90 percent of the votes counted when the race was called by the New York Times. Kawas has made history as the first hijab-wearing Palestinian American to serve in the New York State Legislature. She joins a small list of Palestinian Americans to ever be elected at the state level across the US . Kawas posted a short message to X after the victory saying, "We made history". "Fund dignity, fight destruction" was the slogan Kawas campaigned with. "Fund dignity" refers to her stance on healthcare for all, fast and reliable public transportation, and affordable housing. "Fight destruction" refers to her positions on stopping climate change, protecting immigrants and her "No money for war" stance. Kawas is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, a group that has made unprecedented gains since its member Zohran Mamdani won the historic mayoral race in New York City last year. There is also talk on both sides of the Atlantic of reviving the traditional alliance between Labour and Democrats as the 2028 presidential election approaches. Democrat sources told MEE they watched British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Miliband break with Keir Starmer’s foreign policy towards Israel - and noted how popular it has been in Britain. Congressman Ro Khanna, who was held at gunpoint by settlers in the West Bank last summer, praised the UK’s “important moral step”. Matt Duss, a Washington Middle East expert with strong links to the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, told MEE on Tuesday night that “seeing key allies taking these steps gives a real boost to colleagues in the US”. He added that, “A new class of progressive Democrat is coming into Congress who wants to support Palestinian rights.” Democratic member of Congress, Greg Casar, has already urged a US ban on trade with the settlements. Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, meanwhile, declared that “Congress can and must act”. 'It is time' Emily Thornberry, the chair of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Select Committee, told MEE that if "brave and thoughtful leaders such as Reps Khanna, Casar and Castro are put into a position to develop US policy toward Israel and the occupied territories, real progress could be made." Thornberry added: “I would recommend what we have done [on Israeli settlements] as a model, and I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this in the near future.” In a sign that the Democrats have been inspired by Britain, 19 Senate Democrats - including Castro and Casar - introduced legislation in late September to sanction people or companies facilitating settlement construction as part of the Israeli government’s E1 plan. The plan involves building thousands of new housing units between Jerusalem and the existing West Bank settlement of Maale Adumim, 7km east of the city. It would effectively cut the West Bank in half, making a Palestinian state unviable. Congresswoman Madeleine Dean, one of the lawmakers behind the sanctions bill, said when it was unveiled: “It is time that the United States joined our allies - such as the United Kingdom, France, and Canada - in taking action to help preserve dignity and self-determination for the Palestinian people, which is essential for progress toward peace.” (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Both the Sunak and Starmer governments pursued a general policy of alignment with the US. Then came Burnham’s startling break with the Trump administration over Israel, with Britain leading middle-ranking powers including France and Canada in sanctioning settlements in September. This bold move opened up a new interest in Britain from the US Democrats, who have emerged victorious in the American midterms this week. 'I dearly hope that we’re able to work together on this [policy towards Israel] in the near future' - Emily Thornberry, Foreign Affairs Select Committee chair Polls have shown most of the British public, including a narrow majority of Conservative voters, supported the sanctions package. Democrats are hoping to distance themselves from former US President Joe Biden’s support for Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza. With high-profile Democratic candidates critical of Israel - in particular Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who was relentlessly attacked by Trump but endorsed by former Democratic President Barack Obama - storming to victory in the midterms this week, the appetite within the Democratic Party to take a tougher stance on Israel is nearly certain to increase. This may especially be so if Trump now launches a fresh assault with Israel on Iran - which the midterm results indicate most Americans do not support. In some ways, the burgeoning alliance between the Democrats and Labour recalls the close ties built up between US President Bill Clinton and Tony Blair before he became prime minister in 1997. The relationship between Harold Wilson and Lyndon Johnson in the 1960s is another example. A close relationship between the Democrats and Labour would therefore mark a return to traditional British foreign policy, which has been strongly tied to the United States. Responding to a question about whether the election outcome could make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham said: “Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living. “That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves. But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.” Pressed on the risk of further fighting following the vote, he said: “Well, I’ll be working for de-escalation to make it very clear. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs369.06 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs391.52. The prices are applicable for Nov 4 (Wednesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The latest price cut also comes as international oil prices slid about 2 per cent to a three-week low on Tuesday in volatile trade. The market weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries about additional supply disruptions from recent attacks in both conflicts. Brent futures fell $1.63, or 2pc, to $103.14 a barrel at 8:44pm PKT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude fell 67 cents, or 1pc, to $95.79. Brent was on track for its lowest close since Oct 7 and WTI was headed for its lowest close since Oct 14. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under an arrangement announced on Monday for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This would allow a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. Addressing a press conference today, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said efforts were being made to introduce a similar system for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). He also hinted at the latest reduction in fuel prices, saying “even better news will come before us”. Meanwhile, Jamaat-i-Islami and the government held another round of talks to discuss possible relief to low-income citizens in petroleum prices, and agreed to continue their negotiations in the coming days. Rise in fuel prices The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. On Sept 13, PM Shehbaz also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, the petroleum minister announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene. Additional input by Reuters

Pakistan successfully tests its first indigenously developed air-to-air missile Fa’az: ISPR. Pakistan on Tuesday performed a successful flight test of the country’s first indigenously developed air-to-air missile, Fa’az, “marking another significant milestone in the advancement of national aerospace and defence capabilities”, the military’s media wing said . According to a statement by Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the missile is equipped with a state-of-the-art terminal guidance system and can engage enemy targets at longer ranges. “Fa’az will significantly enhance [the] operational flexibility of [the] Pakistan Air Force, further strengthening the country’s overall defence posture. The successful flight test underscores the technical maturity, innovation and self-reliance achieved by Pakistan’s defence industry,” the statement added. The launch was witnessed by senior military officers, scientists and engineers involved in the development of the system, the ISPR said. It added that President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and the service chiefs congratulated the scientists. Pakistan’s first indigenously developed air-to-air missile, Fa’az, is test-launched from a JF-17 fighter jet in this video released on Nov 3, 2026. — Screengrab via X/DGPR_PAF Meanwhile, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi issued a statement congratulating the nation on the test. “Our scientists and engineers have once again achieved a remarkable feat that makes the nation proud,” the ministry quoted him as saying. “The successful test of the indigenously developed Fa’az missile marks a significant advancement in the field of defence. “We are all proud of Pakistan’s distinguished scientists and engineers.” Pakistan successfully tested two surface-to-surface missiles last month; the Fatah-2 extended range (ER) hypersonic ballistic missile was tested on Oct 13, and the indigenously developed extended version of the Fatah-IV ground-launched cruise missile was tested a week before that. ISPR said that the Fatah-2 ER is equipped with advanced navigation and state-of-the-art avionics. “It is capable of engaging targets with high precision and defeating [the] enemy’s missile defence systems due to its unique trajectory and manoeuvrability features,” it added. For Fatah-IV ER, ISPR said: “Equipped with advanced avionics and state-of-the-art navigational aids, the weapon system is capable of engaging targets at extended ranges with high precision and lethality.” It noted that the test “also validated additional technical parameters of various sub-systems incorporated for improved accuracy and enhanced survivability”.

Govt weighs options to recover $800m from Etisalat. ISLAMABAD: The government is considering international arbitration against Etisalat over the outstanding $800 million payment from the sale of Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL), along with its opportunity cost since 2008 and applicable damages. The matter was discussed at a joint meeting of the Senate standing committees on information technology and privatisation on Tuesday, where members were informed that the Office of the Attorney General for Pakistan (OAGP) had been directed to implement the federal cabinet’s decision under Rule 24 of the Rules of Business, 1973, at the earliest. However, senators from both committees expressed surprise that they were not given access to the sale purchase agreement (SPA) concerning the divestment of 26pc shares in PTCL, along with management control, to UAE-based Etisalat International Pakistan (EIP). The meeting was jointly chaired by Senator Dr Afnanullah Khan, chairman of the Senate Standing Committee on Privatisation, and Senator Palwasha Khan, chairwoman of the Senate Standing Committee on Information Technology and Telecommunications. Cabinet asks attorney general’s office to prepare case for international arbitration At the outset, IT Secretary Zarrar Hasham Khan informed the committees that the agenda item concerning Etisalat’s outstanding $800m payment to the government was sensitive. He requested the chairpersons to ask all unauthorised persons, including media representatives, to leave the meeting, following which the proceedings were held in camera. However, after the meeting, some senators expressed annoyance that they, too, had not been provided details of the PTCL sale agreement. “The strange part is that we parliamentarians cannot handle information, but it is safe with the bureaucrats,” one senator remarked. “There has to be a law in this regard, and parliament should be informed about such sales of national assets rather than depending upon bureaucrats and officers,” the senator added. According to a briefing submitted by the Ministry of Privatisation, a copy of which is available with Dawn, the government sold 26pc shares in PTCL, along with management control, to Etisalat in 2005 for $2.59 billion. Of this amount, $1.76bn was received, while approximately $800m remains unpaid. The briefing said the payment was linked to the transfer of PTCL properties to the new management. Although 99pc of the properties had been transferred, 32 of the total 3,246 properties remained untransferred. Etisalat, which is now known as e&, has continued to withhold the outstanding $800m because of the non-transfer of these properties. The ministry said the government had made extensive efforts since 2015 to resolve post-privatisation issues, including the formation of several committees and negotiations with Etisalat for an amicable settlement. However, the dispute remained unresolved, prompting the government to constitute another committee in July 2026, headed by the adviser to the prime minister on privatisation. The committee included representatives of the ministries of IT and law and the OAGP. Considering the 20-year history of the dispute, the committee recommended that Pakistan consider international arbitration, as provided under the SPA, to recover the outstanding $800m, along with its opportunity cost since 2008 and applicable damages. It also recommended that the attorney general assess the strength of Pakistan’s case, its prospects of success and the associated legal implications. “If merits of the case permit to pursue international arbitration, prior to issuance of the Notice of Intent to Etisalat, the Attorney General should seek approval of the prime minister or the federal government,” the privatisation ministry’s briefing stated. The Privatisation Division informed the committees that a summary had subsequently been submitted to the federal cabinet. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

Govt unveils LPG policy as power costs set to rise. • Directs four SOEs to re-enter LPG import business • Plans subsidised LPG at Rs300-350 per kg for BISP-eligible consumers ISLAMABAD: The government on Tuesday directed four state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to re-enter the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) import business to ease severe supply constraints and soaring prices, while the power division sought an estimated Rs2-4 per unit increase in electricity purchase costs for the next calendar year. Speaking at a news conference at PTV headquarters, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik said the federal cabinet had approved a broad-based LPG policy aimed at creating competition and supplies through procurement by four SOEs under government-to-government (G2G) and business-to-business (B2B) arrangements. He acknowledged that LPG, often described as the poor man’s fuel, was in short supply even before the onset of winter because of disruptions along the western borders. As a result, unscrupulous elements were selling LPG at Rs700-800 per kg, depending on the area, against the maximum price of Rs295 per kg notified by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) for November, he said. “Looking at the Saudi CP (Contract Price) rate and prevailing premiums, its local price in the market would be Rs450-500 per kg” once supplies from SOEs began, the minister said. He added that private-sector importers would remain free to arrange supplies at lower rates to compete. Mr Malik said the prime minister had directed that LPG be provided to deserving and vulnerable consumers at Rs300-350 per kg, using the eligibility criteria of the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP). The subsidy would be financed through a new account funded by the difference between the LPG import parity price and proceeds from auctions of locally produced LPG supplied by refineries and exploration and production companies, under a clawback mechanism. The minister told Dawn that the four SOEs — Pakistan State Oil, Pakistan LNG Ltd, Sui Sout­hern Gas-LPG and Parco-LPG — had already received offers for LPG supplies from Saudi Arabia and Oman. However, even the proposed subsidised price of Rs300-350 per kg for BISP-eligible consumers would exceed Ogra’s current notified maximum price of Rs294.08 per kg. Power purchase costs Separately, a power division team presented six scenarios for rebasing the power purchase pr­ice (PPP) for January-Dece­m­ber 2027 at a public hearing cond­u­cted by the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra). Industrial consumers criticised the government for creating additional entities and hiring staff at exorbitant salaries, arguing that these costs were contributing to higher electricity tariffs. Central Power Purchasing Agency CEO Rehan Akh­tar and Power Planning and Monitoring Company CFO Naveed Qaiser presented the projections, all of which put next year’s power purchase price, excluding taxes and other charges, above this year’s Rs25.32 per unit. None of the scenarios assumed that the US-Iran war would continue into 2027. Under the base-case scenario, the power purchase price was projected at Rs27.31 per unit, an increase of Rs1.99. The ideal scenario, which officials acknowledged was unlikely to materialise, projected Rs25.883 per unit, up Rs0.563. The two worst-case scenarios put the price at Rs28.84 and Rs29.26 per unit, representing increases of Rs3.52 and Rs3.94, respectively. Two other scenarios, involving changes in electricity demand and greater LNG and natural gas availability, projected increases of Rs2.25 and Rs1.12 per unit. Nepra reserved its decision and will issue its determination after examining the record and submissions. The projected annual power purchase cost ranges from Rs3.4 trillion to Rs3.8tr. Explaining the new LPG policy, Mr Malik said the Competition Commission of Pakistan, the National Explosives and Petroleum Safety Agency and Ogra had been tasked with addressing collusive practices, quality standards and price monitoring in coordination with district administrations. He said the quota system benefiting influential groups would be abolished, while local producers would auction LPG in lots of five to 10 tonnes through a competitive process monitored by Ogra and the petroleum division. Under the new arrangement, SOEs would import LPG in bulk and publish the base price, linked to the Saudi Aramco Contract Price. These would be disclosed on their websites as the monthly average landed cost. Ogra would cease issuing price notifications for locally produced and imported LPG. Local producers would receive the producer price determined through auctions, while the difference between the producer price and the SOE-linked base price would be deposited in a fund to subsidise LPG for BISP-eligible consumers. Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

Opposition nominees sought for election reforms panel. • PTI whip says participation ‘difficult’ following developments in KP • Minister says committee seats to be allocated on basis of strength in NA • PPP blames opposition for delay in appointment of new CEC ISLAMABAD: The government on Tuesday formally approached the opp­o­s­ition to seek its representation on the proposed Parliamentary Committee on Electoral Refo­rms (PCER). How­ever, the opposition termed the formation of the committee a “futile exercise” unless its long-standing demands were met. The committee is being formed to make the electoral process fair, transparent and acceptable to all stakeholders. Federal Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry contacted PTI chief whip in the National Assembly Aamir Dogar, asking him to submit the names of opposition lawmakers for the committee. When contacted, Mr Dogar confirmed that the minister had telephoned him to seek nominations. He said the opposition would hold a meeting to discuss the invitation and the decision would be ann­o­unced by National Asse­mbly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai. Questioning how the opposition could join the committee under the prevailing circumstances, Mr Dogar referred to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the alleged detention of the provincial chief minister and the arrest of more than 10 PTI leaders. He also alleged that the PTI’s mandate had been stolen in the last general elections. “How can the government expect the opposition to sit with it on the committee under these circumstances?” he asked. Mr Dogar also expressed reservations over the proposed composition of the committee and demanded equal representation for the government and opposition. Meanwhile, PTI’s interim Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan told reporters that the opposition would not oppose the committee if the dialogue was conducted sincerely. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), a major ally of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), has already approached opposition leaders Mehmood Khan Achakzai in the National Assembly and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas in the Senate, inviting them to join the proposed committee. Nasa's Swift satellite telescope heads for fiery re-entry 22 years after launch. An aging Nasa satellite telescope that a robotic spacecraft was sent to retrieve on a failed rescue mission this summer was headed for a fiery re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday, nearly 22 years after it was launched into orbit. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory , weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452 kg), was set to tumble out of orbit and burn up in the atmosphere somewhere over the tropics, with fragments surviving re-entry unlikely to threaten populated areas, according to Nasa. The US Space Force has put the odds of harm coming to anyone on Earth at one chance in 2,100, Nasa said in an online statement, projecting the time of re-entry at approximately 3:30am EST (0830 GMT). The Aerospace Corporation, a nonprofit national security research entity, projected a re-entry window of 5:19am EST, plus or minus two hours. London-based astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell, an honorary professor at the Durham University Space Research Centre, cited revised US Space Force data predicting re-entry most likely to come around 7:45am EST. “The satellite is in a very circular orbit, skimming the top of the atmosphere,” he told Reuters by phone on Tuesday night. “The question is at what point does it heat up enough that it starts breaking up.” Nasa’s prized $500 million Swift satellite, a first-of-its-kind multi-wavelength space observatory, has been studying gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic phenomena since 2004, using its array of three telescopes. The observatory, which has no onboard propulsion system of its own, has been drifting toward an expected demise for months as it circles the globe at a speed of roughly 17,000 miles per hour (27,359 kph). Astronomers had hoped to extend Swift’s mission for a number of years by giving the satellite telescope a lift. In July, Nasa and Arizona-based startup Katalyst launched a specially built rescue vehicle called LINK on a mission to rendezvous with Swift, latch onto the satellite and tug the observatory back into a higher, more sustainable orbit. But the LINK spacecraft itself began spinning uncontrollably soon after reaching space, and by mid-August, mission managers abandoned the effort, resigned to letting Swift continue to meet its fate. The aborted rescue attempt, the first US mission of its kind, took on heightened significance as a demonstration of a new orbital grappling technology seen as pivotal to the outcome of the US-China space race. The LINK effort was closely watched as a trial run of a key satellite-maintenance technology with potential dual-use military space applications. Katalyst touted the mission as a historic endeavor that designed, built and tested the LINK rescue vehicle on an unprecedented nine-month production schedule under a $30 million Nasa contract. Swift was launched more than two decades ago to explore the most powerful known explosions in the universe, bursts of gamma-ray radiation emanating from the cores of distant galaxies. Originally designed for a two-year prime mission, Swift remained in operation far longer with observations of a wide range of cosmic objects, from galaxies powered by supermassive black holes and stars emitting X-ray flares, to comets and asteroids streaking through our own solar system.

Pakistan's Maliha Ali topples Russia's Drozdova at MMA world championships. Russia arrived at the IMMAF World Championships in Tbilisi, Georgia, with more than 60 athletes, government backing and one of the best-funded programmes in the sport. On Tuesday, a 24-year-old from Hunza, Gilgit-Baltistan, beat one of them. Maliha Ali defeated Veronika Drozdova, a two-time European champion and, at 19, by split decision in their featherweight (65.8kg) bout at the world championships of amateur mixed martial arts. Maliha, who is also a wushu champion and a national kickboxing gold medallist, came into the tournament off a silver medal at the IMMAF World Cup in Angola earlier this year. The fight was won early and nearly lost late. Fighting from a southpaw stance, Maliha started cautiously before closing the distance and pinning the Russian against the cage. She landed clean strikes to finish the opening round strongly, though Drozdova found a couple of overhand lefts. Maliha dominated the second. She secured a takedown, taking the fight to the floor, and moved into full mount, sitting astride her opponent’s torso, to land heavy blows from the top. But she had spent much of her energy in those two rounds and appeared to tire in the third, where Drozdova took her down and controlled the action on the ground. The round went to the Russian, but the first two belonged to Maliha. The judges agreed. When the final bell rang, she stood with her arms raised, not in certainty, but in hope. When her name was announced, Maliha let out a roar. Omar Ahmed, president of the Pakistan MMA Federation, leapt with joy from her corner. She hugged her opponent, then dropped to the mat in prostration, the Pakistan flag draped over her shoulders: a moment of faith and gratitude after a hard-fought battle. “I was listening to the corner and the coach’s instructions during the fight,” Maliha told Dawn . “We worked on our opponent’s game plan, how she fights, and executed our strategy. And thankfully it worked.” Omar said the federation held a six-week camp and brought in an international jiu-jitsu and grappling coach after spotting weaknesses during Maliha’s silver-medal run in Angola earlier this year. “There were some holes in their game which we spotted during the event in Angola,” Omar told Dawn . “The coach worked on the mistakes that she made during her previous fights, and we saw the improvement today.” He acknowledged the disparity in resources between the two nations. “Russia has one of the most well-funded MMA programs,” Omar said. “Compared to them, we are the most underfunded and probably the least-resourced federation competing in this event because of the sports policy in Pakistan. But still, we manage to eke out victories against such formidable opponents.” For Omar, each victory against the odds carries a deeper meaning. “Watching our fighters win against such tough opponents brings me joy which I cannot put into words,” he added. “We come from almost nothing; the only thing we have is our grit and desire to succeed, and I guess that’s what matters at the end of the day.” It is a familiar position for the federation. Pakistan’s campaign at last year’s championships, also held in Tbilisi, was reported to be entirely self-funded through private sponsorship, with no government money. Maliha faces Mexico’s Andrea Gabriela Guzman Salazar in the quarter-finals on Wednesday. Her twin sister Manesha, who won gold in Luanda earlier this year, fights Poland’s Martyna Caruk on the same day. Both are chasing world titles.

Dashain gone, Tihar uncertain: Nepali workers stranded in Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks disrupt flights. KATHMANDU: Rajesh Rai from Khotang was preparing to return home after three years in Saudi Arabia to celebrate Dashain with family. His employer had granted him a month’s leave and he had an exit-re-entry visa. He had booked an October 11 Air Arabia flight from Riyadh to Kathmandu via Sharjah. But a day before departure, Houthi rebels attacked King Khalid International Airport . Thirteen people, according to Saudi authorities, were killed and more than 300 injured. The airport was shut. After a friend told him that flights were operating from Jeddah, Rai travelled nearly 1,000 kilometres by bus for 13 hours, paying Rs7,000. But he remains in a friend’s room, unsure when he can fly home. “I am neither in my company’s camp nor have I been able to reach home,” said Rai. “Dashain has passed, Tihar is around the corner and my leave is about to end.” Rai is among hundreds of Nepali workers whose plans to return home have been thrown into uncertainty. Between October 8 and 25, about 45 per cent of scheduled flights from Saudi airports were cancelled. At Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the rate reached 86pc. Direct Kathmandu-Dammam flights, widely used by Nepali workers, have also stopped. Nepal Airlines and Himalaya Airlines have cancelled 18 scheduled services since October 11. Nepal Airlines operates weekly and Himalaya twice a week; the latter has announced cancellations through November 4. Around 400,000 Nepalis work in Saudi Arabia. The Department of Foreign Employment says about 7,000 people receive labour permits, including renewals, each month; 8,366 did so in the mid-September to mid-October period. Nepali Embassy in Riyadh says the workers whose contracts have ended are under particular pressure. The embassy has asked employers to provide food and accommodation to the workers. The embassy does not have official figures of the stranded Nepali workers. “More people are contacting us to ask where and from which airport they can travel home,” said labour counsellor Kabiraj Upreti. “We are facilitating whatever we can.” Reuters reported on October 26 that 4,071 of 4,736 flights scheduled at Riyadh airport between October 8 and 25 had been cancelled. Cancellations reached 42pc in Dammam and 46.7pc in Abha. More than 7,800 flights, or 45pc of scheduled departures nationwide, were cancelled. There are a total of 18 international airports in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh airport has partially reopened, but regular services have not returned. Some Saudi carrier flights have resumed, while foreign airlines have reduced or suspended Riyadh services. Jeddah and Dammam also face cancellations and rescheduling. Madhendra Rai, an Ilam native working in Dammam, said repeated cancellation notices were causing mental stress. Airlines were not clearly explaining whether passengers could get refunds or transfer to another flight. “When a flight is cancelled, they do not clearly explain the options. They tell us to take a voucher instead of a refund. Employers also say they will look for an alternative only after the cancellation is confirmed,” said Mahendra. “It is not just the ticket date that keeps changing; the day we can meet our families is also being pushed further away.” Connecting flights through Air Arabia, flydubai and Indian carriers are also hard to find. “Even if we get a ticket, the one-way fare has reached Rs100,000. We have never seen tickets this expensive,” he said. Dilip Baraili, another Nepali worker, said repeated flight cancellations had left ticket-holders in limbo. “The feelings of Nepalis who work hard abroad and wait to return home to celebrate festivals with their families must be understood,” he said. Poor information is also adding to workers’ costs. Ganesh Rai’s October 25 Himalaya Airlines flight was cancelled, with rebooking arranged for October 30. That flight was cancelled, too, soon. The travel agency does not answer calls, he complained. Each fruitless trip to the airport costs him about Rs2,000. Nepal Airlines said it had suspended flights for passenger safety. “This is not because of us,” said spokesperson Archana Khadka. “Services will resume as soon as the situation in Saudi Arabia becomes normal.” The airline says passengers can change travel dates without charge or receive a full refund. Himalaya Airlines said its cancellations were also linked to aviation safety and that it could not guarantee a resumption date. Umesh Pandey, working in Dammam, has waited 18 days to return to Nepal. He is considering travelling by road to Qatar or Bahrain but does not know the immigration procedures. “If we cannot fly from Saudi Arabia, I want to travel by road to Qatar or Bahrain. But I do not know how to get the visa or whether border immigration will let us cross. We have never travelled this way,” said Umesh. The problem is more serious for workers whose exit permits are near expiry. Hemanta Thapa, from Jhapa, works in Najran near the Yemeni border, where the regional airport is closed. His ticket has been cancelled and he fears he may miss Tihar. To catch a flight from Dammam, he must travel about 1,400 kilometres, a 17 to 18 hours road journey. “For two years, I have been planning to go home for Tihar. I do not know when Dammam airport will reopen or when flights will operate,” he said. Thapa had left his company after obtaining an exit permit, a process that took six months. If it expires before he can leave, he will have to apply again through the embassy. He says this could take another three months and he would have to bear the costs himself. Workers have urged the government to arrange travel through neighbouring countries. “We are in trouble. The government should arrange flights home from Kuwait, Qatar or Bahrain,” said Shailesh Upadhyay. “Bahrain is the most suitable option.” Balaram Thapa, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association in Saudi Arabia, urged the government and airlines to arrange transport from Dammam to Bahrain. “It is close and we can reach it by bus or taxi. Some people are already travelling through Bahrain without being stopped at the border,” he said. “The government or airlines should arrange buses and direct flights to Nepal from there.” The disruption comes amid wider security concerns. Houthi attacks had heightened fears among Nepalis, including workers in Dammam and Jizan. A report on October 22 said a Nepali and a Filipino were killed in a drone attack at the Shaybah oil field , while a Pakistani and an Indian worker were injured. The embassy has urged Nepalis to follow official alerts and verify flights before going to airports. The foreign ministry says it is monitoring the situation. “The Nepali Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate General in Jeddah are closely following the flights situation and facilities for Nepali citizens. They are in regular contact with Nepali citizens and communities,” said Lok Bahadur Paudel Chhetri, the ministry spokesperson. “The government will take appropriate steps as necessary, keeping the convenience and safety of Nepali citizens in mind.” It’s not only direct flights between Saudi Arabia and Nepal that have been cancelled. Connecting flights have also been affected. IndiGo has suspended services to Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam and Medina until November 14. Air India and Air India Express have suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam until November 7. Similarly, Etihad Airways has cancelled some flights from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until November 5. Air Arabia has also cancelled some services to Riyadh, Dammam, Abha and Taif, but no resumption dates have been confirmed through publicly available sources. Qatar Airways has suspended flights to Riyadh and Dammam and reduced the number of services to Jeddah. However, no new dates have been announced for the resumption of flights to Riyadh and Dammam following October 24.

Numbers that tell the story of the Democrats' midterm blowout. Democrats stormed back to power in Congress and governors’ mansions across America in Tuesday’s midterm elections, a stunning repudiation of Donald Trump’s political agenda. These are the numbers that tell the tale of a historic night. Record turnout Total turnout numbers were not in yet, but Americans cast more than 61.7 million votes even before election day, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. That figure, a runaway record for early voting in US midterms, undoubtedly boosted Democrats, who traditionally cast their ballots early more often than Republican voters. The numbers showed large turnout among African Americans, young people and other groups that typically support Democratic candidates, National Public Radio reported. The surge contributed to a wave election, with Democrats running the table on key races and seizing control of both chambers of Congress. Record fundraising Total spending for the 2026 midterms soared to a record $11.9 billion, substantially higher than the $8.9bn racked up in 2022, according to OpenSecrets, a non-partisan authority on spending in US politics. Campaign fundraising and ad buys jumped in the 2026 races, driven by the outside spending of so-called political action committees. Such outside spending, led by Trump’s mega-billionaire ally Elon Musk, favoured Republicans by some $360m. But Democratic candidates proved adept at raising their own funds. House and Senate candidates spent an unprecedented $3.7bn from their campaign war chests, with Democrats outspending Republicans by $800 million, according to OpenSecrets. In Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico broke records by bringing in a staggering $145m, several times the $22m raised by his Republican rival Ken Paxton, who was forced to rely on outside groups to fund his campaign. First wins in decades Ninety-four years ago was the last time Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate. But on Tuesday night, Adam Hamilton unseated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall. Hamilton, the pastor of a Methodist megachurch who was registered as a Republican until recently, became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the largely rural, conservative state since 1932. Texas also went blue for the first time in decades, with Talarico scoring a massive upset to flip a Senate seat in the Lone Star State for the first time since 1988 — the year before Talarico was born. South Carolina also defied history, ousting Senator Darline Graham — who had been appointed earlier this year to fill the seat of her late brother Lindsey Graham — in favour of Democrat Annie Andrews. No South Carolina Democrat had been elected to the Senate since 1998. Young voters, Latinos turn away Young men and Latino voters — two segments of the American electorate crucial to Trump — turned sharply away from the president and his Republican Party, exit polls showed. Hispanic voters had helped bring Trump to power in 2016, and were instrumental in his victory in 2024, when they only narrowly went to Democrat Kamala Harris in the presidential election, 51 per cent to 48pc, according to Pew Research. But in recent weeks, several Latino voters have expressed anger at Trump, saying they felt betrayed. It showed in NBC News exit polls on Tuesday, when Latino voters backed Democratic candidates by 62pc to 35pc over Republicans. Young voters also soured on Trump. NBC News reported that its exit polls showed 18-29-year-olds, men and women, voted for Democrats by a 72pc to 25pc margin. That is a sharp shift from 2024, when young voters were split between Trump and Harris.

Israel election commission rejects Netanyahu charges of fraud. Israeli electoral authorities on Wednesday rejected allegations promoted by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of fraud by Arab parties, who could hold the key to removing him from power after a divisive vote. President Isaac Herzog will at noon (1000 GMT) officially receive the results of the October 27 election as he decides whether to give Netanyahu or his rival Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form a government, with neither commanding enough votes alone. The Central Elections Committee said it had conducted an audit of 9,069 polling stations following complaints and was confident that the announced results “accurately reflect the will of the voters”. “All complaints submitted by political factions have been reviewed and there were no findings indicating harm to the integrity of the election,” it said in a statement. Netanyahu has repeatedly alleged fraud by Arab-majority parties, pointing to the arrests of several people with envelopes of cash on election day and later claiming lawmakers received money from Qatar — allegations that have been levelled at his own aides in the past. Late on Tuesday, Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said she would not question anyone without evidence after reports that the head of the domestic security service Shin Bet, a Netanyahu ally, had asked to interrogate Arab parties. Netanyahu’s Likud party lashed out at her, saying that she was trying to “obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors”. Eisenkot, a former military chief trying to unite centrists and the centre-right and turn the page on Netanyahu’s long, polarising reign, accused Likud of attempting a “pogrom against democracy”. He had earlier warned Netanyahu against launching a new war with his close ally US President Donald Trump against Iran, which could help the Israeli prime minister push for a unity government or to run out the clock until new elections. No unity government Yair Lapid, a former prime minister and key force in the opposition bloc, pointed to the midterm elections in the US in which Democrats resoundingly trounced Trump’s Republicans. The Shin Bet “outbursts” paired with the US election results “eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has been in power on and off for nearly two decades, has called for a “broad national government” — with himself at the top. Herzog’s statements have raised speculation that he could sound out leaders on a possible unity government, hoping to bring stability in a country sharply split after three years of war and over Netanyahu’s hard-right politics. Herzog holds a largely ceremonial role as head of state, but carries the decisive vote on who will have the first chance to try to be prime minister — a process that could last weeks or even months and may end in failure and new elections. After officially receiving the results, Herzog begins two days of consultations with parties, starting with the smaller ones. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot holds the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the 120-member parliament. Netanyahu’s bloc has an edge, with 53 seats as opposed to Eisenkot’s 48. Eisenkot could reach the threshold if he were to ally with parties from the Arab minority, whose seat count surged to 19 on outrage against the actions and rhetoric of Netanyahu’s government. But some in the opposition have baulked at relying on non-Jewish lawmakers’ votes. ‘Fresh thinking’ Herzog, a mild-mannered lawyer whose political career was in the defunct left-wing Labour Party but is now officially nonpartisan, has said he wants to encourage “fresh thinking” and avoid a new election. Once Herzog tasks someone, they will have 28 days to form a government, with a potential 14-day extension. If no one succeeds, Herzog will give the mandate to someone else. If that too fails, a majority of lawmakers could come together to nominate someone within 21 days — or else Israel heads to new elections. It took Netanyahu, who at the time had a better showing by Likud, 58 days to form a government after the last election in November 2022. Israel held five elections between 2019 and 2022 after repeated deadlocks. Netanyahu faces corruption charges and the risk of jail if he loses power and, with it, immunity. Yousef Jabareen, the head of the largest Arab-majority party in the next parliament, told AFP this week that the opposition needed to accept “political reality” and team up to remove Netanyahu. Netanyahu has persistently warned Jewish Israelis that the opposition will work with Arab parties, which he accuses of backing Hamas.

SSGC announces winter gas supply schedule for Sindh, Balochistan. KARACHI: The Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) on Wednesday announced the gas supply schedule for the winter season, under which three slots have been fixed for supply to domestic consumers, in line with federal government directives. An SSGC spokesperson told Dawn that the schedule covers supply to domestic consumers in Sindh and Balochistan and comes into effect immediately. Gas availability under new schedule: 6:30am-9am (Breakfast) 12pm-2:30pm (Lunch) 6pm-9pm (Dinner) The SSGC shared the schedule on its website and social media platforms, saying that it was “prioritising domestic consumers by ensuring supply during meal times”. For the past some years, SSGC’s consumers have not been getting round-the-clock gas supply. On Tuesday, a severe gas crisis gripped Karachi. The situation was further complicated by multiple contradictory gas supply schedules attributed to SSGC that began circulating on social media from Monday. However, the utility had not issued any clear and consolidated statement until late Tuesday evening, adding to the confusion.

US midterms: Democrats win US Congress in midterm rout of Trump. Democrats seized control of the US Congress on Wednesday, capturing the Senate and House of Representatives in a stunning, nationwide rejection of Donald Trump set to put the brakes on the final two years of his presidency. The Democratic landslide will give the opposition power to block legislation, launch broad investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments. The vote reflected deep anger over living costs, tariffs and Trump’s war against Iran, which has sent fuel prices soaring and compounded dissatisfaction with an already deeply unpopular president. Trump struck a conciliatory note despite his history of questioning election results, telling The New York Times : “I am absolutely willing to accept those results” and promising to “work with the Democrats”. “I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do,” the 80-year-old told Fox News, in rare praise for his political opponents. “They fought hard.” But he sought to distance himself from his own party’s poor showing, adding: “I don’t view it as a hit on me.” He acknowledged that the Iran conflict had contributed to the defeat but defended the military campaign, and he suggested the rival parties could find common ground on immigration, long one of the most divisive issues of his presidency. But minutes later on social media the 80-year-old signalled how he intends to deal with Democratic attempts to pass laws, posting a picture of a red baseball cap emblazoned: “VETO.” The Democrats’ decisive Senate breakthroughs came in Kansas and Iowa, the fifth and sixth Republican-held seats to fall in the extraordinary “blue wave” election night. In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton defeated Republican incumbent Roger Marshall, becoming the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the reliably conservative state since 1932. Iowa had not elected a Democratic senator since 2008, again illustrating the scale of party’s inroads into Republican strongholds. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton speaks following her victory in the US midterm elections at a Democratic Election Night rally, in Columbus, Ohio, US, November 3, 2026. — Reuters The upsets followed victories in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio, where voters rejected Republican candidates despite Trump’s intensive efforts to rally his supporters. Democrat James Talarico ousted a Trump-backed Senate candidate, while Gina Hinojosa unseated Republican governor Greg Abbott, ending decades of Republican control of the state’s top office. Talarico said that “we defeated Goliath” after winning a US Senate seat over Texas attorney General Ken Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump who was heavily backed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. “In this race, we went up against our own Goliaths. The richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world, and the entire Washington, DC establishment,” Talarico told a victory rally in the Texas capital, Austin. Democrats also protected key Senate seats of their own, including Jon Ossoff’s in Georgia and an open seat in New Hampshire. In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra handily defeated Donald Trump-backed Republican Steve Hilton in the race to become the governor, US networks said. Partial results showed Becerra, a career politician who served in the cabinet of former president Joe Biden, had a nearly two-to-one advantage over Hilton, with about half of the ballots counted. Becerra had run a low-key campaign in a state where Democrats heavily outnumber Republicans and where the Trump brand is almost toxic. The son of Mexican immigrants, he will be the first elected Latino governor of California, a state that would be the world’s fourth-largest economy if it were a country. “Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era,” the former US Health and Human Services secretary told his supporters at a victory party in Sacramento. “I didn’t run to make history,” he said. “I ran to make a difference for anyone and everyone who calls California home, whether you voted for me or not.” Becerra will replace term-limited Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democratic Party big-hitter who is believed to have his eyes on a tilt at the White House in 2028. California Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra speaks at an election night event on November 3, 2026 in Sacramento, California. —AFP Hilton, a British-born conservative former pundit who was once an adviser to former UK prime minister David Cameron, had always been a long shot. He conceded he had lost a difficult race. “Maybe this isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican when we see what’s going on around the country,” he said. Republicans had held a 53-47 Senate majority. The six-seat Democratic gain proved sufficient for networks to project a takeover despite some races remaining unresolved. Republican heartland Democrats also captured the House after flipping Republican-held districts in states stretching from Pennsylvania and New Jersey to Kentucky, Arizona and North Carolina. Some victories came in territory Trump had carried comfortably in 2024, despite Republican attempts to shore up House seats by redrawing electoral boundaries. One bellwether was Indiana, where Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican congresswoman Victoria Spartz in a district Trump won by 17 points. Analysts had identified an upset there as a warning of a much wider Democratic advance. Supporters react to early election results in favor of US Senator Jon Ossoff at an election night watch party hosted by the Democratic Party of Georgia after the midterms election in Atlanta, Georgia on November 3, 2026. — AFP In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history, while other Democratic gains extended to statehouses across the country. Republicans had some bright spots in Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds won the governorship, becoming the state’s first Black governor, and Ashley Moody kept a Senate seat. George Washington University professor Todd Belt called the Democratic advance “a big wipeout and a strong repudiation of Donald Trump and his policies,” citing voters’ concerns about the economy, corruption and the Iran conflict. Trump on defensive Democrats will now be able to block Trump’s legislation, investigate his administration over corruption allegations, the Iran war and immigration enforcement, and use Senate control to thwart judicial appointments and senior nominations. Robert Garcia, a Democrat expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks during a press conference with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) at the AC Hotel Washington DC Capitol Hill Navy Yard on November 03, 2026 in Washington, DC. Jeffries is also positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January, if elected by his colleagues. As speaker, Jeffries, representing a New York City congressional district, would preside over a majority that will be sworn in the first week of January, taking the reins from Republicans who controlled the House for the past four years. “Today begins the great American comeback,” Jeffries proclaimed in a victory speech late on Tuesday after media outlets projected the likelihood of Democratic majorities in the House and Senate. For many voters, the central concern was Trump’s stewardship of the economy. “Rent, groceries, utility bills, and property taxes keep climbing,” 24-year-old Los Angeles voter Taylor Cook told AFP. A rebuke to Trump, winner says “In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party. In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about three percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today , further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats. Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least nine percentage points, according to media projections. Cait Conley, Democratic candidate for the US House of Representatives in New York’s 17th Congressional District, reacts following her victory in the US midterm elections, in Pleasantville, New York, US, November 3, 2026. — Reuters Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, on Tuesday was elected governor of the state of Georgia, becoming the first Black woman elected to that office in the US, media projections showed. CNN and NBC News called the race in her favour. Bottoms defeated billionaire health care executive Rick Jackson, who ran as a Republican. Current Governor Brian Kemp is term-limited and could not run again. Midterm elections are typically viewed as a referendum on the president, and that is especially true for Trump, who dominates attention like no other politician. Trump himself told his supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and held dozens of rallies in the closing weeks. According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets, including major television networks and the Associated Press , half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed. In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president. History is against Republicans: the sitting president’s party has lost ground in Congress in all but two midterms since World War Two. Trump’s approval rating is hovering near his career lows, with voters frustrated by war on Iran , higher fuel prices and wider affordability concerns. Led by Trump, Republicans have portrayed Democratic candidates as radical, un-American and even communist, labels Democrats flatly reject. Opinion polls show voters are most concerned about affordability and disapprove of Trump’s handling of the issue.
