His tariffs on imports, many of which the courts threw out, and his decision to attack Iran in February raised prices for consumers. Trump deploys election monitors The US Justice Department said it had deployed 1,000 election monitors and observers to all 50 states in what it called the largest Election Day monitoring effort in history. Democrats criticised the plan as potential voter intimidation. In roughly two-thirds of the jurisdictions the department listed, voters supported Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump in the 2024 presidential election, a Reuters analysis found. Election officials in several states reported no issues with the monitoring effort. New Mexico’s secretary of state’s office said it had received reports of federal monitors asking “unusual questions” in one county and that the Justice Department offered assurances that the conduct would be addressed.

Schools in Sindh to remain closed on Nov 9 on account of Iqbal Day. The Sindh government announced on Wednesday that all public and private schools across the province would remain closed on Nov 9 (Monday) to mark the birth anniversary of Dr Allama Muhammad Iqbal, the national poet of Pakistan. The Sindh Information Department posted a notification by the School Education and Literacy Department on the social media platform X. “In pursuance of the decision taken in the meeting of Steering Committee on Education held on Feb 12, all public and private educational institutions under the administrative control of the School Education and Literacy Department, government of Sindh, shall remain closed on Nov 9 (Monday) on account of Allama Iqbal Day,” it said. The notification was sent to the principal secretaries of the Sindh governor and chief minister, as well as other senior officials. Born on November 9, 1877, in Sialkot, Iqbal was a distinguished poet, a scholar, a gifted philosopher and Pakistan’s ideological founder. It was at the Allahabad session of the Muslim League in 1930 that Iqbal became the first politician to articulate the two-nation theory that ultimately led to the creation of Pakistan on August 14, 1947. Iqbal Day was on the calendar of national public holidays for decades, but the interior ministry, through a circular issued on November 4, 2015, announced the cancellation of the day as an annual holiday without specifying a reason. However, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government restored the holiday in 2022.

Pakistan, UK express concern at threat posed by terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan: FO. Pakistan and the United Kingdom on Wednesday expressed concerns over the ongoing threat from terrorist groups operating in and from Afghanistan, the Foreign Office said. According to a statement by the FO, the two countries held their annual bilateral dialogue on counter-terrorism in Islamabad, in which they reviewed ongoing bilateral and multilateral counter-terrorism cooperation and reaffirmed their shared commitment to combatting terrorism in all its forms. “The two sides discussed in detail the evolving regional and global security environment and exchanged views on the threats posed by terrorist entities, including transnational terrorist networks,” it said. “Both sides expressed concerns over the continuing threat posed by terrorist groups, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), operating in and from Afghanistan,” the FO said, adding that they underscored the “urgent need for a stable, secure Afghanistan as a cornerstone for lasting peace and prosperity across the region”. The UK delegation also expressed condolences over the loss of innocent lives in terrorist attacks in Pakistan and reiterated that it stood with the country in the fight against terrorism, the statement added. Another focus of the dialogue was the exchange of best practices and the exploration of new avenues for partnership to counter new trends in terrorism, including campaigns of misinformation and disinformation, exploitation of social media platforms and emerging technologies, it said. “Both sides acknowledged Pakistan’s contributions to regional stability and security,” the FO said, adding that they agreed to strengthen institutional linkages and maintain regular engagement to advance shared counter-terrorism objectives. According to the statement, the delegations agreed to hold the next round of the dialogue in London in 2027, on mutually agreed dates. Earlier this year, the two countries agreed to enhance cooperation in counterterrorism, combating illegal migration and human smuggling, institutional collaboration and police training. Pakistan and the European Union (EU) have also agreed to strengthen cooperation at multilateral forums, including the United Nations. Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

Asif says Chaudhry Salik's remarks about corruption in Punjab 'beyond my understanding'. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Wednesday that Minister for Overseas Pakistanis Chaudhry Salik Hussain’s remarks regarding corruption in Punjab were “beyond my understanding”. During a talk show on a private television channel on Monday, the Pakistan Muslim League-Quaid (PML-Q) leader had lavished praise on former Punjab chief minister Chaudhry Pervez Elahi. However, he had also criticised the present provincial administration, headed by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, alleging that he regularly heard complaints of corruption. On Tuesday, CM Maryam had sent a Rs5 billion defamation notice to the minister, demanding that he retract his remarks. In a post on the social media platform X on Wednesday, Asif said, “Chaudhry Salik Sahib is very respected in my eyes; I respect his elders just as I respect my own. “His statement regarding corruption in Punjab is beyond my limited political understanding. Corruption is the biggest issue in our society and it is the collective responsibility of the political leadership, both at the central and provincial levels, to rid the country of this curse,” he said. He went on to say that Salik was a part of “both the federal and provincial governments and the leadership of both these governments lies with the PML-N”. “If this statement is part of some future political agenda — to target Maryam Nawaz’s government and carve out space for himself in Punjab and at the Centre to secure his political future — then it starts to make sense,” he said. He also praised Maryam’s performance, saying her work across Punjab’s cities and villages and the service standards being set by her government would pose a “very difficult challenge” for its opponents. What did Salik say? During his interview, Salik had also questioned lavish government spending , particularly the use of official aircraft , arguing that public representatives should remain mindful of the country’s economic difficulties. Officials using government aircraft, he said, should be required to demonstrate the tangible outcomes and public benefits of their trips. He further called for greater ministerial accountability, proposing that the federal as well as provincial ministers should be empowered to perform their duties, but also be held answerable for their performance. The remarks carry particular political significance given the fractured relationship between the Chaudhry family and the PTI leadership. Salik, the younger son of PML-Q president Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain, belongs to a family whose political loyalties have diverged sharply since the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in 2022 through a no-confidence vote. While Elahi and his son, former federal minister Moonis Elahi, aligned themselves with the PTI, the Shujaat family chose to stand with the Sharifs. Salik’s elder brother, Shafay Hussain, is also part of CM Maryam’s cabinet in Punjab. On Tuesday, CM Maryam said the PML-Q leader’s anger stemmed neither from corruption nor progress. She said the issue was that she had changed the deputy commissioner of Gujrat a few days earlier, whereas Salik wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed. The defamation notice — sent to Salik, ARY News host Naeem Ashraf Butt and the channel’s chairman — said the minister’s remarks were not just an expression of disagreement with policy or “ordinary political criticism”, but conveyed “serious imputations” of widespread corruption in the province. The notice called on them to retract the remarks, publish an “unconditional and unequivocal apology and clarification” and “remove or suitably correct” the portions of the interview in question. It also demanded a sum of Rs5bn in damages. Meanwhile, responding to Maryam’s remarks, Salik said he stood by his statement and had responded honestly to a question during the interview. The minister’s remarks had also drawn a sharp rebuttal from Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, who advised Salik not to “bite the hand that feeds him”. Bokhari also alleged that his displeasure stemmed from a request to appoint a deputy commissioner of his choice being turned down.

Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price. US President Donald Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot in the midterm elections and handpicked Republican candidates in some of the country’s most consequential Senate races. By Tuesday night, voters had rejected them . Trump-backed candidates in South Carolina, North Carolina and Texas all lost, while the president’s preferred pick trailed in early results in Michigan. The defeats handed Democrats control of the chamber and exposed the limits of Trump’s political power. Trump has spent more than a decade reshaping the Republican Party around his ‘Make America Great Again’ (MAGA) movement, dictating primary matchups and pushing aside conservative figures he felt were insufficiently loyal or not aligned with his vision. Trump repeatedly favoured loyalists and ideological allies over more established Republicans with stronger statewide networks and proven electoral track records, betting that his endorsement could overcome their political liabilities. Tuesday’s results revealed he was unable to persuade the broader electorate to back his choices. People react at a US midterms elections night watch party hosted by the Congressional Progressive Staff Association (CPSA) and Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America (MDC DSA), in Washington, DC, the US on November 3, 2026. — Reuters One of the most stunning repudiations came in South Carolina, which had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998 and which Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024. Trump backed Darline Graham, the sister of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham . But Democrat Annie Andrews won the seat in a stunning upset. In North Carolina, Trump endorsed former national Republican campaign official Michael Whatley, who lost in a rout to former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper. In Texas , Trump intervened in a messy Republican primary election to promote scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton over Senator John Cornyn, a Trump ally who some in the party considered a safer pick in the general election. Democrat James Talarico glided to a victory on Tuesday night, delivering Democrats a seat the party had not won since 1988. Republican senatorial candidate Ken Paxton addresses supporters after his defeat in the Texas US Senate race at The Westin Galleria Dallas in Dallas, Texas, on November 3, 2026. — AFP Former US Representative Mike Rogers , Trump’s choice in Michigan, trailed Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in an uncalled race. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate. The losses came as Trump’s popularity was lower heading into Tuesday’s vote than in the aftermath of the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol, according to Reuters/Ipsos polls. That helped fuel concerns among Republicans that the president had become a drag on the party he remade around himself. This is a “Trump Quake”, said Doug Heye, a veteran Republican strategist, pointing to voter frustration over high prices caused by tariffs and the war in Iran. “Trump spent the year telling voters what was important to him, not to them.” Trump struck a defiant tone as election returns arrived. “I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won in a landslide!” Trump wrote in a Tuesday night social media post . One White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves. A senior White House official, also speaking anonymously, told Reuters the administration had polling data as far back as six weeks ago showing Republicans would lose both the House of Representatives and Senate, and Trump embarked on a month-long nationwide campaign to try to salvage Republicans’ prospects. ‘Gave that seat away’ Some independent analysts said the Senate losses bore Trump’s fingerprints specifically. Thomas Kahn, a professor at American University, said the president’s intervention in the Texas Republican primary had cost his party a safe seat, arguing that a nomination for Senator John Cornyn “would have been a slam dunk for Republicans to win.” North Carolina, Kahn said, was another clear case. The Republican incumbent senator, Thom Tillis, said he would not seek re-election last year after a public split with Trump, who threatened to back a primary challenger against him after Tillis baulked at Medicaid cuts in the president’s tax-and-spending bill. “He essentially gave that seat away to Democrats,” Kahn said. “Roy Cooper would not have run if Thom Tillis had run for re-election.” Former North Carolina Governor Pat McCrory, a Republican, said Trump’s interventions in his party’s primaries had divided Republicans in state after state. Democrat senatorial candidate Roy Cooper and his wife Kristin Cooper celebrate victory during an election night event in Raleigh, North Carolina, the US on November 3, 2026. — AFP In South Carolina, McCrory said, the president went against two local congressmen, a fight that “really divided the party”, an example, in his telling, of a president spending his political capital against his own side. McCrory’s sharpest criticism was aimed at Trump’s connection with the voters who built his coalition. “I think President Trump’s greatest strength was that he had a common touch with the working-class people,” McCrory said. “He lost that skill. He better regain that skill for the good of the country.”

Federal cabinet ratifies defence agreement with Kuwait. The federal cabinet on Wednesday ratified the defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait, according to a handout by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). “The federal cabinet ratified a defence cooperation agreement between Pakistan and Kuwait. This agreement, which aims to foster cooperation in the defence sector between the two brotherly nations, was concluded on June 11, 2023. The Kuwaiti government had ratified the agreement on July 19,” the handout said. In 2023, Pakistan and Kuwait signed a defence pact to further strengthen defe­nce cooperation and institutional linkages between the armed forces of the two countries. The statement also said that the cabinet approved the transfer of powers delegated to the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister to the province’s governor. The Centre declared an emergency and governor’s rule in the province on Oct 11. It said the powers included “the conduct of day-to-day affairs during the period of emergency in the province, to facilitate the smooth handling of administrative matters in KP and further improve governance”. “The KP governor will submit a review report to the federal government every month regarding the exercise of all such powers,” the statement said. It stated that the federal cabinet welcomed the decision and expressed the hope that the KP Advisory Council , under the leadership of the Governor Faisal Karim Kundi, would make full efforts for the welfare and prosperity of the people of the province and for establishing peace and security. Moreover, the federal cabinet, on the recommendation of the Ministry of Finance, approved the design of new currency notes, the statement added. “The cabinet was given a detailed briefing on the new currency notes. The briefing stated that proposals were solicited from artists and designers across the country for the design of the new currency notes and a cabinet committee established by the prime minister conducted detailed consultations on it with all stakeholders,” the handout said. According to the statement, the meeting was informed that, along with enhancing security features to prevent counterfeit notes, modern materials would be used, which would also extend the lifespan of the notes. The federal cabinet also approved the introduction of a Rs10 coin in place of the Rs10 banknote, the PMO statement said. ‘Pakistan continuing efforts for peace in Middle East’ Addressing the federal cabinet during televised remarks, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif noted that global oil prices had “skyrocketed” due to the instability in the region. “Pakistan is playing its role as before in restoring peace in the region,” he said, recalling Pakistan’s recent engagements with Tehran and other regional actors in the matter, as well as engagements under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. Last month, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, accompanied by Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, visited Iran as part of Pakistan’s efforts to mediate between Washington and Tehran. In another meeting in October, held under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, CDF Munir, the Saudi defence minister, and the Turkish spymaster met top Iranian officials in Tehran. Last week, the military’s spokesman said Pakistan remained “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between the US and Iran. On Tuesday, PM Shehbaz also recalled that the government had planned to hike fuel prices by Rs15 on Friday. “Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik [..] talked to the refineries to bear the burden in their windfall profits. We will not let a common man bear this burden,” he added. Speaking about the fuel subsidy scheme, launched in September, the premier said it would run till the end of December. “Rs28 billion has been spent so far,” he said, adding that the scheme was running “successfully and transparently” and that the Intelligence Bureau (IB) continued to monitor it. On liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), the prime minister said that the “era of mafiaa” was over and it was now being arranged transparently. “Now when LPG is imported, competition will be promoted and it will be auctioned in lots. The government will take the profits and subsidise it for the common man,” he said. He also stressed that the federal government was holding meetings “day and night” to meet LPG, liquefied natural gas (LNG), petrol and gas requirements ahead of winter despite challenges arising from the closure of maritime routes. LPG supply has been disrupted in the country due to the closure of Iranian border crossings, resulting in gas cylinders being sold at twice the official rate in the open market. PM Shehbaz also said that the federal government had finalised a proposed Rs160bn package for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “Security is our number one, two and three priority in KP,” the premier remarked. He further noted that counterterrorism efforts continued in the region. With the efforts of law enforcement agencies, the new government in KP and the support of the federal government, we will crush terrorism,” he said.

'Clear message' by Americans: US politicians react to Democratic win in US midterms. In a sweeping midterm rout , Democrats won control of the US Congress, with a series of upsets delivering a major rebuke to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The victory handed Democrats both the House of Representatives and Senate, giving them power to block Trump’s agenda and investigate alleged corruption for the last two years of his presidency. Many politicians, Democrats and Republicans alike, reacted as news of America’s choice broke, with the former rejoicing countrywide. Former US president Bill Clinton said Democrats will lower costs, protect healthcare, end senseless wars, while also stopping tariffs that make life more expensive. “You deserve a government that works as hard for you as you do for your family,” Clinton posted on X. “It’s high time we put people first again!” Former US president Barack Obama said the results were a “clear message” from the Americans. “They want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” Obama said on X. “These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country,” he added. “While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future,” Obama further asserted. President Trump, meanwhile, in comments to Fox News , said, “Congratulations to the Democrats — they did a good job. They’ve been looking for this one for 11 years and they finally got it.” He added, “I don’t view it as a hit on me.” US Senator Bernie Sanders called the news “great” on X. “At a time of massive income and wealth inequality, we must do more. We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” he wrote. Former US vice president Kamala Harris reacted to the news with a video of herself saying, “Hallelujah!” Democratic Representative Robert Garcia, now expected to lead the powerful House Oversight Committee, in a post on X warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries declared Trump’s MAGA movement “on the run from sea to shining sea”. Jeffries could become the first Black speaker of the House when the new Congress convenes in January. Former secretary of transportation Pete Buttigieg, in the wake of a number of Republican strongholds flipping blue, said, “Tonight proves it: there is no such thing as a permanently red seat.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, in a post on X, vowed: “As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democratic Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done.” He expressed gratitude that Trump was still in the White House, hoping that the Republicans will “work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism. We cannot let their fringe positions become the mainstream”. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis pointed out that it was “unlikely” Republicans would recapture Congress in 2028, looking at the Senate map and given the “massive” margin in the House. “Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032,” he added. CNN cited DeSantis as saying that Republicans underemphasised the impact of high gas prices due to the Iran war, although he did not name Trump specifically. “Listen, we’ve just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of the Iran conflict […] If you can’t admit that to voters, then you’re gaslighting them,” DeSantis said on Stephen A. Smith’s podcast “Straight Shooter” on Monday, according to CNN . Former US Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene, reacting to the development, said it was a “total referendum” for Trump, accusing the US president of “covering up the Epstein files, protecting rapists and paedophiles” and starting the US-Iran war. She said Trump “killed a school full of kids, put his rich elite donors before the struggling Americans who put him in office, made life unaffordable with his tariffs, and caused gas and diesel prices to skyrocket while he played the market and sold crypto.” “And Republicans stood behind him silently clapping like trained baby seals,” she said. “And tonight they sent him a clear message,” she added, warning that Republicans “need to learn the lesson and drastically change course”. “And I’m not sure if they’re capable of that.”

Iran supreme leader says those expecting US policy shift 'seriously mistaken'. Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said on Wednesday that anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, hours after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website. Democrats seized control of the US Congress in Tuesday’s midterms, reflecting anger over living costs , tariffs and the US war against Iran , which has sent fuel prices soaring . Khamenei’s remarks come with diplomatic efforts underway to avert renewed fighting in the war, which broke out on February 28 . US and Israeli leaders have in recent days threatened to resume attacks against Iran. “Should such aggressions be repeated, the war’s scope will become much wider,” said Khamenei, who has yet to appear in public since he took power in March. Earlier, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said Americans had voted against war. “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he posted on X. “If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Ghalibaf said. Iran’s judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei also hailed the election results, saying Trump had been “defeated both militarily and politically”. “We will certainly inflict further defeats on him,” he added.

'We did it!': Democrat El-Sayed hails US Senate win, becomes first Muslim elected to upper chamber of Congress. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s US Senate race over former Republican lawmaker Mike Rogers, US networks said early on Wednesday, making him the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress. “Michigan, we did it!” El-Sayed said in a speech attended by hundreds of supporters who screamed and hugged each other at his election headquarters in Detroit. “I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.” El-Sayed won despite a last-minute curve ball in his campaign when congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to El-Sayed, came out in support of Rogers at the 11th hour. The Michigan medical administrator rallied voters on leftist campaign promises, including universal health care, to win a key US Senate seat for Democrats, taking over from the retiring Gary Peters. El-Sayed held a nearly six-point lead on Rogers when networks called the race. Party-goer entrepreneur Trunetta Roach, 75, who attended El-Sayed’s victory party in downtown Detroit wearing US flag-design diamante high-heels, said: “We are sick and tired of being sick and tired. And I’m so proud of all the work. It was boots on the ground. We were always out, but we were never outworked.” “I’m feeling elated. The kids are all right. I was concerned about them. They didn’t seem very engaged, but I was wrong. They showed up.” ‘Swear me in’ Republicans ran a scorched-earth campaign to paint Democrats as communists and branded El-Sayed a terrorist who would endanger Americans. But the straight-talking 42-year-old El-Sayed pledged to help cash-strapped voters navigate America’s fractured, for-profit health care system. “You deserve to be able to see a doctor without getting a huge bill,” he told Michiganders on the eve of the vote, vowing to upend America’s divisive multi-billion-dollar for-profit medical system. During the race, El-Sayed drew huge campaign crowds across the state, even in deeply conservative Republican areas. El-Sayed also vowed to get “money out of politics” and address the harsh economic woes that have voters yearning for a political newcomer to shake up the status quo. The victory made El-Sayed the first Democratic doctor in the Senate since 1969. “Everybody in politics is so trash. So to see ethical Muslims be at the forefront representing us and showing everybody what we’re actually about … it means everything,” said micro-influencer Maryam Bozai, 28. At the victory party, crowds gathered around TVs tuned to left-leaning cable news channel MS NOW , cheering jubilantly each time the Democrat’s trademark blue flashed on screen to announce another race won by the party. “Tsunami! Tsunami!” chanted Ondine Fortune, 64, a Democratic Party media planner. El-Sayed supporters rubbed shoulders with left-leaning influencers and union activists, a group that lent El-Sayed their formidable campaign infrastructure to reach Michigan’s large organised labour community. Eboni Taylor, a vice-president at Higher Heights which promotes Black women seeking office, said El-Sayed had “gone places where I just would not expect to see him.” “What’s most remarkable is that he’s showing up in places that are not the usual prescription for the Democratic Party. He’s going wherever the people want him to be,” Taylor said between social media livestreams and celebratory dancing. El-Sayed faced Islamophobic attacks and mockery for his Arabic name from US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. But El-Sayed may yet have the last laugh. Addressing the vice president, El-Sayed said in his victory speech, “you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January”. Dr Arif Alvi congratulates El-Sayed Pakistan’s former president Dr Arif Alvi congratulated El-Sayed on his victory in a post on X and said it “resonates far beyond one election”. “It is a reminder that democracy matters: that the people’s mandate is sacred, that every vote counts, and that the will of the people cannot be wished away, manipulated or denied with guns,” he said, wishing El-Sayed success in his role. Alvi added that “being Muslim should never make anyone a target of hatred, prejudice or intimidation. No one should have to face the vile excesses of Islamophobia.” He noted that the “people’s voice will prevail”, expressing his hope that the lesson would reach beyond US shores.

38 detained in Karachi as police baton-charge protesters headed towards CM House. KARACHI: Thirty-eight people were detained on Wednesday as police used tear gas and baton-charged protesting teachers headed towards Chief Minister House from Karachi Press Club (KPC). Hundreds of teachers had gathered outside the press club on the call of the All Sindh Primary Teachers Association. They were headed towards CM House to present their demands that pertained to the service structure and called for delegating powers for transfers and postings to district officers. The protesters chanted slogans and attempted to move towards the CM House. However, when they arrived near Fawara Chowk, police baton-charged them and used tear gas shells to push them back toward the press club. Adjoining roads near the KPC were closed to traffic, according to a traffic police spokesperson. South Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Syed Asad Raza told Dawn that a teachers’ organisation had announced a protest at the KPC, with a march planned toward the CM House. He said prior to the protest, the administration made concerted efforts to resolve the matter through negotiations and engaged officials from the education department to facilitate meaningful dialogue. The official said the protest leadership was categorically told that entry into the Red Zone — a term used to denote the area surrounding Governor House and Chief Minister House — would not be permitted. Nevertheless, the administration was directed to exhaust all available resources and make every effort to ensure a peaceful resolution through dialogue, he said. Raza alleged that around 3:15pm, the protesters turned “violent, abandoned the course of negotiations and forcibly started advancing towards the CM House.” He claimed that the protesting teachers “breached police barricades and resorted to pelting police personnel with stones, causing injuries to one official.” “Upon reaching and crossing Kabir Masjid on Governor House Road, the situation escalated, compelling police to resort to shelling to disperse the violent mob and restore order,” said the South police chief. He said during the operation, 38 protesters, including the president of the All Sindh Primary Teachers Association, Ghulam Rasool Mahar, and the general secretary, Aijaz Ali Chandio, were taken into custody. Raza insisted that police took drastic action as the teachers tried to enter the Red Zone. Meanwhile, Rafiq Nizamani, the vice president of the teachers’ association, told Dawn that in 2021, the Sindh government had chalked out an “education policy” under which it was decided that teachers would not be promoted and they would remain in the same pay scale. He said they launched a protest against this “arbitrary” decision as others were being promoted, but not them. He said that at the time, the government had assured them that their demands would be addressed, but this did not happen. He said apart from the service structure, their other demands pertained to delegating the powers of posting primary teachers to district government officials. He said that they wanted recruitment and the transfer/posting of teachers to be delegated to district officials. According to Nizamani, as the protesters moved from KPC towards CM House, police resorted to tear gas and a baton charge. He claimed that two teachers were also injured. Nizamani said that they had decided to set up a protest camp outside the KPC for the fulfilment of their demands. He admitted that the education officials had approached them for talks, but said they considered it “delaying tactics” in view of their past unfulfilled promises and decided to hold a protest march.

ECP objects to retired SC judge's remarks about 2023 ruling on polls in Punjab and KP, reserved seats case. The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Wednesday objected to remarks made by former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, Mansoor Ali Shah, regarding polls in KP and Punjab and the reserved seats case pertaining to the PTI. Shah made the remarks at an event organised by the US-based Community Alliance for Peace and Justice on October 29, where he was asked about his dissenting opinion in the 2023 SC ruling on provincial elections in Punjab and KP and whether it was a “turning point” and the beginning of a “division” within the SC. In its 3-2 verdict, the SC, after taking a suo motu notice, directed that elections should be held within 90 days in both provinces. Two judges, including Shah, had dissented from the ruling, saying that the suo motu proceedings initiated by then-chief justice of Pakistan Umar Ata Bandial, were “wholly unjustified”, besides being initiated with “undue haste”. In their detailed reasoning , they explained that the SC by a majority of 4-3 and not 3-2 had dismissed the suo motu hearing on polls delay in Punjab and KP and therefore the same should be considered as the “Order of the Court”. It had resulted in a controversy, with the government igniting a raging debate claiming that the ruling was a 4-3 majority decision in its favour and not a 3-2 verdict against. In response to the question, Shah said that this was the time when the ex-chief justice was “forming like-minded benches”. He said that at the time, two SC judges — Justice Yahya Afridi and Justice Athar Minallah — had dismissed suo motu proceedings and petitions in the case. He said that it was “decided that the high court would decide the case” and the appeal would “naturally come to the SC”. He alleged that the whole judgement was centred around the concept of a “one-man show”. Shah also defended the 2024 verdict in the reserved seats case , wherein PTI was declared eligible for seats reserved for women and minorities, in a setback to the ruling coalition. “We said that the PTI was a political party and it was wrong to deprive [them of their symbol] … and illegal,” he said, recalling that this was a decision “that nobody liked”. In a statement on Wednesday, the ECP referred to the remarks made by Shah, saying that they ignored “basic constitutional and legal facts related to the election matters and judicial decisions”. “It is highly inappropriate to present the judicial record for specific purposes through selective quotations, incomplete perspectives and one-sided interpretations,” the statement said. The electoral watchdog said that Shah had claimed that the SC’s majority decision about the elections in 2023 was a 4-3 verdict and that the suo motu notice and relevant petitions were dismissed. The ECP also stated that according to Shah’s claims, the election ruling was a “minority decision” and the commission could not have held polls. Regarding the PTI case, it said that Shah had declared the order for withdrawal of the party’s electoral symbol during the 2024 elections as “illegal”. The commission said that the election symbol was subject to transparent intra-party elections as per Sections 208 and 209 of the Election Act 2017. It added that “till date, PTI has not been able to fulfil the requirement”. The ECP said PTI was supposed to hold intra-party elections by June 30, 2021, and the commission had given the party three chances; however, the party failed to hold intra-party elections. As a result, the commission said that the party’s election symbol was withdrawn, which, the ECP added, was also upheld by the SC in 2025, along with rejecting review petitions filed by the PTI. The ECP further stated that PTI held intra-party elections after five years and its proceedings remained pending before the commission as the “PTI itself has taken a stay order from a high court”. It further stated that as per the commission’s records, the PTI was still enlisted as a political party. The ECP added that only political parties which contested the elections had a right to the reserved seats. “These political parties are required to submit a preferred list of candidates before the elections, while PTI has not submitted any preferred list,” it stated. It further stated that it was mandatory for a political party to win at least one seat and that independent members were not entitled to reserved seats and therefore, the ECP gave the seats to the eligible parties. It said that if the PTI was entitled to the reserved seats, then “Articles 51 and 106 of the Constitution and Section 104 of the Elections Act 2917 become ineffective”. The ECP said that it was “unfortunate” that a retired judge was taking a position against the Constitution and the law. In November 2025, Shah had resigned as an SC judge alongside Minallah, hours after the 27th Constitutional Amendment — which made significant changes to the country’s judicial system and established the Federal Constitutional Court — was signed into law by President Asif Ali Zardari. “By fracturing the unity of the nation’s apex court, it has crippled judicial independence and integrity, pushing the country back by decades,” he wrote in the letter sent to the president. “Staying on would not only amount to silent acquiescence in a constitutional wrong, but would also mean continuing to sit in a court whose constitutional voice has been muted,” he said.

Govt says Islamabad's One Constitution Avenue to be turned into a five-star hotel. The federal government on Wednesday said that a joint investigation team had revealed that Islamabad’s One Constitution Avenue was built on “irregularities and rigging” and announced that the residential building will soon be turned into a five-star hotel. The building, a skyscraper in the federal capital that houses residential apartments, had its lease cancelled by the Capital Development Authority (CDA) due to the company behind the project defaulting on payments. The decision was upheld by the Islamabad High Court (IHC) in April. The building was initially supposed to be a five-star hotel project; however, instead of functioning as a five-star hotel, it was converted into residential apartments and commercial areas. The IHC’s order led to the mass evictions of residents in May, following which Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif formed a joint investigation team (JIT) to probe the matter. Addressing a press conference on Wednesday alongside Information Minister Attaullah Tarar and State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the JIT presented its report to the federal cabinet today, noting that the project was fraudulent. He said that the report had input from the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), the Federal Investigation Agency, the Federal Board of Revenue, the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan, the Intelligence Bureau and Inter-Services Intelligence. “They carefully assessed this project and presented the report, and it was approved,” Iqbal said. “The JIT has clearly identified that the project was created based on irregularity and rigging and that the bidding process was manipulated.” Iqbal added that, according to the report, rules were ignored to provide benefits and the company which was given the lease had no rightful claim. “In this whole matter, the CDA was found complicit, and similarly, the conditions of the bank guarantee were removed to provide benefits to the developers,” he stated. “The work which was carried out was conducted in a very suspicious manner and the apartments were sold illegally.” He noted that the project was initially approved as a five-star hotel two decades ago, but later it was turned into apartments. “The JIT has identified Abdul Hafeez Sheikh, who has been called the mastermind and was found to be in connivance with CDA officials,” the planning minister added. “CDA officers such as Kamran Lashari, who was chairman at the time, Dr Faisal Awan, Azhar Ali Chaudhry, Brigadier (retired) Nasrullah and Marhoom Rai Nawaz Kharal were found to be colluding in fraud,” he said. Iqbal said that as a result of the scheme, the national exchequer suffered losses, while the aforementioned people “gained financially and defrauded the Pakistani people of their invested capital”. “The JIT recommended that Sheikh and his company be blacklisted from future public projects and that proceedings be launched against him,” the minister added. It was further recommended that the project be reviewed and work undertaken to achieve its original purpose as a hotel. Additionally, the report recommended that the project be started anew and auctioned in a transparent manner, he said. “Security clearance and clearance from other institutions should also be sought so that future projects have a steady framework to prevent this type of fraud from happening again,” Iqbal said, adding that fire safety and other protocols must also be ensured. He added that according to the JIT, the project should be renamed, as the name ‘One Constitution Avenue’ was the same address as the finance ministry. “They used this address for marketing purposes only,” the minister asserted. “There will be action taken against those found involved in fraud. The government has a responsibility to protect those who were robbed or swindled.” Iqbal said it was decided that those defrauded would receive compensation, their principal investments would be refunded and payments would be adjusted against their Kibor interest “so they do not suffer losses”. “It was also recommended that the CDA and its ordinance be overhauled and that an independent master plan commission be formed to shut the door on such fraud in the future,” he announced. Iqbal added that all of the records must be digitised and officers should be rotated between the state planning, enforcement and building control departments every two years. “People have held offices for 20 years and opened offices of fraud. With this constant rotation, it will close the door on these corrupt projects,” he explained. “In the same way, pre-audit auctions and contracts from third parties will be consulted, and in light of this JIT report, NAB has been ordered to take action against anyone involved in this project, and those who facilitated it,” Iqbal said. Meanwhile, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also addressed a press conference on Wednesday and said that the government had now regained possession of the skyscraper, vowing to turn the building into a five-star hotel within months. “In official documents, we always had possession of this building, and after the cabinet’s approval, it is now legally in our possession,” Naqvi maintained. He regretted that the government’s decision to regain control of the building earlier this year had been portrayed as a “crime”, decrying how Islamabad’s land had been infringed upon. “We will try our best to convert this building into a five-star hotel in months,” the interior minister announced, reaffirming that this had been the project’s primary objective. “There is a severe shortage of hotels in Islamabad. We will soon try to make an agreement with a large chain of hotels and convert this building into a five-star hotel,” he stated. He commended the CDA chairman and legal team for pursuing this case; however, Naqvi also reproached the CDA for being at fault. “NAB will tell who is responsible,” he said. “As per JIT recommendations, we will try to make rightful payments to the occupants,” Naqvi said. “This is binding for us after the report.” The interior minister said he was grateful to PM Shehbaz, recalling that the prime minister had assured him that the right decision would be taken. Naqvi further said that a residents’ committee, which was overseeing the building’s affairs, had been abolished. “A CDA member will look after the building’s matters from now on,” he said, reiterating that the hotel would be operational soon and be a “gift to the people of Islamabad”.

Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them. Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”. The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down. But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last. The full article can be read on the Time website. The Central African Republic (CAR) is grappling with the effects of Sudan’s conflict. Instability in north-eastern CAR is strengthening local rebel groups, some of which are taking advantage of the war economy to rebuild their capabilities. Bangui’s partnership with Abu Dhabi exposes CAR to retaliation from the Sudanese army. Together, these developments could jeopardise the country’s security gains. What should be done? CAR should work with its partners to provide better security in the north east, while keeping aid levels constant. The UN should maintain its peacekeeping mission. Executive Summary The Central African Republic (CAR) is dealing with dangerous spillover from the civil war ravaging neighbouring Sudan. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudanese army’s main opponent in that conflict, have nearly free rein in the north-eastern border prefecture of Vakaga, where they are endangering the population. The hostilities in Sudan have also revived a war economy that a number of CAR rebel groups are exploiting to rebuild capabilities that had eroded in the last five years under pressure from government forces. Meanwhile, CAR’s growing ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the RSF’s main outside patron, are testing Bangui’s relations with the Sudanese army and exposing the country to blowback. To prevent instability in the north east from undoing progress in protecting the public, Bangui and its partners should mount a more robust security response and maintain humanitarian aid levels. UN peacekeepers should keep patrolling the area. Finally, CAR should request that the UAE desist from supplying the paramilitaries via its territory while keeping channels of dialogue open with the RSF to reduce violence. The conflict in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023, has forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to flee the country. More than 43,000 people – Sudanese refugees and CAR returnees – have sought safety in CAR. Most of the new arrivals have settled in Vakaga prefecture, which abuts Sudan and Chad. Birao, the regional capital, has seen its population double in three years. The sudden influx has severely strained the capacity of Vakaga, a remote region that is among the poorest in the country, to accommodate newcomers, while making access to water and food increasingly difficult. The closure of many international NGO offices in the area since 2025, following cuts in U.S. aid, along with budget restrictions affecting UN agencies, has further weakened the humanitarian response. Accessible by vehicle only via dirt tracks during the dry season, since the 2000s Vakaga has been a haven for several CAR armed groups, which accuse the central government of neglecting the region. These insurgents later joined the Séléka rebel coalition, which seized power in 2013 and plunged the country into civil war. The 2019 peace deal between Bangui and fourteen armed groups, followed by government offensives from 2021 onward, weakened rebels across the country. Vakaga nevertheless remains home to armed movements that either rejected the peace agreement or emerged after it was signed. Chronically under-funded, the national army lacks the capacity to exert effective control of the region, despite support from its partners, notably MINUSCA, the UN peacekeeping mission in CAR, and Russian mercenaries from the Wagner Group. Taking advantage of the porous border and the weakness of state forces, fighters affiliated with the RSF – which has a stronghold in South Darfur, adjacent to Vakaga – have been crossing regularly into north-eastern CAR since 2023. Over the same period, security in Vakaga has deteriorated sharply, a development that observers on the ground attribute largely to the RSF combatants. Heavily armed and poorly disciplined, these fighters engage in criminal activity, including robbery and kidnapping. They have also taken up occupations such as livestock herding and artisanal gold mining, competing with locals and increasingly settling disputes through violence. In response, Bangui has reinforced its garrison in the area, but it has been unable to stem the RSF’s movement across the border. The Sudanese conflict is ... creating new opportunities for CAR armed groups active in the north east. The Sudanese conflict is also creating new opportunities for CAR armed groups active in the north east. Drawing on their cross-border networks, these groups have hired out their fighters to both warring sides in Sudan, acquired weapons and forged new alliances. This war economy has allowed them to recoup some of the financial and material resources they lost over the past five years, jeopardising CAR’s security gains. A rebel attack on the border town of Am-Dafock on 30 June, which left 30 people dead, underscored the growing threat. Backed by well-equipped Sudanese fighters, the assailants managed to push back government and UN forces and occupy the town for several days before withdrawing. Finally, the war in Sudan has strained CAR’s relations with the Sudanese army. Informal cooperation between Bangui and the RSF aimed at containing violence along the border has caused friction between CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, who heads the Sudanese army. Meanwhile, CAR has forged closer ties with the RSF’s main external ally, the UAE. The wealthy Gulf state has shown growing economic interest in CAR since 2023, particularly in the gold and energy sectors. This partnership puts Bangui in a delicate position. The UAE has reached agreements with other neighbours of Sudan, notably Chad, to channel weapons to the RSF through their national territory, though Abu Dhabi denies the existence of such supply networks. According to several sources, a small number of Emirati arms shipments destined for the RSF have passed through CAR, including via Vakaga. Attracted by Emirati funding but wary of reprisals from the Sudanese army, Bangui is trying to strike a balance. There is still time to prevent violence from escalating in Vakaga. With support from partners such as the European Union and UN agencies, the CAR authorities should continue to provide humanitarian assistance, despite limited resources, and launch long-term projects to better connect the north east to the rest of the country. Bangui should also strengthen its security partnerships in the area, notably by reviving cooperation with Chad, another neighbour affected by the war in Sudan. Despite severe budget pressures, MINUSCA should retain a robust presence in the area, even if that means redeploying troops from regions facing fewer security threats. UN member states should also avoid prematurely downsizing the mission when they renew its mandate in November. Finally, CAR should ask the UAE to stop using its territory as a supply corridor while creating conditions for peaceful coexistence with the paramilitaries to reduce violence. To preserve its fragile stability, CAR should reaffirm its neutrality in the Sudanese conflict. Introduction La guerre civile qui sévit au Soudan depuis avril 2023 a plongé le pays dans la pire crise humanitaire au monde. 1 Voir briefing Afrique de Crisis Group N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 avril 2026 ; et Alan Boswell, « As the Horn of Africa Nears Boiling Point, Time for Urgent Diplomacy », commentaire de Crisis Group, 17 juillet 2026. Le conflit oppose deux branches de l’appareil militaire : l’armée soudanaise, dirigée par le général Abdel Fattah al-Bourhane, et les Forces de soutien rapide (FSR), un groupe paramilitaire mené par Mohammed Hamdan Daglo, dit « Hemetti ». Chaque camp contrôle désormais une partie du pays, faisant craindre une partition durable du territoire ; en 2025, ils ont chacun nommé un gouvernement revendiquant sa souveraineté sur l’ensemble du Soudan. 2 L’armée soudanaise contrôle la capitale Khartoum et l’est du pays, tandis que les FSR ont consolidé leur emprise sur le Darfour, une vaste région de l’ouest du Soudan, qui borde la Libye, le Tchad, la RCA et le Soudan du Sud. La guerre a contraint jusqu’à quatre millions de Soudanais à fuir le pays, déplacé au moins trois fois plus de personnes à l’intérieur de ses frontières et soumis plusieurs régions à des épisodes prolongés de faim ou de famine. L’ONU estime que 33,7 millions de Soudanais ont un besoin urgent d’aide humanitaire. 3 Briefing de Crisis Group, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , op. cit. « Nos actions humanitaires au Soudan », Unicef, consulté en juin 2026. Les effets du conflit se sont rapidement fait sentir au-delà des frontières du Soudan, le Tchad étant sans doute le pays voisin le plus touché. 4 Charles Bouëssel, « Sudan’s War Risks Fracturing Eastern Chad », vidéo de Crisis Group, 23 juillet 2026. L’afflux de plus d’un million de réfugiés soudanais et de rapatriés tchadiens dans l’est du Tchad a détérioré les conditions de vie dans les provinces de l’Ennedi Est, du Wadi Fira, du Ouaddaï et du Sila, déjà confrontées à une forte pauvreté, ainsi qu’à des difficultés d’accès à l’eau et aux terres. 5 Briefing Afrique de Crisis Group N°202, Tchad : limiter l’impact de la guerre au Soudan dans le Ouaddaï , 14 novembre 2024 ; et commentaire de Crisis Group, « Préserver la stabilité du Tchad face au conflit soudanais », 1er septembre 2025. Ces derniers mois, les accrochages entre l’armée tchadienne et des miliciens des FSR, les frappes de drones et les tensions intercommunautaires se sont multipliés le long de la frontière entre les deux pays. 6 Enrica Picco, « L’est du Tchad happé par la guerre au Soudan », Analyst’s Notebook de Crisis Group, 19 mai 2026. En parallèle, les Emirats arabes unis (EAU), principal parrain des FSR, utilisent le Tchad comme base logistique pour livrer des armes aux paramilitaires soudanais. Cet appui – que les EAU et le Tchad ont toujours démenti malgré un vaste faisceau de preuves émanant de rapports onusiens, d’enquêtes journalistiques et de témoignages de diplomates – a provoqué l’ire de l’armée soudanaise, qui a menacé N’Djamena de représailles. 7 Voir « Boeings identified in Reuters report carried weapons for Sudanese paramilitary », Reuters, 28 juin 2026 ; « Sudan’s civil war fueled by secret arms shipment from UAE and Iran », The Washington Post , 15 octobre 2024 ; « Talking peace in Sudan, the U.A.E secretly fuel s the fight », The New York Times , 29 septembre 2023 ; « Secretary of state Marco Rubio before the house foreign affair s committee on the FY27 departmen t of state budget request », ambassade des Etats-Unis au Soudan du Sud, 4 juin 2026 ; et « Leaked UN experts report raises fresh concerns over UAE’s role in Sudan war », The Guardian , 14 avril 2025 ; « The UAE in Africa: Power, influence and conflict », Bloomberg, 25 juillet 2025. Les hostilités au Soudan ont également des répercussions sur un autre de ses voisins : la République centrafricaine (RCA). Frontalière du Darfour, la préfecture de la Vakaga (nord-est), l’une des plus défavorisées du pays, accueille aujourd’hui plusieurs dizaines de milliers de personnes – réfugiés soudanais et rapatriés centrafricains – ayant fui les violences soudanaises. 8 « The Central African Republic’s response to the Sudan crisis », Sudan Regional Crisis – Development Action Platform, consulté en mai 2026. « Situation du Soudan, République Centrafricaine », HCR, décembre 2025. Cet afflux de population, couplé aux ruptures d’approvisionnement en biens de première nécessité depuis le Soudan (aussi liées au conflit), complique l’accès à l’eau, à la terre et à la nourriture. 9 Entretiens de Crisis Group, responsables humanitaires, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Il a en outre provoqué une inflation des prix des marchandises et des loyers, accentuant l’insécurité alimentaire. 10 Entretiens de Crisis Group, habitants, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Le climat sécuritaire s’est aussi dégradé : la région subit des incursions fréquentes de combattants soudanais, pour la plupart affiliés aux FSR. 11 Entretiens de Crisis Group, responsables humanitaires et sécuritaires, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Ces derniers se livrent à des actes de criminalité armée et investissent certains secteurs de l’économie locale, tandis que les rebelles centrafricains actifs dans la zone ont su tirer parti de l’essor d’une économie de guerre pour s’enrichir. 12 Ibid. Ces évolutions pourraient fragiliser les progrès sécuritaires des dernières années en RCA. 13 Charles Bouëssel, « Centrafrique : après les élections, consolider les gains sécuritaires », commentaire de Crisis Group, 27 janvier 2026. La guerre au Soudan a en effet éclaté alors que le pays commençait à se relever d’une longue crise, déclenchée en 2013 lorsqu’une coalition rebelle à majorité musulmane, la Séléka, a renversé le président François Bozizé. Après plusieurs années de guerre civile, l’accord politique pour la paix et la réconciliation, conclu en 2019 à Khartoum entre l’Etat centrafricain et quatorze groupes armés, a permis la reddition de la plupart des insurgés. 14 Rapport Afrique de Crisis Group N°277, Dernier accord de paix en RCA : les conditions du succès , 18 juin 2019. Depuis, l’armée nationale, ses alliés russes et rwandais et la Mission multidimensionnelle intégrée des Nations unies pour la stabilisation de la RCA (Minusca) ont repris le contrôle des principales villes du pays et sécurisé Bangui, la capitale. 15 Pauline Bax, « Russia’s Influence in the Central African Republic » , commentaire de Crisis Group, 3 décembre 2021 ; Bouëssel, « Centrafrique : après les élections, consolider les gains sécuritaires », op. cit. Les opérations militaires ont contraint les groupes rebelles à se replier vers des espaces périphériques de plus en plus réduits, asphyxiant leurs réseaux de financement minier et routier et affaiblissant leurs capacités opérationnelles. Malgré des fragilités persistantes, le déroulement relativement paisible des élections générales de décembre 2025 a témoigné de ces avancées. 16 Le 28 décembre 2025, la RCA a organisé simultanément des élections présidentielle, législatives, régionales et municipales, qui se sont déroulées dans un calme relatif sur l’essentiel du territoire. En dépit d’inquiétudes quant à l’intégrité du scrutin, la contestation des résultats par l’opposition n’a pas débouché sur une crise politique majeure. Le 5 janvier, l’Autorité nationale des élections a proclamé la réélection du président Faustin-Archange Touadéra dès le premier tour. Bouëssel, « Centrafrique : après les élections, consolider les gains sécuritaires », op. cit. Ce rapport analyse les conséquences humanitaires et sécuritaires de la guerre au Soudan sur le nord-est de la RCA et l’influence des partenariats géopolitiques de Bangui dans la gestion de ces défis. Il repose sur une cinquantaine d’entretiens avec des responsables de l’Etat aux niveaux national et régional, des représentants de groupes armés centrafricains et des FSR, des sources sécuritaires locales, des chefs religieux et communautaires du nord-est du pays, des responsables humanitaires et administratifs, et des opérateurs économiques. Menées en 2026, ces entrevues ont eu lieu à Bangui, dans les villes de Birao et d’Am-Dafock (Vakaga), ainsi que par téléphone. Crisis Group a pu échanger avec quelques femmes et a pris en compte leur point de vue dans ses recherches. Le faible nombre d’entretiens avec des femmes reflète les structures de pouvoir inégalitaires en RCA. Enfin, le rapport s’appuie sur les précédentes publications de Crisis Group et sur celles d’organismes humanitaires et de recherche. Un groupe de déserteurs armés des Forces de soutien rapide (FSR) arrive à bord de véhicules dans l’ouest d’Omdurman, où ils seraient venus se rendre à l’armée soudanaise, le 19 août 2026. L’impact de la guerre au Soudan sur la Vakaga Eloignée de Bangui et du pouvoir central, la préfecture de la Vakaga, frontalière du Soudan, a longtemps servi de base arrière à de nombreux groupes armés. Depuis l’accord de paix de 2019, les forces de défense et de sécurité de la RCA ont toutefois repris pied dans la zone, repoussant les rebelles aux confins de la région. Mais les hostilités au Soudan, qui ont éclaté en avril 2023, ont mis un coup d’arrêt à cette dynamique. Le conflit a favorisé les déplacements de combattants soudanais dans la Vakaga, en particulier des FSR, entrainant une hausse de la criminalité armée. Il a aussi permis aux groupes armés locaux de reconstituer une partie de leurs forces grâce au trafic d’armes et de mercenaires. En juin, le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a alerté sur ces risques, se disant « profondément préoccupé par les répercussions de la guerre au Soudan », qui font peser « une grave menace sur les civils et la stabilité dans le nord-est » de la RCA. 17 « Rapport du Secrétaire général sur la République centrafricaine », UNSC S/2026/494, 15 juin 2026. A. La Vakaga, une région fragile sous l’emprise de groupes armés La Vakaga est une région périphérique de la RCA qui borde le Tchad, le Soudan et le Soudan du Sud. La préfecture souffre de malnutrition chronique et fait partie des plus défavorisées du pays, le deuxième plus pauvre d’Afrique avec un PIB par habitant de 492 euros par an. 18 « Central African Republic: IPC food security snapshot, September 2022-August 2023 », Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), 11 novembre 2022. « PIB par habitant - Africa », Banque mondiale, consulté en septembre 2026. La Vakaga est dotée d’un climat aride à semi-aride soudano-sahélien, marqué par une saison sèche de sept à huit mois. 19 « Troisième communication nationale de la République centrafricaine, sous la convention cadre des Nations unies sur les changements climatiques », ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement durable de la RCA, 2022. Les principales activités économiques incluent l’agriculture, l’élevage (avec des éleveurs transhumants qui sillonnent la zone pendant la saison sèche), l’exploitation minière et le commerce. 20 Ibid. La région dispose d’un potentiel aurifère largement sous-exploité mais qui fait l’objet d’un intérêt croissant de la part d’opérateurs miniers centrafricains et étrangers – y compris soudanais, tchadiens, russes et émiratis – autour de Birao, chef-lieu de la préfecture, et le long de la frontière soudanaise (sur l’axe reliant les localités d’Am-Dafock et de Tiringoulou). Depuis l’indépendance de la RCA en août 1960, les autorités centrales ont peu investi dans le développement de la Vakaga. La région a longtemps manqué de préfets, de douaniers, de gendarmes, de juges, de médecins et même d’enseignants. 21 « Centrafrique : Birao, capitale à la dérive du Nord "abandonné" », AFP, 27 décembre 2017. L’accès à l’eau et à l’électricité y demeure également très limité. 22 Si la situation s’est légèrement améliorée à partir de 2019, avec le retour de militaires à Birao après dix ans d’absence et la mise en place d’un embryon d’administration, les populations s’estiment encore abandonnées par l’Etat. Entretiens de Crisis Group, habitants de la Vakaga, avril 2026. La préfecture souffre en outre d’un profond enclavement : seules des pistes en terre permettent d’y accéder, et uniquement pendant la saison sèche. 23 Entretiens de Crisis Group, usagers de la route et habitants, Birao, avril 2026. Rejoindre Birao depuis Bangui, située à plus de 1 000 kilomètres, prend entre deux et quatre jours en véhicule, seuls les 180 premiers kilomètres étant goudronnés. 24 Ibid. En mars, Bangui a signé un préaccord avec une société privée pour la construction d’une autoroute reliant la ville de Sibut (chef-lieu de la préfecture de la Kémo) à Am-Dafock, mais le financement n’est pas encore bouclé. « Un mémorandum signé pour le financement de l’autoroute Sibut-Am-Dafock », Oubangui Médias , 6 mars 2026. Le peu d’attention accordé à la Vakaga s’explique en partie par les différences ethniques et religieuses qui la distinguent du reste du pays. 25 Entretiens de Crisis Group, responsables de partis politiques et analystes politiques, Bangui, avril 2026. Pour des questions logistiques et financières, les populations du nord-est préfèrent en outre s’approvisionner en produits de première nécessité et en carburant via la ville soudanaise de Nyala – la capitale de l’Etat du Darfour méridional, située à environ 300 kilomètres de Birao – ou via le Tchad, plutôt que par Bangui. En mars 2023, par exemple, des combattants du PRNC ont pris en otage une vingtaine de soldats centrafricains. Depuis 2022, deux groupes rebelles tchadiens ont aussi ouvert des avant-postes dans la Vakaga : le Rassemblement populaire pour la justice et l’égalité au Tchad (RPJET) et une faction dissidente de l’Union des forces républicaines (UFR). 35 Le RPJET est un groupe rebelle tchadien apparu au début des années 2020 et principalement implanté dans le sud de la Libye. De taille modeste, il s’oppose au régime du président Mahamat Déby, mais n’a jamais mené d’offensive majeure contre N’Djamena. En RCA, il ne compterait qu’une centaine d’hommes issus des communautés du nord du Tchad, arrivés en 2023 et positionnés dans des grottes autour de Hadjar Fatna (Vakaga). L’UFR, fondée en 2009 par Timan Erdimi, a longtemps constitué l’une des principales rébellions tchadiennes. Si le groupe a signé l’accord de Doha en 2022 et si son chef est rentré au Tchad pour participer à la transition, sa composante militaire n’a pas été intégralement désarmée. L’UFR conserve une existence politico-militaire, mais son activité armée est aujourd’hui réduite. C’est le cas du Mouvement démocratique pour le rassemblement du peuple centrafricain (MDRPC), dirigé par Arda Hakouma, un ancien cadre du FPRC. Créé en 2023 dans le Bamingui-Bangoran, il a depuis relocalisé une partie de ses forces dans la Vakaga voisine. 37 « Naissance d’un nouveau groupe politico-militaire, le MDRPC du général Arda Hakouma », Corbeau News, 16 février 2023. Parmi les autres groupes ponctuellement présents dans le nord-est figurent l’Unité pour la paix en Centrafrique (UPC), dirigée par le chef rebelle peul Ali Darassa et opérant dans le centre et le sud-est, ainsi que le Mouvement patriotique pour la Centrafrique (MPC) de Mahamat al-Khatim, implanté dans le nord et le nord-est. Ces deux groupes, eux aussi issus de l’ex-Séléka, ont réintégré l’accord de paix en 2025 grâce à une médiation de N’Djamena. 38 Après avoir un temps repris les armes, trois des groupes les plus puissants de la RCA – l’UPC, Retour, réclamation et réhabilitation (3R) et le MPC – ont réintégré l’accord en 2025 à la suite de négociations menées sous l’égide du Tchad. Voir « Le Président de la commission salue la signature de l’accord de paix du 19 avril en République centrafricaine et la dissolution des groupes armés UPC et 3R », Union africaine, 18 juillet 2025 ; et « Le gouvernement centrafricain et le MPC signent un nouvel accord à Ndjamena », Radio Ndeke Luka, 20 novembre 2025. Certains de leurs généraux refusent cependant de déposer les armes, estimant que l’accord ne leur est pas favorable. Ils se déplacent parfois dans la Vakaga, où ils entretiennent des liens commerciaux ou militaires avec les rebelles locaux. Nourredine Adam, chef du FPRC, l’un des principaux groupes armés centrafricains, pose à Birao, dans le nord de la République centrafricaine, le 20 décembre 2017. ALEXIS HUGUET / AFP B. L’emprise croissante des FSR dans le nord-est de la RCA Avant la guerre au Soudan, des éléments armés soudanais, parfois affiliés à l’armée soudanaise ou aux FSR, circulaient déjà dans le nord-est de la RCA, profitant de la porosité de la frontière et de la faible présence des forces de sécurité centrafricaines. 39 « Coup d’Etat au Soudan : l’armée reprend le contrôle et réprime les protestations dans le sang », Le Monde , 26 octobre 2021. Des milliers de combattants soudanais du Darfour avaient rejoint les rangs de la Séléka et des centaines sont restés dans les groupes issus de son éclatement, par solidarité communautaire ou en quête d’enrichissement. 40 Certains sont restés plusieurs années en RCA. C’est le cas du général Wadal Ounda, qui a combattu avec l’UPC avant de retourner au Darfour méridional, sa région d’origine, et de rejoindre les FSR. Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, représentants de groupes armés, avril 2026. Des officiers des FSR et de l’armée soudanaise participaient aussi à des trafics d’armes avec des groupes armés comme le FPRC. 41 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Enfin, d’autres membres des FSR y voyageaient régulièrement pour des raisons familiales : le général Abdallah Djazouli, commandant des FSR au Darfour méridional, est ainsi marié à l’une des filles du sultan de Birao, l’une des principales autorités coutumières de la région, et se rend souvent dans cette ville. 42 Nourredine Adam, le chef du FPRC, est marié à une autre fille du sultan de Birao, illustrant l’interconnexion de tous ces acteurs armés. Entretiens de Crisis Group, habitants d’Am-Dafock, représentants de groupes armés actifs dans la zone et sources sécuritaires, Vakaga, avril 2026. Différents partenariats établis avec Bangui ont contribué à normaliser, aux yeux des FSR, la possibilité de circuler en armes en RCA. En 2019, les autorités centrafricaines et leurs alliés russes ont fait venir dans le nord-est du pays un groupe de miliciens arabes du Darfour – les Janjawid, d’où sont issus les FSR – dirigés par le commandant Ali Kushayb ; ces derniers ont appuyé les forces gouvernementales dans une offensive lancée la même année contre le FPRC. 43 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, juin et juillet 2019. Fin 2022, les FSR ont également conclu avec l’exécutif centrafricain un accord (non public) les autorisant à pénétrer en RCA. Cet arrangement visait à sécuriser la frontière et à y empêcher la circulation des groupes armés centrafricains, en contrepartie de l’exploitation d’une mine d’or près de la ville de Gordil (Vakaga). 44 La mine reste aujourd’hui occupée par des proches des FSR. Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. « Rapport final du Groupe d’experts sur la République centrafricaine reconduit dans son mandat par la résolution 2648 (2022) du Conseil de sécurité », UNSC S/2023/360, 18 mai 2023. Destiné à pallier la très faible présence des forces étatiques dans la zone et leur manque de moyens logistiques, l’accord n’a toutefois pas survécu au conflit soudanais. Depuis le début des combats au Soudan, la Vakaga a connu une forte dégradation sécuritaire. En 2022, la région enregistrait une dizaine d’incidents violents par mois, impliquant des groupes armés, les forces armées nationales et leurs alliés russes, ou des criminels. A partir d’avril 2023, les violences se sont multipliées, avec un pic de 60 incidents par mois en décembre de la même année ainsi qu’au mois de janvier suivant. Les années 2024 et 2025 ont connu un niveau de violence supérieur à celui d’avant-guerre, bien qu’inférieur à celui observé fin 2023. Le nombre de ces incidents est reparti à la hausse en 2026, avec environ 40 cas mensuels répertoriés entre février et juillet. 45 Entretien de Crisis Group, source confidentielle, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. La Vakaga connait une forte dégradation sécuritaire depuis le début de la guerre au Soudan, en avril 2023. Le nombre d'incidents violents a bondi de 162 pour cent entre 2022 et 2023 et se maintient depuis à un niveau élevé. Décompte de crisis group basé sur des sources sécuritaires / CRISIS GROUP La hausse de l’insécurité dans la Vakaga s’explique d’abord par l’afflux d’hommes armés venus du Soudan, dont beaucoup sont affiliés aux FSR. Ces trois dernières années, les paramilitaires ont consolidé leur emprise sur le Darfour : ils y ont établi un embryon d’administration civile et mis en place, en 2025, un gouvernement parallèle, basé à Nyala. 46 « Soudan : un gouvernement parallèle nommé, l’éclatement du pays se poursuit, la crise humanitaire aussi », L’Humanité , 29 juillet 2025. « Sudan war takes turn as paramilitary force captures Darfur, threatening to split the country », Associated Press, 29 octobre 2025. Les FSR disposent aussi d’une base dans la partie soudanaise d’Am-Dafock, une localité située à cheval sur la frontière. Certains d’entre eux en profitent pour circuler en RCA. Plus de la moitié des incidents recensés dans la Vakaga depuis avril 2023 relèvent de la criminalité armée et impliquent souvent des miliciens soudanais proches des FSR. 47 Entretiens téléphoniques de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, août 2026. Ces attaques se concentrent surtout le long des axes routiers et près de la frontière. 48 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Les autorités, les ONG et les habitants s’accordent à dire que ces violences ne s’inscrivent pas dans un projet politique, mais résultent du nombre accru de combattants indisciplinés dans la zone. 49 Entretiens de Crisis Group, autorités, habitants et sources sécuritaires, Vakaga, avril 2026. Certains membres des FSR viennent aussi régler des différends avec des habitants ou des réfugiés. 50 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, responsables humanitaires et habitants, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Ces derniers sont particulièrement exposés à ces violences, comme l’explique un responsable sécuritaire : « Les FSR considèrent parfois les réfugiés des communautés arabes comme des lâches qui ne contribuent pas à l’effort de guerre avec eux. Ils ont forcé certains d’entre eux à rejoindre leurs rangs en les menaçant physiquement ». 51 Entretien téléphonique de Crisis Group, source sécuritaire à Birao, juin 2026. Les paramilitaires soudanais franchissent aussi la frontière pour traquer certains de leurs hommes ayant déserté et fui en RCA avec leur équipement militaire. 52 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources confidentielles, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Ils mènent enfin des représailles contre les habitants qu’ils soupçonnent de signaler leur présence aux autorités centrafricaines. 53 Entretiens de Crisis Group, habitants, Birao et Am-Dafock, avril 2026. Les activités économiques développées en RCA par des individus associés aux FSR sont aussi sources de tensions, notamment dans les secteurs de l’élevage transhumant et de l’exploitation minière. En cas de dispute avec des agriculteurs, les éleveurs proches des FSR ont tendance à recourir à la violence ou à solliciter l’appui des paramilitaires, contribuant à la multiplication des conflits agropastoraux dans la Vakaga. 54 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, responsables de la Minusca, chefs communautaires, opérateurs économiques et habitants, Vakaga et Ouaka, avril 2026 ; et par téléphone, avril 2026. L’exploitation aurifère supervisée ou financée par des Soudanais affiliés aux FSR a également pris de l’ampleur. 55 Ibid. Depuis le début de la guerre, le site de Mandjan, situé à 20 kilomètres de Gordil et exploité par des hommes d’affaires soudanais liés aux paramilitaires, a connu plus d’une trentaine d’incidents, dont des braquages, parfois suivis de représailles. 56 Entretiens de Crisis Group, sources sécuritaires, Vakaga, avril 2026. L’implication de membres des FSR solidement armés dans ce secteur favorise le règlement des litiges par la violence. L’insécurité générale perturbe la vie quotidienne et les activités économiques dans la région. En 2024 et 2025, la circulation sur l’axe Am-Dafock-Birao a souvent été interrompue en raison des violences, tandis que de nombreux agriculteurs n’osent plus se rendre dans leurs champs par crainte d’attaques. 57 Entretiens de Crisis Group, habitants et usagers de la route, nord-est de la RCA, avril 2026. Les femmes sont exposées aux violences sexuelles, notamment lorsqu’elles s’éloignent des centres urbains pour aller chercher de l’eau ou effectuer des travaux agricoles. 58 Les FSR ont fréquemment recours à la violence sexuelle, notamment au Darfour. « Soudan. Homicides délibérés et violences sexuelles commis par les FAR à El Fasher : nouveaux témoignages de victimes », Amnesty International, 25 novembre 2025.
