On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/30/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 30 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 30 October 2026 ISRAEL Israelis went to the polls Tuesday for elections in which the majority voted against the incumbent coalition but without producing a clear path to a new government. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has the largest number of parliamentary seats, at 53, but it is eight short of the 61 needed to govern by itself. Retired general Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc finished second with 48 seats. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the biggest story is the huge turnout among Israel’s Palestinian Arab citizens, whose parties reached a record nineteen seats in total. The election is over, but the fight for power has just begun. Netanyahu, who will remain caretaker premier for the time being, could seek to form a coalition with elements of Eisenkot’s camp. Or Eisenkot, though he repeatedly pledged not to do so during the campaign, could cobble together a government with one of the Arab lists. A third scenario – neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot forms a large enough coalition, meaning another round of balloting in a few months’ time – may be the most probable. In the meantime, the prime minister has accused Palestinian Arab voters of “stealing the election”, in an effort to undermine the results and stoke anti-Arab prejudice in the Eisenkot bloc’s ranks. SOMALIA The UN is closing its political mission in Somalia, as per a Somali government request made two years ago. For more than three decades, a series of UN missions have used their good offices to help repair relations among various political groups amid persistent civil strife. Mogadishu asked this last one to wind down its work as a sign of the country’s progress toward stability. Despite Somalia’s advancements, the UN is leaving at a delicate time, says Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood. Somalia is in the throes of another political crisis over the timing and format of elections. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud called for a dialogue with opposition factions on these matters in mid-November, but it will take place without UN behind-the-scenes support to help broker compromise. Discord among politicians in Mogadishu, along with dissension between the federal and several regional governments, is a major reason why the authorities struggle to wear down the Al-Shabaab insurgency that holds swathes of the country’s south. VENEZUELA Opposition politician María Corina Machado made a dramatic return to Venezuela Sunday after ten months abroad. The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize winner got a warm reception as she travelled to Caracas, with tens of thousands cheering as her motorcade passed by. Machado intends to mobilise her supporters to demand an election to replace Delcy Rodríguez, who has been heading an interim government since January, when the U.S. grabbed former President Nicolás Maduro. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says many Venezuelans, whose living conditions continue to deteriorate, would like to see a vote soon. But Machado’s comeback poses a challenge to the slow-paced transition being conducted under U.S. tutelage, especially to the negotiations between the government and an opposition sector led by Dinorah Figuera. Her strategy could even provoke a backlash from those in the interim government – the old guard of Maduro’s chavista movement – who view staying in power as an existential issue. 23 October 2026 CUBA The UN General Assembly will vote next week on its annual resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba, in place for more than six decades. Last year’s resolution passed 165-7. Washington is seeking to reduce the resolution’s backing as the Trump administration pursues a broader economic pressure campaign on the island (including restrictions on oil shipments and new secondary sanctions). U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents, who argued that supporting the resolution excuses the Cuban government’s human rights abuses while obscuring its role in the country’s economic crisis. Cuban diplomats denounced the panel as an attempt to deflect attention from the embargo’s effects. Crisis Group expert Michael Bustamante says the confrontation illustrates the unfortunate either-or terms in which the debate is often framed. Decrying the humanitarian consequences of U.S. measures need not mean absolving the Cuban government of responsibility for its economic policy failures or its suppression of dissent. STRAIT OF HORMUZ October has already seen Iran hit more ships in or around the Strait of Hormuz than any previous month of the war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February. Tehran’s escalation comes after the volume of crude oil moving through the strait reached pre-war levels, largely through a scheme by which a few risk-tolerant tankers are assuming the danger of hauling barrels through the waterway before transferring their cargo to more risk-averse vessels outside it. Crisis Group expert Chris Newton says the question now is whether Iran can make these “shuttle runs” too costly. If it cannot, it will lose leverage in any negotiations with the U.S. and Gulf Arab countries that may transpire. But if it can, its attacks could prompt retaliatory U.S. strikes. U.S. - UKRAINE Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Tuesday that U.S. intelligence sharing, crucial for advance warning of incoming Russian ballistic missiles, had been restored. At the same time, there were conflicting reports on a slowdown in Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite system, which it depends on for battlefield communications and defensive drones. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the “throttling” of Starlink, which is run by billionaire Elon Musk's company SpaceX, was a technical error that “no one ordered”. The incident nonetheless fuelled speculation that the Trump administration is scaling back intelligence and technological support for Ukraine to strong-arm Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow ahead of the 3 November U.S. midterm elections. Wednesday’s meeting between Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Witkoff called Putin a “humanitarian”, has done the same. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says Zelenskyy’s resistance to U.S. pressure has boosted his approval ratings at home. Polls show that a majority of Ukrainians oppose ceding territory in return for a peace settlement. 16 October 2026 IRAN Iranian attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in October to date, with more than two dozen vessels struck since the month began. Meanwhile, Washington is maintaining its blockade of Iranian ports while backing oil shipments along the Omani coast, where smaller tankers transfer cargo to larger vessels outside the strait. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick in Iranian strikes is an effort to counter a rebound in oil flows that showed Tehran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz was weakening. Iran wants Washington to accept its proposed terms for a ceasefire that reopens the waterway in exchange for sanctions relief and an end to the U.S. blockade. But a diplomatic breakthrough appears less likely than the two sides setting off another escalatory spiral. SUDAN The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a UN-backed hunger monitor, warned Monday of growing famine risks in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan regions, driven by conflict, displacement and inadequate aid funding, and compounded by an El Niño-induced drought. This news comes as Sudan’s army reports advances against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in parts of North Kordofan and West Darfur. Meanwhile, the RSF continues to mount attacks in Blue Nile and to target El Obeid in North Kordofan with drones. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says the army’s gains could make it more confident of victory, while continued RSF offensives suggest that this group, too, sees opportunities for battlefield gains. The continued fighting is likely to further complicate diplomatic efforts to end the war and ease Sudan’s humanitarian crisis. UKRAINE This past Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, saying each had agreed to halt attacks on the other’s energy infrastructure, following a deal he made to buy Russian diesel and ease related U.S. sanctions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he learned of the ceasefire through social media, adding that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian refineries. Ukrainian forces also reported restrictions on Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service, which they depend on for communications and drone operations. Washington says it continues to share intelligence with Ukraine. Zelenskyy this week announced the resumption of refinery attacks as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued unabated. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says any disruption to intelligence or communications would compound Ukraine’s difficulties in protecting its cities and power grid as winter approaches, leaving civilians more vulnerable to prolonged heating and electricity outages. 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Diplomats need to press Israel to release its chokehold on Gaza and push for continued progress on the truce’s terms. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. But these events are bound to increase tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which are already high following clashes between Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces last October, and to further chill relations between Islamabad and New Delhi. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. The standoff began last week, when Ecuador announced a 30 per cent tariff on Colombian imports, blaming Bogotá for insufficient action to stop drug trafficking along the shared border. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Iran is unlikely to meet the White House's sweeping demands, which encompass nuclear, missile and regional concessions, raising the likelihood of confrontation at a time when the Islamic Republic already faces increasing diplomatic isolation, mounting economic problems and outrage at its brutal crackdown on dissent. SOUTH SUDAN The South Sudanese army announced Sunday it is launching a major offensive to recapture territory in Jonglei state that has been seized by opposition forces and allied militias since hostilities intensified in December. The UN warned this week that mass troop mobilisation and inflammatory rhetoric from senior commanders have significantly heightened the risk of violence against civilians. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the escalation signals a clear slide toward full-scale war. The rapidly expanding conflict threatens to draw in neighbouring states, including Uganda, and to deepen South Sudan’s dangerous entanglement in the war in Sudan. 23 January 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO M23 rebels withdrew from Uvira, near the Burundian border, over last weekend, ending a tense month in which they controlled the South Kivu town. They had promised to pull out, likely due to U.S. pressure following a December summit in Washington between their main outside backer, the Rwandan president, and his Congolese counterpart. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating. Another M23-aligned armed group, the Twiraneho, is involved in fighting around Uvira, also pointing to a pattern of inter-communal violence. GUATEMALA President Bernardo Arévalo declared a 30-day state of emergency Monday after inmates had taken more than 45 guards hostage at three prisons two days earlier. After the authorities regained control of one of the facilities, gang members outside jail killed ten policemen in retaliation. The state of emergency limits citizens' rights and gives state forces special powers such as making arrests without cause. It echoes the iron-fist approaches to public safety pursued by leaders in El Salvador and Ecuador. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Arévalo, who won the 2024 election touting a progressive reform agenda but has since lost popularity, listened to demands from Guatemalans for a decisive response to an uptick in violent crime. If the measure delivers immediate results, it could help the president’s political standing. UGANDA Tensions simmered this week after the 15 January elections, which saw President Yoweri Museveni win another term with 71.65 per cent of the vote. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. He remains in hiding after dodging a police raid – staged for reasons that remain unclear – on his residence. The president's powerful son, army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said on social media Tuesday Kyagulanyi would be treated as an "outlaw/rebel" if he did not surrender within 48 hours. (He later deleted this and other inflammatory posts.) Meanwhile, authorities charged more than 100 NUP members with involvement in election day violence. An internet blackout has made details of the incidents difficult to verify. The official death toll is twelve, but both Kyagulanyi and Muhoozi have cited higher figures. The government says ten died when its forces were attacked at an opposition legislator's home, a version of events sharply contested by others who were present. Crisis Group expert Meron Elias says the opacity of events, along with Muhoozi’s threats, will likely keep the political temperature high following the polarising vote. 16 January 2026 CUBA The bodies of 32 Cuban soldiers killed during the 3 January U.S. raid in Venezuela arrived in Havana Thursday. Cuba is facing considerable uncertainty after U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday urged its government to “make a deal” or face the consequences, vowing that the U.S. would cut the Venezuelan oil supply to the island nation, which is heavily dependent on these deliveries for its energy needs. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says Washington appears to be calculating that a deepening economic crisis in Cuba will mobilise the masses to bring about the regime’s collapse. The Cuban regime retains a strong military and solid ties to Russia and China, however, and previously has not hesitated to crush dissent. GREENLAND Several European NATO members have deployed troops to Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, to beef up infrastructure and carry out joint military exercises after U.S. President Donald Trump repeatedly stated that the U.S. intends to acquire the island, by force if necessary. Wednesday’s meeting among the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in Washington failed to resolve “fundamental disagreement” on Greenland’s future, according to the Danish foreign minister. With Europe already buffeted by Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, says Crisis Group expert Olga Oliker, this crisis will have dire implications for the future of NATO and European security writ large if the U.S. does not back down. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. Since the last Kurdish fighters left the city Sunday, fighting shifted eastward, raising the risk of sustained confrontation. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The U.S., which supports both sides, has kept a ceiling on escalation thus far and should use its leverage to bring the parties back to the negotiating table. 9 January 2026 CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC Provisional results show that President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has secured a third term after general elections on 28 December. Two challengers – Anicet-Georges Dologuélé and Henri-Marie Dondra – have called for annulling the vote, alleging fraud, while the main opposition coalition boycotted the ballot, citing an uneven playing field. The disputed poll coincided with renewed violence in the south east. Fighters linked to the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) – a Zandé self-defence militia – disrupted voting in Bambouti. Clashes then spread, including AAKG attacks on government forces around Zémio in early January. The AAKG was initially aligned with Bangui but later broke with the government after its rapprochement with a Fulani-led armed group that the militia accuses of encroaching on Zandé land. Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji says the AAKG may be digging in to battle the state. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country. Iran and the U.S. publicly exchanged threats while privately trading proposals to end the war. Troops from Eritrea briefly crossed the border to support their faltering Tigrayan allies, accelerating the downward spiral in bilateral relations. Former President Joseph Kabila in DR Congo launched a new political-military coalition incorporating the Rwanda-backed M23 rebellion and its political wing, further undermining prospects for progress in the fragile peace process between the group and Kinshasa. Russia expanded its bombing campaign against Ukraine , killing scores of civilians in round-the-clock attacks, while Kyiv’s relations with Washington deteriorated amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow and reported disruptions of U.S. intelligence and technological support to Ukraine. Government and allied forces in Mali recaptured the separatist bastion of Kidal following the withdrawal of the Azawad Liberation Front, marking a significant symbolic victory in their struggle to reassert territorial control. Sri Lanka: Organized Crime Bill Violates Rights Standards. Click to expand Image A police anti-riot unit in Colombo, Sri Lanka, January 30, 2024. © 2024 Thilina Kaluthotage/NurPhoto via AP Photo (New York) – The Sri Lankan government’s Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, submitted to parliament on October 20, 2026, risks enabling arbitrary detention, torture, and other rights violations, Human Rights Watch said today. The proposed law, alongside the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill submitted on October 6, reproduces abusive provisions in existing counterterrorism laws that would allow continuing abuses that the government had pledged to end. President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s National People’s Power alliance pledged in its 2024 election manifesto to abolish all “oppressive” laws and ensure “civil rights of people in all parts of the country.” In particular, the Dissanayake government—like its predecessors—pledged to repeal the notorious Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). Both bills presented in October replicate some of the worst aspects of the PTA, shifting abusive provisions to create parallel legal structures outside existing criminal law and without basic safeguards. “Sri Lanka’s organized crime bill would enable prolonged detention without adequate judicial oversight or evidence of criminal conduct, and could encourage torture by allowing convictions based on confessions obtained by the police,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “If this law is adopted in its current form, it risks unleashing serious rights violations just as previous similarly draconian legislation has done.” The purported objectives of the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill are to combat organized crime and support international law enforcement cooperation. It is presented as giving effect to the 2003 United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime, yet fails to adhere to international standards of precision and legal certainty and removes basic due process safeguards provided in ordinary Sri Lankan criminal law, enabling the authorities to use arbitrary powers in a wide range of ill-defined circumstances. The bill defines “serious crime” as any offense punishable with at least four years in prison and lists a large number of offenses that fall under other laws, placing a wide variety of alleged criminal activity within its extraordinary authority. It defines an “organised criminal group” as three or more people acting in concert with the aim of committing one or more serious crimes to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit. Courts may consider whether a person is a member of an organized criminal group based on factors including physical or virtual meetings with known members; their style of dress, hand signs, language or tattoos; association with known members of the group; and habitually visiting premises known to be used by the group. Such provisions risk criminalizing association rather than conduct, allowing the authorities to detain a person without any evidence of criminal activity. The bill would allow the secretary to the Ministry of Public Security to issue a detention order for two months at a time, for up to a year, without giving the magistrate discretion to set the detention order aside. Bail may be granted only by the High Court, with suspects accused of a serious crime only released on bail in exceptional circumstances. In the past, the PTA incentivized torture by allowing convictions based on confessions obtained by the police. Recent reform attempts including the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill required instead for confessions to be made to a magistrate. Nevertheless, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill reproduces the abusive practice of making confessions to the police admissible in court, incentivizing coercion, ill-treatment, and torture. The bill provides police with broad surveillance authority, including to intercept and record communications, carry out forensic extraction of data from electronic devices, and access data from telecommunications companies and online services, through court orders. The police could, even without a court order, obtain any telecommunication, satellite, or digital service provider information relating to the identity of the owner or subscriber, calls, and the tower location, of any device, sweeping powers to expose personal communications and information and infringe rights, including of privacy and assembly. Sri Lankan law enforcement and security agencies have a long record of misusing surveillance to target human rights defenders and the families of victims of rights violations. The organized crime bill also contains sections that could curtail freedom of expression by making it an offense to publish the name or anything that could identify a victim of crime. Further restrictions are placed on media reporting of court proceedings without court permission. The bill also gives the police broad powers, on “reasonable suspicion” of a serious crime, to stop and search individuals and vehicles, or make arrests and seize relevant items. They could enter and search premises without a warrant. Taken together, the additional police powers with little or no judicial oversight are wide open to abuse, Human Rights Watch said. Sri Lanka’s experience with the PTA demonstrates the potential for serious rights violations under the Organised Crimes Bill. Repealing the PTA would fulfill a key commitment that Sri Lanka made to the European Union, in exchange for tariff-free access to the EU market under its Generalised Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) program. However, the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill preserves the terrorism act’s abusive features, further weakening Sri Lanka’s compliance with its GSP+ human rights commitments. The government did not appear to conduct consultations while drafting the bill. The government should withdraw the bill, undertake a genuine, open, and inclusive consultation, ensure legislation with robust safeguards to prevent arbitrary detention, torture, and ill treatment, and ensure judicial oversight and due process, in compliance with the government’s international legal obligations. “Every government has a duty to combat organized crime but needs to do so in compliance with international human rights standards,” Pearson said. “The European Union should make it clear that this bill would not meet Sri Lanka’s obligations under the GSP+ trade program.”

US: New Hurdles to Having Votes Counted. Click to expand Image US election workers open and inspect mail-in ballot envelopes during processing inside the Maricopa County Tabulation and Election Center (MCTEC) on Election Day, November 5, 2024, in Phoenix, Arizona. © 2024 Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images (Washington, DC) – US states’ use of a tool to verify citizenship that is marred by inaccurate and incomplete data is creating new hurdles for the right to vote with the midterm elections only days away, Human Rights Watch said today. The Supreme Court ruled in late September 2026 that states could use the tool, Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE), to screen lists of registered voters for citizenship status, at least for the time being. “The use of the SAVE tool is causing new hurdles for some voters,” said Katherine La Puente, US democracy researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Sending vaguely worded letters as early voting began or offering federal-only ballots to some registered voters risks a discriminatory impact on people’s right to vote.” The Trump administration expanded use of the problematic SAVE online system, which previously had been used only for public benefits and was not designed for verifying voter eligibility, in 2025 to now use it for these purposes. Some states have adopted their use of SAVE to verify voter eligibility, and the recent Supreme Court ruling has allowed its use for individualized inquiries. Federal law does not require proof of citizenship when registering to vote, but states have passed these laws requiring proof for state and local races, resulting in bifurcated voter systems. In Utah, thousands of voters flagged by the SAVE database were sent notification letters over the summer, and in October over 4,000 who didn’t respond were mailed ballots with only federal races. In South Dakota, nearly 6,000 voters have been categorized as federal-only voters as well as 47,000 in Arizona. In Utah and Arizona, they can provide proof of citizenship and vote in person on Election Day but can’t vote by mail, a method relied on by most voters. In North Carolina, vaguely worded letters sent to 1,400 registered voters flagged through SAVE asking for proof of citizenship may deter people from going to the polls. Earlier in 2026, Utah audited its voter rolls, finding that it could not verify the citizenship status of over 5,000 registered voters. It sent them letters indicating that they needed to provide documentary proof of citizenship. Many were older voters who did not need documentation when they registered to vote. Fewer than 2,000 have responded. The others will receive ballots only for federal offices. In South Dakota, new state laws requiring documentary proof of citizenship and residential addresses quadrupled the voters in the “federal-only” category because they did not submit proof of citizenship or list a mail forwarding service or P.O. Box as their address when they registered. County clerks sent notification letters to these voters that misstated the reasons for their change in status. After advocates filed a federal lawsuit against the state, officials issued corrected notices in September. South Dakota’s online Voter Information Portal does not tell voters if they are registered as federal-only and changes were only allowed until the state’s October 19 registration deadline. The North Carolina State Board of Elections sent letters to nearly 1,400 registered voters flagged through SAVE just two days before early voting began on October 15. The board of elections has since confirmed that all citizens are still entitled to vote even as it resolves these queries, and voting rights groups are emphasizing that all those flagged should still be able to vote. But people who got the letters may think they cannot vote or may run into issues at the polls. In July, with less than a month to the August primary, the director of Alaska’s Division of Elections admitted in a legislative hearing that her office had mailed letters to more than 3,000 voters asking to confirm their citizenship and marked them inactive. Though hundreds have had their registration restored, others will only be able to vote with a questioned ballot, which is only counted once the voter’s eligibility is verified. Earlier in 2026, a new law took effect in Ohio that requires the Office of the Secretary of State to review its voter registration database at least monthly and direct elections officials to promptly cancel a flagged person’s registration. Citizen groups have raised concerns that this could lead to mistaken removals close to elections, with 75 people removed in September and 90 in October. In Arizona, the Maricopa County recorder flagged 207 voters identified through SAVE as “not eligible” to vote, which means the voters would stay on the rolls, but would not receive mail-in ballots and would need to use a provisional ballot. Of an initial investigation of 60 of these voters, the Maricopa County attorney determined at least 52 were citizens. But the county did not restore some people’s eligibility until the state attorney general filed suit and a resolution was negotiated. Arizona has required proof of citizenship to register to vote in state and local elections since 2004. Clean Elections Arizona estimates that 47,000 voters are now in this federal-only category. Naturalized citizens, people who automatically became citizens during childhood when their parents naturalized, US citizens born abroad, and those without easy access to documentation are particularly at risk as a result of these moves. Often, individuals who secured their citizenship through a parent’s naturalization or at birth abroad may not have access to the original documents confirming their status, which they obtained as children. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which the United States has ratified, requires governments to ensure the right to vote without unreasonable restrictions or discrimination. The International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination requires the United States to eliminate racial discrimination and to guarantee the right to vote “without distinction as to race, colour, or national or ethnic origin.” In its concluding observations for its review of the United States in 2022, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination expressed concern about practices that “constrain the exercise of the right to vote with a disproportionate impact on people of African descent, indigenous peoples, persons of Hispanic/Latino origin and other ethnic minorities,” and said that the United States should “facilitate access to voting and eliminate unreasonable restrictions to the exercise of the right to vote.” A survey by the Brennan Center found that more than 9 percent of those polled did not have proof of citizenship readily available, which would mean 21.3 million people nationally if the results are accurate. A study by the Center for American Progress found that fewer than half of US citizens held a valid US passport in 2024. Communities of color, immigrants, low-income, and older people are less likely to have identity documents such as passports or birth certificates. There is no evidence of widespread, unlawful voting by noncitizens in US elections, and such claims have been disproven in other states like Nevada and Missouri. Nationwide, CBS News reported, 156 people had been charged with offenses related to voter fraud since January 2025, out of approximately 227 million registered voters. Other statements and actions made by the Trump administration leading up to the elections could deter people from voting. In several states, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents have questioned people in their homes about their immigration status and voting history, though a judge recently restricted these operations in nine states. Neither President Donald Trump nor the heads of the DHS and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been willing to rule out the possibility that federal agents, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, may be at polling places. “Election officials should take steps to eliminate hurdles to vote and ensure that voters feel confident to go to the polls,” La Puente said.

Activist in DR Congo Faces Military Trial. More than three months have passed since plainclothes security officers arrested pro-democracy activist Clovis Kakule Mutsuva on July 18 in North Kivu province in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Mutsuva, 32, is awaiting trial before a military court on several charges. Click to expand Image Clovis Kakule Mutsuva. © Private The Allied Democratic Forces, a Ugandan-origin armed group active in eastern Congo, has been carrying out deadly attacks in the North Kivu city of Beni, near the Ugandan border. Mutsuva and other activists used videos and public speeches to call for a city-wide shutdown of public activities. The shutdown, which was peaceful according to Beni’s mayor, occurred on May 14.Nonetheless, two months later Mutsuva was arrested and charged with incitement to disobey the law, criticizing public authority, organizing unauthorized demonstrations, insulting the army, spreading false rumors, and spreading false information on social media. The prosecution has accused Mutsuva of calling on demonstrators to “set fire” to the streets at night in protest of insecurity and to demand that the government protect civilians. Mutsuva has been outspoken about martial law orders issued under the region’s “state of siege” in North Kivu and Ituri provinces since 2021. The state of siege is an exceptional regime introduced by President Félix Tshisekedi to address insecurity and armed group violence in eastern Congo. It grants expanded powers to military authorities and restricts certain fundamental freedoms including by allowing military courts to try civilians. The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights has emphasized that military courts should not have jurisdiction over civilians under any circumstances. Mutsuva has been in pretrial detention for more than three months, despite serious concerns about his deteriorating health. He was hospitalized on August 11 for nearly two months before being sent back to Kangbayi Central Prison in Beni on October 7. Mutsava’s lawyer said that the Higher Military Prosecutor's Office of North Kivu has rejected requests for his provisional release. Human Rights Watch has repeatedly called on Congolese authorities to try civilians in civilian courts, including in provinces where martial law is in place. Mutsuva’s case should be transferred to a local court, and he should be released on bail pending trial so he can have access to appropriate health care.

UN Finds Age-Based Persecution of Palestinian Children. Click to expand Image Children on their way to school in the West Bank, September 16, 2026. © 2026 John Wessels/AFP via Getty Images A UN Commission of Inquiry concluded on October 14 that Israeli authorities have committed the crime against humanity of persecution against Palestinian children. Their findings recognize an important dimension that has not been given enough attention: children in the West Bank have been deliberately targeted—not just because of their nationality, race or ethnicity but also due to their age—in attacks causing serious bodily and mental harm. After making the same determination about Gaza in June, the commission expanded its finding to the West Bank, explaining: “the harm inflicted on children is not incidental or collateral to the broader violence affecting civilian population, but forms part of a pattern of intentional violence.” Age-based persecution is not limited to Gaza or the West Bank. Last November, judges at the International Criminal Court confirmed 39 charges, albeit in absentia, against Joseph Kony, leader of the Lord’s Resistance Army, for crimes in northern Uganda including persecution on age grounds. None of these findings required new laws. Currently, the International Law Commission’s agreed upon definition of persecution includes the catch-all “other grounds that are universally recognized as impermissible under international law.” Age is one such characteristic that someone could be persecuted for, as is disability. But investigators and prosecutors work best from lists in front of them. That’s why, when creating a new treaty to codify crimes against humanity, countries should explicitly list “age” as a ground for persecution. This would make children, older people and other groups targeted for their age more visible as subjects of persecution and make it easier for judges to confirm charges when the evidence is there. Codifying age-based persecution better recognizes a fact that courts and investigators already know. Children are targeted because of their age, whether for sexual violence against very young girls in the Democratic Republic of Congo, systematic denial of education in Cameroon from armed separatists' attacks on schools, or recruitment and use as soldiers in Myanmar. Already, sixteen countries proposed amendments adding age to the working draft of the new treaty on crimes against humanity’s definition of persecution. More should support the proposal before countries begin formal negotiations in 2028. Making the law more explicit will pave a clearer path to justice for children who are targeted simply because they are children.

Mbappé, Mao, and La Liga. Click to expand Image An advertisement featuring French soccer star Kylian Mbappé in Shanghai, China, June 30, 2026. © 2026 Chinatopix via AP Photo This week a Chinese sports forum unearthed an April 2026 interview with Real Madrid football star Kylian Mbappé jokingly likening himself to a “Chinese dictator” (dictateur chinois). While Mbappé, known for dictating terms on the pitch, did not name names, the broadcaster added art showing him as Chinese Communist Party founder Mao Zedong. Beijing’s reaction was swift. China’s Foreign Ministry claimed the words “hurt the feelings of the Chinese people.” Chinese state broadcaster CCTV blacked out all Spanish football league La Liga matches. The Chinese Communist Party under Xi Jinping has low tolerance for anything that could be interpreted as an affront to China, even a comment about Mao made in jest. Javier Tebas, the Spanish football league’s president, issued an apology praising La Liga’s ties with China’s “government departments.” Mao launched China’s Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, disasters that caused massive loss of lives and suffering. In his 2008 book Tombstone: The Untold Story of Mao's Great Famine, journalist Yang Jisheng estimates that at least 36 million people starved to death or died from related abuse during the country’s famine from 1958 to 1961. There were periods when people in China could discuss aspects of these horrors. But, currently, under Xi’s ever-tightening grip, such questions won’t be tolerated. While Mbappé, who swiftly apologized, might lose Chinese sponsors, it’s China’s people who pay the greatest price. In 2021, the Chinese government passed a law punishing those who slander “heroes and martyrs” with up to three years in prison. The authorities later fined a comedian’s company 14.7 million yuan (about US$2.1 million) after he made a joke about the People’s Liberation Army. The authorities also recently sentenced artist Gao Zhen to three years in prison under the same law for his provocative Mao sculptures; in one, he depicted Mao kneeling and apologizing to his victims. Beijing’s response to Mbappé’s offhand remark is a reminder that, when it comes to controlling thought and speech, the Chinese Communist Party will always play to win.

Women Should Never Give Birth in Shackles. Click to expand Image A woman in Australia. © 2008 Getty Images An incarcerated Indigenous woman was reportedly shackled during a hospital stay earlier this month to deliver her baby by caesarean section in a Queensland hospital in Australia. Queensland Corrective Services promised an internal review but did not confirm the shackling. Shackling a woman during childbirth contravenes international human rights standards. The incident happened days before Australia’s two major political parties blocked a vote in parliament on October 14 on a bill to ban the shackling of prisoners during childbirth. United Nations human rights experts criticized the Australian parliament’s failure to vote on the bill. Prisoners and detainees do not lose their rights to health or to be treated humanely and with dignity. Restraining a woman during childbirth raises grave concerns about degrading treatment and interference with care, which constitute obstetric violence. Obstetric violence is the physical and emotional abuse of pregnant people seeking sexual and reproductive health services and information, including maternal health. It is a form of gender-based violence and a violation of fundamental human rights. As a UN member state, Australia has endorsed the Bangkok Rules, a UN resolution that sets out minimum standards for the treatment of women in prison. The resolution specifically prohibits the use of restraints on women during labor, birth or immediately after birth. The well-being of the mother and the needs of her newborn should take priority over punitive practices. Australian authorities should investigate who authorized the shackling, whether clinicians objected and how those objections were handled. There should be accountability for any wrongdoing and an effective remedy for the woman. She should have independent legal advice and support, without pressure to disclose her experience or identity publicly. The Australian government should also promptly adopt consistent national safeguards and prohibit the practice of shackling prisoners in labor. It should introduce reforms that outline appropriate hospital and prison protocols for pregnant women, staff training, rapid escalation for clinicians, and independent monitoring. A prison sentence must never be a justification for woman to give birth without dignity.

Critic of Mali’s Junta Forcibly Disappeared Six Months On. Click to expand Image Lawyer and junta critic Mountaga Tall, Mali, 2025. © Private Six months after their abductions, Mountaga Tall, an outspoken critic of Mali’s junta, and his son, Cheick Mamadou Tall, remain missing, their fate unknown, and the Malian authorities silent. Every day that passes without news raises fears for their safety and deepens their family’s anguish. Unidentified gunmen abducted Tall in Bamako, Mali’s capital, on May 2. Tall’s son went missing on May 16 after receiving a call informing him that he could deliver belongings to his father, who was reportedly being held at an undisclosed location. Radio France Internationale reported in July that the United Nations Committee on Enforced Disappearances had urged Mali’s authorities to locate and protect Tall and his son. International media suggest that Malian intelligence services may be holding Tall in a secret facility. Malian authorities, however, have neither acknowledged detaining Tall or his son nor provided information about their location, legal status, or health, despite requests from Tall’s family and a legal team. Tall, who was a government minister between 2014 and 2017, was initially aligned with Mali’s military authorities but later emerged as a critic of the junta who opposed the military-led government’s dissolution of political parties. The disappearances of Tall and his son fit a broader crackdown on political opposition, media and dissent under Mali’s military junta, which seized power in 2021. Authorities have suspended and banned media outlets, dissolved civil society groups, ended multiparty politics and subjected critics to arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Since Tall’s abduction, other political figures and their relatives have reportedly been abducted by masked gunmen, a modus operandi associated with Malian intelligence services and some remain missing. Under international human rights law, an enforced disappearance occurs when state authorities or their agents detain a person and then refuse to acknowledge the detention or disclose the person’s fate or whereabouts, thereby placing the person outside the protection of the law. Victims of enforced disappearance face a heightened risk of torture and execution. Enforced disappearance inflicts profound suffering on families, leaving them uncertain about whether their loved ones are alive or dead and denying them justice. Malian authorities should immediately disclose the whereabouts of Mountaga Tall and his son, ensure their safety, and release them.

“They Killed Us”. Click to expand Image Nobel Peace Prize laureate Dmitry Muratov of Russia during the award ceremony for the Nobel Peace prize on December 10, 2021, in Oslo, Norway. © 2021 Odd Andersen/AFP via Getty Images When I woke up this morning to the news that Novaya Gazeta is closing its doors, it felt like a personal blow. To me, Novaya’s office in a small grey building in central Moscow always felt like home. The newsroom moved to Moscow almost three decades ago. I got to know its every nook and cranny, as I went there, in my capacity of a Moscow-based Human Rights Watch researcher, for meetings, celebrations, commemorations, or simply to swap stories with a friendly journalist over coffee or wine. Click to expand Image Novaya Gazeta staff members with a portrait of Anna Politkovskaya" next to their office building in Moscow". © Novaya Gazeta archive I was there on the night of Anna Politkovskaya’s murder in October 2006 and stood outside seven years later as her memorial plaque was affixed to the wall. I celebrated with the newsroom when editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. For years, I worked alongside Novaya journalists in conflict zones. Together, we travelled to Chechnya, remote mountain villages in Dagestan, South Ossetia (Georgia), and Ukraine. It was more than collaboration; it was a true partnership. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the authorities set out to stifle Novaya Gazeta. By the end of 2022, the newspaper had lost its print and online media registrations, and its website had been blocked. Some journalists left Russia, launching Novaya Gazeta Europe and other projects in exile. Others stayed against all odds, continuing to publish investigations, interviews, and commentary online, accessible outside Russia and through circumvention tools inside the country. Despite mounting pressure, they persevered. In April 2026, police searched the newsroom for 13 hours and arrested a journalist on criminal charges carrying up to six years in prison. In September, the authorities designated Novaya Gazeta a “foreign agent” and listed over 100 staff and contributors as “affiliated individuals.” On October 29, the newspaper was told to vacate its offices. Its donation-processing system was also disabled, cutting off reader contributions. Today, Novaya Gazeta announced it would cease operations on November 9. In a statement titled “They Killed Us,” the editors wrote: “This is not just our own story. It is the story of a country and a society that are being destroyed in exactly the same way.” Novaya Gazeta’s story is also one of extraordinary courage and journalistic integrity. The authorities may silence a newspaper, but they cannot extinguish the voices of those who refuse to be silenced.

New US Sanctions Target Rwanda’s Abusive Role in Eastern Congo. Click to expand Image A member of the M23 looks on during an enrollment of civilians, police officers, and former members of the Congolese armed forces who have been recruited in Goma on February 23, 2025. © 2025 Michel Lunanga/AFP via Getty Images The United States Treasury announced new sanctions this week against Rwanda's Ministry of Defense and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution that the US Treasury found facilitated payments for the Rwandan army and the abusive M23 armed group. The sanctions freeze all named parties’ assets and interests in the US and effectively bar their use of the US dollar in international transactions. Thousands of Rwandan soldiers have fought alongside the M23 in eastern Congo since the group’s resurgence in late 2021. The Rwandan army has also provided the M23 with significant logistical and material support. In announcing the new sanctions, the US Treasury noted the M23 has perpetrated serious human rights abuses. The armed group has carried out unlawful killings, sexual violence, forced recruitment and forced labor, unlawful detentions, forced population transfers, and torture or other physical abuses in areas under its control. The treasury also stated that a Zigama branch enabled the transportation of gold sourced from rebel-controlled territory in eastern Congo to the Rwandan capital Kigali and facilitated financial transactions for the M23 worth tens of millions of dollars. While prior US sanctions issued in March targeted the Rwanda Defence Force and individual senior commanders, sanctioning the ministry targets the institution overseeing all military operations in support of M23. The sanctions come weeks after former Congolese president Joseph Kabila announced the creation of a political-military coalition that includes the M23, called the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (Front pour la Refondation de la Nation, FRN). Washington already sanctioned Kabila in April for his alleged support to armed groups. Sanctions alone, however will not protect civilians and should be accompanied by concrete measures to secure an end to abuses. The United Nations identified the M23 as the leading perpetrator of documented human rights violations in 2025, with the Congolese army second. The US and other governments should also press Congo to investigate and prosecute its own forces responsible for abuse, ensure they respect humanitarian law, and to end support for abusive groups. Above all, greater pressure is needed to ensure that protection of civilians and accountability are central to peace efforts.

Pakistan: Rights Lawyers Receive 10-Year Sentences. Click to expand Image Human rights lawyers Imaan Mazari (right) and Hadi Ali Chattha, during a court hearing in Islamabad, Pakistan, December 5, 2025. © 2025 Aamir Qureshi/AFP via Getty Images (New York) – An anti-terrorism court in Pakistan imposed 10-year prison sentences on two human rights lawyers on October 29, 2026, in an escalation of the government’s crackdown on civil society, Human Rights Watch said today. Pakistani authorities should immediately quash the convictions, release Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha, and cease criminal proceedings aimed at punishing human rights advocates. The sentences were handed down following a trial held inside Adiala prison in Rawalpindi. The lawyers were accused of obstructing police at a road closure in Islamabad in October 2024. Instead of prosecuting them for a misdemeanor or common crime, the police charged them under Pakistan’s anti-terrorism act, which carries far greater penalties and a longer sentence. This was the second time in recent weeks that the two have been prosecuted in an apparent attempt to prevent them from carrying out their legal work. “Prosecuting two human rights lawyers for terrorism sends a chilling message to everyone who speaks up for fundamental rights in Pakistan,” said Patricia Gossman, senior associate Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should quash the outrageous 10-year sentences handed down to Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha.” Mazari and Chattha have represented journalists as well as political and human rights activists. They have defended people facing blasphemy charges, victims of sexual violence and enforced disappearances, and prisoners facing the death penalty. In addition, the court sentenced both lawyers to three years in prison for “obstructing and assaulting public servants,” to run concurrently. Family members allege that during the trial, Mazari and Chattha were denied legal representation of their choice and access to key legal documents, raising serious concerns about the fairness of the trial, due process, and the right to prepare and present an effective defense. On September 17, the Supreme Court had suspended their sentences in a separate case involving social media posts and ordered their release on bail, but police rearrested them hours later. On September 30, United Nations human rights experts called for their immediate release and said that successive proceedings appeared intended to punish them for their views and their human rights advocacy. Pakistani authorities have used vague and overbroad anti-terrorism legislation to sentence and imprison those protesting government policies. The authorities should prosecute alleged violence under appropriate criminal laws while protecting the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. Allegations of obstructing officials or disrupting public order should not be treated as terrorism, Human Rights Watch said. The authorities should ensure that counterterrorism laws are narrowly drawn and applied and are not used to punish dissent or circumvent fair-trial protections. The UN Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provide that governments should protect lawyers from intimidation, harassment, and improper interference, as well as from prosecution for carrying out recognized professional duties. “Punishing lawyers and human rights activists for defending rights leaves those they represent without protection,” Gossman said. “Concerned governments should press Pakistan to end its crackdown on human rights advocacy.”

Australia: Solitary Confinement Harming Prisoners with Disabilities. Click to expand Image The Adelaide Women’s Prison, South Australia, 2026. © 2026 Dean Faulkner/ABC News Prison authorities in the Australian state of South Australia are harming people with disabilities by using solitary confinement.Solitary confinement has a disproportionately harmful impact on people with disabilities and can amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and even torture. Australia’s federal and state governments should take urgent action to ensure proper independent oversight of prisons and invest in alternatives to incarceration. (Sydney) — Prison authorities in the Australian state of South Australia are harming people with disabilities by using solitary confinement, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The 50-page report, “‘They Just Locked Me Away’: Solitary Confinement and Abuse of People with Disabilities in Prisons in the State of South Australia,” documents the use of solitary confinement on people with psychosocial disabilities, mental health conditions. It details broader problems facing people with disabilities in South Australian prisons, including inadequate access to individualized mental health care and lack of prison oversight.
