November 1, 2026 “They Just Locked Me Away” Solitary Confinement and Abuse of People with Disabilities in Prisons in the State of South Australia Download the full report in English Appendix: Response from the Department for Correctional Services The United Nations Committee Against Torture, an international expert body that, in November 2026, is reviewing Australia’s compliance with international legal obligations to prevent torture and ill-treatment, has asked the federal government to provide information on its efforts to ensure that solitary confinement is prohibited for people with disabilities when it would exacerbate their mental health conditions. “Prison authorities in South Australia need to recognize and stop the use of solitary confinement of prisoners with mental health conditions,” said Daniela Gavshon, Australia director at Human Rights Watch. “Solitary confinement has a disproportionate harmful impact on people with certain types of disabilities and can amount to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and even torture.” In 2025 and 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed more than 40 people, including 17 people with disabilities—14 of them with psychosocial disabilities—who had previously been incarcerated in South Australia. Interviewees also included family members and friends of people with disabilities who had been incarcerated, lawyers, staff of nongovernmental organizations, advocates, mental health and medical professionals, and academics. Twelve of the people with psychosocial disabilities interviewed said South Australian authorities had subjected them to solitary confinement, referred to as “separation orders” under South Australian policy, in some cases repeatedly. All said it was distressing and damaged their mental health. South Australian laws provide few limitations on the circumstances under which correctional authorities can impose solitary confinement. Reasons prison authorities can send people to solitary confinement can include when they are deemed to be at a real or perceived risk of self-harm. Human Rights Watch found that fear of being sent to solitary confinement deterred people from disclosing mental health conditions. One woman with a psychosocial disability said that she had tried to hide her self-harm scars to prevent prison officers from sending her to solitary confinement. International research has consistently found that solitary confinement can increase the risk of self-harm and suicidal thoughts. People with physical disabilities also described a lack of physical accessibility in South Australian prisons. One man who uses a wheelchair said he had spent eight days in Adelaide Remand Centre without access to a bathroom. Solitary confinement for people with disabilities is a nationwide problem. Human Rights Watch has also documented the use of solitary confinement for prisoners with psychosocial disabilities in prisons in Western Australia and Queensland in 2018 and 2020. The use of solitary confinement on people with disabilities is contrary to international human rights standards. The UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules) prohibit the solitary confinement of people with psychosocial or physical disabilities “when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures.” The UN Human Rights Committee, which monitors compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, has called for prohibiting “solitary confinement for … persons with intellectual or psychosocial disabilities in prison.” In 2022, the UN Committee Against Torture, in its sixth periodic review of Australia, said that the government should “ensure that persons with disabilities cannot be held in solitary confinement.” However, the government has yet to act. Not a single state or territory law prohibits solitary confinement for people with disabilities. Human Rights Watch also found a lack of data on the number of people with disabilities incarcerated in South Australia and nationally, although it is widely accepted that they are overrepresented in Australian prisons. One reason is that the Australian Bureau of Statistics does not allow incarcerated people to fill out their own census forms. Any data collection should follow human rights principles, including the right to privacy and consent. The final report of the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of People with Disability, a national inquiry that concluded in 2023, found that data gaps “present challenges for governments when designing and delivering supports and services for people with cognitive disabilities involved in the criminal justice system.” The South Australian government should enact laws banning the use of solitary confinement on people with disabilities, increase independent oversight of prisons, and ensure incarcerated people have proper access to disability-related requirements including mental health care and support, Human Rights Watch said. The government should also invest in alternatives to custody for people with disabilities. “Prison authorities across Australia are violating the rights of imprisoned people with disabilities,” Gavshon said. “The federal and state governments should take urgent action to ensure proper independent oversight of prisons and invest in alternatives to incarceration.” Selected Accounts “My mental health was bad enough, but [solitary] just made it worse…. They put me in there because of self-harming, not taking medication…. I thought I had to punish myself for the things I'd done, I wanted to punish myself. They never asked [why], they just put me in D-Wing.” — A woman with a psychosocial disability repeatedly held in solitary confinement in Adelaide Women's Prison, South Australia. “If you go there for suicidal thoughts or whatever, it makes you [even more suicidal] from going there. I had a really rough time down there.… I felt isolated from the whole world.” — A man with a schizoaffective condition, with respect to being held in G Division, the solitary wing of Yatala Labour Prison, South Australia. “No shower, no toilet…. Eight days.… They had nothing — no toilets which were accessible, no shower. I didn't even get to see the toilet or the shower.… They need to facilitate for people in wheelchairs. They can't just put them in there and say, deal with what you've got.” — Man held in Adeliade Remand Centre in 2020 without access to a wheelchair-accessible bathroom.

Zambia: Widespread Repression in Post-Election Crackdown. Click to expand Image A police vehicle on the outskirts of Lusaka, Zambia, August 14, 2026. © 2026 Alfonso Nqunjana/AP Photo Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members, lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August. The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices.The authorities should immediately halt the crackdown, allow access to lawyers and medical care to detainees, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses. (Johannesburg) – The Zambian police and military forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. The authorities have also yet to credibly explain or investigate the killing of an opposition leader in contested circumstances. “Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” said Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.” President Hakainde Hichilema was reelected in the August 13 election, which observers said was marred by irregularities such as a suspension of counting and limited fundamental freedoms. From August 24 to 28, the authorities suspended judicial services and prevented legal challenges to the presidential election results, closing and cordoning off court premises. Zambian police stated that the closures were an “intelligence-led and preventive measure,” without providing details. Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases in August that appear to have been enforced disappearances, in which the authorities refused to reveal the situation and whereabouts of a detained person. Several of these people were initially forcibly disappeared for days. Victims, family members, and lawyers said that the military held some of them. Human Rights Watch also documented 61 cases in which detainees or their lawyers and relatives allege that they were beaten or otherwise violently abused during their arrest, in detention, or both. Eighteen have been charged with treason, with two also facing sedition charges. In many cases, the people detained were never charged with a crime while in others, the charges against them appear to be politically motivated. The government has not disclosed how many people were arrested during the crackdown or the charges against them, prompting concerns that the number of people detained is higher than presently known. Human Rights Watch has also documented two cases in which the Zambia-based relatives of government critics living abroad say government authorities harassed and threatened them. The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices, Human Rights Watch said. On September 11, the government announced the cancellation of six government critics’ passports, including that of an academic, Sishuwa Sishuwa, for “security reasons.” On August 14, security forces raided the home of the Tonse Alliance opposition leader, Brian Mundubile, in a suburb of Lusaka, the capital. Opposition members present allege that security forces killed a former government minister, Mutotwe Kafwaya, during the raid. Inspector General of the Zambia Police Service Graphel Musamba said members of a “joint intelligence-led operation” were met with “gunfire and resistance from unknown individuals” that “prompted officers to return fire,” and that Kafwaya had been killed in the process. Kafwaya’s fate was not known until August 19, after his wife filed a habeas corpus petition to compel authorities to disclose his whereabouts, bring him before court, and show sufficient and lawful cause for his continued detention. Public officials made contradictory statements about the raid and who was responsible for it. On August 15, the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA) sent out a text message to all registered phones in Zambia stating: “Beware of false reports of shootings and abductions. Stay calm and peaceful.” The Ministry of Information and Media dismissed reports of the raid and shooting as “disinformation intended to alarm and mislead the public.” The police also issued a media statement denying that there had been a raid and that Mundubile was in police custody. Police Inspector General Musamba later admitted that there had been a “joint security-led intelligence operation” at Mundubile’s home. Mundubile, who was later arrested and charged with treason, stated in a High Court petition that Human Rights Watch has seen that he saw a member of the military fatally shoot Kafwaya. Given the conflicting statements by government officials about who was responsible for the raid on Mundubile’s home and the circumstances surrounding Kafwaya’s killing, Zambian authorities should institute an independent, impartial, and thorough investigation into the matter, Human Rights Watch said. Detainees have implicated Zambia’s military in arbitrary detention and enforced disappearance. Forty-three opposition members acting as election monitors were detained on August 14. Their lawyer said their whereabouts had been unknown for eight days and that the police had denied holding them. When a lawyer finally saw them, he told Human Rights Watch that “most of them were swollen and had terrible injuries, including broken bones. They said they had been brutalized by the military.” Their lawyers filed a habeas corpus application and, on September 10, a court in Lusaka ordered their immediate release. Under Zambian law and international human rights law, all detainees have the right to due process, including to be promptly informed of the charges against them, to have access to counsel if charged with a crime, to have their detention reviewed by a judge, and to be presumed innocent. They should also have access to adequate medical care and be able to communicate with their families. In a September 2 call, the United Nations special rapporteur on the rights to freedom of assembly and of association said that the authorities should “release all political detainees, respect fundamental freedoms, and restore democratic accountability.” The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said in response that the call was “inaccurate, undiplomatic and falling short of the standards of objectivity, moderation and discretion expected of UN mandate holders.” The ministry said that being a member of opposition party “does not place a person beyond the reach of the law, nor does it convert a criminal suspect into a political detainee… The government is committed to ensuring that these protections are respected in every case, and Zambia’s courts are open to test them.” Zambia will serve as a member of the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027-2029 term. As a council member, Zambia is expected to “uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights.” “The Zambian government’s needs to end its brazen human rights crackdown,” Budoo-Scholtz said. “Leaders in Southern Africa and Zambia’s development partners should encourage President Hichilema to restore the rule of law and ensure that civic and political spaces are protected.” Enforced Disappearances, Including by Military Personnel Human Rights Watch documented 14 cases of apparent enforced disappearances of opposition members and supporters, including some in which the authorities denied holding people who were later produced after habeas corpus applications. The authorities claimed to have arrested 11 men during the August 14 raid on Mundubile’s home. Lawyers and family members of seven of the men said that they were made to lie down and were beaten using fists, rifle butts, and sticks, kicked by men in military uniform, then blindfolded and driven away in military vehicles. Victims and witnesses identified members of Zambia’s military through their uniforms and military vehicles. During the same raid, security forces picked up several opposition members and supporters and forcibly disappeared them for days before family members or their lawyers found them. They included Bishop Trevor Mwamba, an opposition leader; Patrick Mwansa, a leading opposition campaigner; and security aides Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Brazil Soko, Francis Mulenga, and Richard Banda. According to their lawyers and court documents seen by Human Rights Watch, the men were taken to a “military command center” where they were “screened and processed” then detained in “various police stations around Lusaka.” Lawyers and family members said they went around police stations in Lusaka looking for the detainees, but authorities denied holding the men. However, some were found days later at the same stations where the police had denied holding them. Mwansa’s family said he had a broken finger and swollen face when they finally located him four days later in Lusaka’s Central Police Station. On September 6, Mwansa was moved to a maximum security prison in Kabwe, 150 kilometers from Lusaka, and has not yet received medical treatment, a family member said. The family of Bishop Mwamba, president of the opposition United National Independence Party, who was also picked up during the raid at Mundubile’s home, said they searched for him in police stations in and around Lusaka for four days before locating him at Matero Police Station. Earlier, including on the day he was located, officers at Matero Police Station had denied holding Mwamba. “He had spent days without food and without taking his prescription medication,” the relative said. “The police had first denied [holding him] but we insisted to see him, because we had received an anonymous tip informing us that he was at Matero. When they brought him out and we asked what he was arrested for, police said they had no charge for him ‘because he was brought in by the military who asked us to keep him in the cells for them.’” On August 30, when the family took food and pain killers to Benard Chewe at Kabwata Police Station, where he had been detained, officers there told them that he had been moved but claimed that they did not know where. When the family traced him two days later to Mwembeshi Correctional Facility on the outskirts of Lusaka, they were denied access. Men in unmarked vehicles who introduced themselves as “state intelligence officers” picked up Harry Findlay, a Lusaka businessman and opposition supporter, from his residence on August 4, a family member said. Neither his lawyer nor family had access to him, and the authorities did not inform them of his whereabouts. Findlay’s lawyers sent two letters to Zambian authorities, on August 7 and August 17, requesting his whereabouts and calling for his immediate release and access to doctors, lawyers, and family. On August 20, Findlay was taken to court under a judge’s order to inquire into the legality of his detention. On August 29, he was charged with treason and moved to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison, where he remains without trial. All the men detained in the August 14 raid were eventually charged with treason and remain in detention without having appeared in court. Human Rights Watch believes that in these cases, Zambian authorities are using treason charges, which are nonbailable, and sedition, which carries a heavy penalty, to stifle dissent and political opposition. On August 27, police arrested Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, and subsequently also charged them with treason and seditious practices. The charge sheet, which Human Rights Watch has seen, alleges that Mundubile and Zulu went on Facebook live on August 14 stating that the opposition had won the election. The government alleges that this was meant to “raise discontent or disaffection among the people of Zambia.” On September 22, the Law Association of Zambia raised concerns about prolonged detentions without court appearances. Zambia’s Human Rights Commission on September 3 said it was following 84 election-related detainees whose cases it cast as part of a “disturbing pattern of prolonged detention, delayed notification of charges, restricted access to family and legal representation and failure to bring detainees before a competent court without undue delay.” Abuse and Ill-Treatment in Custody Human Rights Watch documented that 61 people had been mistreated in custody by reviewing court documents and interviewing family members. Lawyers for the 43 opposition members acting as election monitors who were detained on August 14 said that state security agents kicked and beat them and denied them food during the first 8 days of their 21-day detention. Lawyers representing 18 detainees accused of treason state in court documents that the detainees were abused and assaulted in custody and denied medical attention. The lawyers also said 10 of the 18—George Chisanga, Patrick Mwansa, Trevor Mwamba, Francis Mulenga, Brazil Soko, Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chewe, Richard Banda, Emmanuel Mulenga, and Darius Mwila—had been restricted from accessing their lawyers or family members. In a court petition filed on September 11, Ezra Topola, Dickson Tembo, and Victor Muzyamba alleged that security personnel waterboarded them and suspended them from a metal bar and beat them. Findlay alleged that he was kept in solitary confinement in Mwembeshi Correctional Facility and denied access to his prescription medication. Mwansa alleged that he suffered serious injuries, including cuts to his face and a fracture on his hand, but was denied access to medical attention. Family members told Human Rights Watch that when they found Mutyoka on August 17 at Lusaka’s Central Police Station, three days after military detained him at Mundubile’s home, he showed signs of having been physically abused. “When we saw him, his face was swollen, he was coughing blood and was limping,” a relative said. “He said they had been made to lie down in the yard of Mundubile’s home and beaten using rifle butts and whips by masked men in military unform. All he wanted was to see a doctor, but that request was denied and, to this day, he has not been seen by a doctor.” When Chewe’s family members found him at Kabwata Police Station three days after he was taken from Mundubile’s home, they said that he too showed signs of physical abuse. “He had a swollen forehead, busted lips, and complained of body pains,” a relative said. “He said he had been assaulted by the military at their headquarters before they took him to the police station.” Lawyers for Chewe, Mutyoka, and Soko at Mwembeshi Correctional Facility said that Zambia Army Special Forces personnel interrogated them and that on September 10, authorities moved the three to Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison without informing family or lawyers. On October 27, family members said medical doctors have not yet seen the three despite urgent letters written on September 9, seen by Human Rights Watch, to the commissioner of the Zambia Correctional Service and the officer-in-charge of Mwembeshi Correctional Facility. Eight election monitors for the opposition, men aged 21 to 26, said a group of armed soldiers wearing uniforms and masks jumped over the perimeter wall into a house in Lusaka’s Emmasdale township on August 15 around 8 p.m., where the monitors were meeting. They said the armed soldiers dragged them out of the house, kicked them with boots, and beat them with fists and sticks. They were forced into a military truck and taken away but could not identify where they were held. For the next three days, security forces beat them several times a day, demanding confessions that they belonged to “Brian Mundubile’s militia.” All eight were released on August 18 without charge. Human Rights Watch has also examined a petition filed on September 11 by lawyers for the 18 accused of treason that implicates the army in interrogations and abuse of detainees. In the petition, lawyers allege that special forces personnel led by Gen. Moses Shapwaya threatened and intimidated some of the detainees in prison to force them to incriminate Mundubile and Zulu. Arbitrary Arrests and Detention From court records and interviews with victims, family, and lawyers, Human Rights Watch documented 71 cases in which opposition members and supporters, as well as government critics, were arrested on charges that may be politically motivated or held in prolonged detention without charge. These include the 43 election monitors and 17 musicians and comedians who were detained after performing at an opposition rally, among others. The arrest of the 43 monitors came after the opposition leader stated that he planned to challenge the election result in court, while the government accused him of plotting an insurgency. In an electoral court challenge, the monitors would have been potential witnesses for the opposition’s case. After their 21 days in detention without charge, the court ruled that their arrest was unjustified and ordered their immediate release. Human Rights Watch interviewed a 44-year-old Lusaka mathematician who was hired to tally numbers for a potential court challenge to President Hichilema’s election. He said that on August 15 at about 9:30 p.m., about eight armed men who identified themselves as intelligence and police officers broke into his house and harassed him. They demanded access to his phone and laptop, he said, and to know who was funding the court challenge. He said they dragged him outside, put him into a vehicle, and took him to the police headquarters in Lusaka, where he was interrogated further about the election petition. The next day, he was transferred to Ridgeway Police Station, where he spent 18 days without being charged. On August 28, his lawyer filed a habeas corpus application in the Lusaka High Court, which Human Rights Watch has seen. Five days later, police charged him with a misdemeanor offense and released him the same day. Before the election, on August 5, a group of 17 people were arrested after performing at an opposition rally in Mongu, Western province. Police detained them for over two weeks on what was initially said to be a traffic offense of travelling in a vehicle without numbered plates, a lawyer familiar with the case told Human Rights Watch. The lawyer said that the group’s arrest and prolonged detention were politically motivated because of their vocal and visible mobilization for the opposition. Police later charged and prosecuted the 17 for “riotous assembly or behavior.” In a court document seen by Human Rights Watch, the state alleges that the 17 did “unlawfully assemble and begun to execute a common purpose by a breach of peace and the terror of the public.” A court released them on bail on August 30, after over three weeks in detention. Driven into Hiding Human Rights Watch interviewed seven people, including lawyers and a journalist, who said they had fled their homes because they believed they had been targeted for arrest in the days after the August 13 election. A lawyer and a journalist showed Human Rights Watch messages on their phones alerting them that they were on a “wanted list.” Some left and others were in hiding within the country. A statement by seven international lawyers’ associations said some lawyers involved in preparing or lodging election-related legal challenges had fled Zambia due to threats to their safety. A lawyer said that he went into hiding on August 15 after scores of security agents came to his home and office. The lawyer had been acting on behalf of Tonse Alliance, including working on a court petition to challenge President Hichilema’s election. “There was no reason for the security agents to chase me in that manner,” he said. “If the police wanted me for any reason, they should have alerted me, and I would have presented myself with my legal representatives.” Mulenga Kapwepwe, an opposition leader who worked closely with Mundubile and Zulu, said she went into hiding on August 15 after confidential sources alerted her that she was “on a wanted list.” “I have had to rearrange my life,” she said. “Many of my colleagues are in detention charged with treason, and I have been warned that the moment I come out of hiding, I will be targeted.” On August 17, a journalist who runs an investigative journalism website and has previously been detained for his journalism crossed the border into a neighboring country hours before security agents went to his house looking for him. “My website was following up on the raid at Mundubile’s house,” he said. “That is when I received messages on my phone saying: ‘Stop what you are doing. We are coming after you.’ I was once arrested and detained without charge for nearly two weeks. I know what these people are capable of. So, fearful for my life, I left.” While he was fleeing, the journalist said, he received a call from a family member that about five people who identified themselves as officers from Office of the President were at his house looking for him. They told his family that he was wanted for sedition. Harassment of Family Members Human Rights Watch documented two cases in which the authorities allegedly harassed and threatened the Zambia-based family members of government critics living abroad. Police allegedly detained two siblings of a well-known diaspora critic of the government and harassed their 76-year-old father, demanding that their sibling abroad, who runs a popular social media page with hundreds of thousands of followers, take down material critical of the government. One sibling was detained in a 3 a.m. raid on their home, in which armed police officers demanded access to their phones and laptop, a close source said, adding that one of the police officers “had a gun and said: ‘This is a high security operation.” The officers said the foreign-based sibling’s “political commentary was ‘a problem’ and that they needed it to stop.” The authorities allegedly demanded the removal of specific videos as a condition for their release. In one of these videos, the social media personality demanded an independent inquiry into the August 14 killing of Kafwaya. In another case, a government critic in the United States with investments in Zambia said that three men who identified themselves as intelligence officers from the Office of the President approached family members in Zambia days after the election and threatened to “squeeze” her businesses if she continued to criticize President Hichilema’s administration on social media. “They told my sister, a civil servant, that she risked losing her job if I did not tone down my criticism,” the critic said.

Türkiye: European Court to Rule on Istanbul Mayor’s Detention. Click to expand Image Ekrem İmamoğlu in front of the courthouse in Istanbul, Türkiye where he received his official mandate to serve a second five-year term as Istanbul mayor after winning the March 31, 2024 municipal election, April 3, 2024. © 2024 Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images The Turkish authorities are misusing powers of detention and prosecution against opposition politicians in Türkiye to prevent them from participating effectively in elections or political life, the Turkey Litigation Support Project, Human Rights Watch, and the International Commission of Jurists said today. The three groups have submitted a third-party intervention—or amicus brief—to the European Court of Human Rights with information on patterns of human rights violations, abuse of the criminal law, and the erosion of judicial independence in Türkiye. The intervention was made in a case brought by the Istanbul mayor and opposition politician Ekrem İmamoğlu to the Strasbourg court asserting that his detention violates his rights protected under provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights, including article 5 (right to liberty and security), article 18 (limitation on use of restrictions on rights), and article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the convention (right to free elections). “Detaining political opponents and perceived dissenting voices to remove them from political life and to silence them has become a familiar playbook in Türkiye,” said Ayşe Bingöl Demir at the Turkey Litigation Support Project. “The case before the European Court of Human Rights reviewing the detention of Ekrem İmamoğlu raises issues also highlighted in earlier cases reviewed by the court.” The Turkish authorities arrested İmamoğlu on March 19, 2025, and a court placed him in pretrial detention the same day the Republican People’s Party (CHP) designated him as a candidate for the future presidential election. He remains detained and has been suspended from his office as mayor during his ongoing trial on charges including “establishing and leading a criminal organization,” “accepting bribes,” and “interfering with public tenders.” İmamoğlu’s detention is part of a larger wave of arrests, detention, and prosecutions carried out since 2025 targeting the CHP, which was Türkiye’s largest opposition party at the time of his arrest. Between March 2025 and August 2026, 43 municipalities run by the party reportedly became subject to judicial proceedings, and 31 CHP mayors were detained. In May 2026, the Ankara regional court of appeal issued a controversial decision to remove Özgür Özel, as the elected head of the CHP, under whose leadership Ekrem İmamoğlu’s candidacy had been declared. Following Özel’s removal, the party leadership split, with the majority of its members of parliament opting to establish and join the New Party (Yeni Party) in July 2026. The use of detention and prosecution against İmamoğlu and other elected officials recalls the 2016-17 waves of arrests of the leadership and members of parliament from the opposition Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP). The European Court of Human Rights found that the detention of HDP co-chairs Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ Şenoğlu and 15 other members of parliament and politicians from the party pursued an ulterior purpose of “stifling pluralism and limiting freedom of political debate, the very core of the concept of a democratic society.” “In reviewing the legitimacy of Ekrem İmamoğlu’s detention, the European Court of Human Rights will be examining a case that bears many similarities to the detentions of the Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtaş and others it has already adjudicated,” said Aisling Reidy, senior legal advisor at Human Rights Watch. “In those cases, the court immediately ordered their release and found that Turkish authorities are responsible for politically motivated detentions aimed at removing elected officials from political life, a fundamental violation of their rights, the rights of voters and of the democratic process.” Recalling the safeguards imposed by human rights law and standards on the prosecution and detention of opposition politicians, the three groups assert that the Turkish authorities have shown systematic disregard for those safeguards, and instead are engaged in a pattern of abusive application of the criminal law using “terrorism,” “organized crime,” and other serious charges against elected officials of Türkiye’s main opposition parties. The groups stressed that the misuse of detention orders and the institution of spurious criminal charges is likely to engender a chilling effect on pluralism and to thereby interfere with the right to run for election and to hold elected office, and therefore with the right of voters to their chosen representatives. The European Court will also scrutinize whether the Turkish authorities have violated article 18 of the convention that prohibits restricting rights for ulterior purposes. In cases against Georgia, Azerbaijan, and Ukraine, the court has found government authorities invoked criminal charges such as “abuse of office” and “misappropriation” against political opposition or civil society figures to pursue ulterior motives. Since 2019, the court has issued eight judgments concerning HDP politicians and the human rights defender Osman Kavala, in which it found Türkiye had violated article 18. The amicus brief also sets out that the erosion of judicial independence in Türkiye, including the failure of lower courts to comply with decisions of the Constitutional Court, deprives opposition politicians of meaningful domestic protection. “As the intervention argues, for over a decade the erosion of the rule of law and judicial independence in Türkiye has had a damaging effect on democratic pluralism and on the right to free elections”, said Temur Shakirov, Director of Europe and Central Asia Programme at the International Commission of Jurists. “Given that context, we trust that the European Court of Human Rights will continue to apply the closest scrutiny to the prosecution and detention of opposition politicians in Türkiye.”

World Court Set to Rule in Myanmar Genocide Case. Click to expand Image People watch the ICJ hearing at a restaurant in a Rohingya refugee camp in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, on January 23, 2020. © 2020 Allison Joyce/Getty Images (The Hague) – The International Court of Justice has announced that it will deliver its judgment on November 19, 2026, in the case brought by Gambia against Myanmar for alleged violations of the Genocide Convention, Human Rights Watch said today in releasing a question-and-answer document on key issues in the case. In August 2017, Myanmar’s security forces began a sweeping campaign of massacres, rape, and arson against ethnic Rohingya in northern Rakhine State that forced more than 700,000 people to flee to neighboring Bangladesh. In November 2019, Gambia filed a case before the International Court of Justice alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya constitute genocide and violate the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This is not a criminal case against individuals, but a request for a legal determination of Myanmar’s state responsibility for genocide. “The International Court of Justice’s Myanmar judgment will mark a crucial moment in the Rohingya’s quest for justice,” said Maria Elena Vignoli, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch. “The ruling will also be a stark reminder that the oppression of the Rohingya is ongoing, and that rights-respecting countries need to act decisively to support them, promote justice for atrocities, and ensure their safe and voluntary return.” The judgment, which is final with no possibility to appeal, will conclude the proceedings in this case before the court.

Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper. Click to expand Image A man reads the Ethiopian Reporter in Addis Ababa on December 11, 2019. © 2019 Eduardo Soteras/AFP via Getty Images In what has become the new normal, the Ethiopian government has silenced yet another independent media outlet. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced in a November 2 Facebook post that it is indefinitely suspending the print and online license of the Reporter, one of Ethiopia’s oldest media institutions. Publishing in English and Amharic, the Reporter is also the country’s last privately owned Amharic newspaper. Stating that the suspension would take effect immediately, the Media Authority accused the Reporter of violating the country’s laws and media ethics by repeatedly publishing content that was against “national interests.” The authority added that the outlet published “distorted content that negatively affects foreign investment, tourism, and diplomacy.” The action is part of the government’s ongoing assault on the media and civic space in the country and points toward increasing use of vague claims about “national interests” to shut down any critical reporting. Since 2025, Ethiopian authorities have banned numerous media outlets, deported foreign correspondents, and targeted local journalists through arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and office raids. In October, undercover police detained journalists Samuel Getachew and Amanuel Gebremedhin, charging them with reporting news that would cause disruptions in Addis Ababa, the capital. The two were jailed for eight days. The Reporter, one of the few remaining independent outlets in the country, hasn’t been spared. Authorities have arrested its journalists, while the outlet itself has been under government pressure. Days before the suspension, the Reporter published an editorial warning that Ethiopia’s privately owned press was “navigating one of its most precarious periods in history” and calling for immediate reforms to prevent its total collapse. The Ethiopian government should heed the warning; the country’s concerned partners should urge the government to immediately reverse course.

Changes to Chile’s Human Rights Institute Risk Leaving Victims Behind. Click to expand Image Chile's President Jose Antonio Kast waves on his inauguration day at Congress in Valparaiso, Chile, March 11, 2026. © 2026 Esteban Felix/AP Photo Chilean President José Antonio Kast introduced in Congress on October 19 a proposal to change the country’s National Human Rights Institute. Founded in 2009 as an autonomous state body, the institute has worked to promote and protect human rights in Chile, including by taking legal action on behalf of human rights abuse victims. If passed, the legislation would weaken some of the tools the institute uses to protect human rights and diminish its independence. The bill would remove the institute’s eleven-member board of directors, replacing them with a new five-member transitional board that would draft new bylaws for the institute. Unlike the current board, which has four members who were selected directly by civil society groups, the new transitional board would be proposed by the president, approved by the Senate, and would have no members selected directly by civil society. This sits uneasily with the standards set out in the Principles relating to the Status of National Human Rights Institutions (the Paris Principles), which recommend that members be independent from the government and selected through a process that ensures broad civil society representation. According to a financial report by the Finance Ministry’s Budget Office, the proposal would also reduce the institute’s staff. The number of staff members in the institute’s regional offices outside of Santiago de Chile would be cut in half, and the number of lawyers in the institute’s protection unit, who handle the institute’s legal actions, would be reduced by 70 percent. As a result, people in many parts of Chile could lose access to in-person assistance from the institute. The proposed legislation would also end the institute’s ability to represent victims in criminal cases—a power it has often used in cases of torture, ill treatment, or human trafficking. That would mean that victims who cannot afford a lawyer would lose legal support and would rely on prosecutors to decide whether to pursue their case and how to move it forward. The National Human Rights Institute itself has welcomed other parts of the bill meant to improve its transparency and governance but has warned that some aspects of the bill would undermine its work. Chile’s Congress should reexamine these worrying provisions and make sure the institute can protect the rights of all Chileans.

Japan: Raise Rights With Vietnam’s Leader. Click to expand Image Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (left) and Vietnamese President To Lam before a meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, May 2, 2026. © 2026 Kyodo News via AP Photo (Tokyo) – Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi should urge Vietnamese President To Lam to make concrete progress on human rights during his official visit to Japan from November 8 to 11, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. Human Rights Watch wrote to Prime Minister Takaichi expressing concerns about Vietnam’s intensifying crackdown on human rights. The repression violates obligations that Vietnam accepted under the 2018 Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, to which Vietnam and Japan are parties. “The Vietnamese government has broken its pledges for reform and continues to crack down on basic freedoms,” said Kanae Doi, Japan director at Human Rights Watch. “Prime Minister Takaichi should communicate clearly and publicly to President To Lam Japan’s serious concerns about human rights and labor rights violations.” The Vietnamese government has sharply intensified its repression of basic freedoms over the past decade, Human Rights Watch said. To Lam served as Vietnam’s minister of public security from 2016 to 2024, heading the country’s national police force. He is now both general secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam and president. Japan is among Vietnam’s top trade partners and one of the largest sources of foreign direct investment in the country. As Vietnam’s largest bilateral donor of development assistance for more than 20 years, and a major trade partner, Japan is in a very favorable position to persuade Vietnam to improve the country’s human rights. On To Lam’s watch, Vietnamese police initiated a far-reaching crackdown that decimated the country’s civil society, stepped up transnational repression, and expanded the scope and use of draconian laws that criminalize the exercise of freedom of expression, in contravention of international human rights law. Vietnam currently has more than 160 political prisoners, convicted under laws that violate their rights to free expression and peaceful activism for human rights and democracy. These include: Pham Doan Trang, a writer and human rights advocate; Can Thi Theu, a land rights activist; Pham Chi Dung and Nguyen Tuong Thuy, independent journalists; Hoang Duc Binh, a labor activist; and Le Dinh Luong, Nguyen Van Tuc, Tran Duc Thach, Tran Van Bang, and Nguyen Trung Ton, democracy campaigners. During the first nine months of 2026, Vietnamese courts convicted and sentenced at least 31 activists, including the prominent bloggers Hoang Thi Hong Thai and Huynh Ngoc Tuan, to long prison terms. Police arrested at least 46 other people for allegedly criticizing the government. The Vietnamese government has failed to put in place legal reforms it pledged to undertake, Human Rights Watch said. In article 19.3 of the Trans-Pacific Partnership, Vietnam committed to “adopt and maintain in its statutes and regulations, and practices thereunder,” the rights in the International Labour Organization (ILO) Declaration, including the “freedom of association and the effective recognition of the right to collective bargaining.” Vietnam also pledged to ratify ILO Convention No. 87 on Freedom of Association and Protection of the Right to Organise by January 2024 but has yet to do so and continues to thwart the establishment of independent trade unions. Japan’s own Diplomatic Bluebook 2026 states that the Trans-Pacific Partnership “has great strategic significance in that it will establish a free and fair economic order with countries sharing fundamental values and principles, including freedom, democracy, fundamental human rights and the rule of law,” values that the Vietnamese government has systematically disregarded. Japan has not meaningfully responded to Vietnam’s worsening human rights record. In November 2023, the two countries upgraded their relationship to the highest level, a “comprehensive strategic partnership for Peace and Prosperity in Asia and the World.” “Japan should stop giving Vietnam a free pass on repression,” Doi said. “As one of Vietnam’s most important partners, Japan should make clear to To Lam that respecting basic rights and its labor commitments are crucial for a strong and lasting partnership.”

Thailand: Two Uyghurs at Risk of Return to China. Click to expand Image Detainees stand behind cell bars at the police immigration detention center in Bangkok, Thailand, January 21, 2019. © 2019 Sakchai Lalit/AP Photo (Bangkok) – Thai authorities should not forcibly return two Uyghur men to China, where they face grave risks of torture and other serious abuses, Human Rights Watch said today. The two men, whose names are not public for security reasons, were transferred from prison to immigration detention in Bangkok after receiving a royal pardon, apparently in preparation for deportation. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul should end forced returns to China and allow the two Uyghur men to travel to a safe third country.” The two Uyghur men have been detained by Thai authorities since 2014, when one of them was only 14 years old. They were serving a prison sentence for offenses related to an escape attempt from immigration detention in January 2020. On October 21, 2026, the authorities transferred them from Bangkok Central Prison to the Bangkok Immigration Detention Center Suan Phlu after they had served most of their seven-year sentence. Thai Foreign Ministry officials told a parliamentary committee that in August the Chinese embassy in Bangkok demanded their return to China. Under Thai immigration law and regulations, the two Uyghur men will be deported to China unless they object to the deportation and are resettled to a third country. Lawyers representing them told Human Rights Watch that they have already informed Thai authorities that the two do not consent to be sent to China. Thai immigration authorities have repeatedly refused to allow the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) access to the men to determine their refugee status. The Thai government is obligated to respect the international law principle of nonrefoulement, barring anyone’s forcible return to a place where they would face a genuine risk of persecution, torture or other ill-treatment, or a threat to their life or other comparable serious human rights violations. Refoulement is prohibited by the UN Convention Against Torture, to which Thailand is a party, as well as customary international law. Thailand’s Prevention and Suppression of Torture and Enforced Disappearance Act prohibits deportation when there is a substantial risk of torture or ill-treatment. In March 2014, Thai police in Songkhla province, near the Malaysia border, arrested about 220 Uyghur men, women, and children, charged them with immigration violations, and soon after transferred them to an immigration detention facility in Bangkok. In several separate incidents around the same period, the authorities arrested dozens of other Uyghurs and placed them in immigration detention facilities around the country. In July 2015, about 170 of the Uyghur women and children detained in Songkhla were released to Turkey. A week later, however, the Thai authorities forcibly transferred over 100 Uyghur men to Chinese authorities, who flew them to China. On February 27, 2025, Thai authorities took 40 Uyghur men from immigration detention and forcibly returned them to China. Upon the men’s return, the Thai authorities participated in a Chinese government-organized propaganda trip to show some of these men with their families. Despite promises by the Thai and Chinese authorities, there has been no credible monitoring of those Uyghurs since their return. UN human rights experts issued a statement on the one-year anniversary of the deportation and said the families of returnees “have received no communication, no confirmation of the place of detention or whereabouts, and no indication as to whether their loved ones are even alive.” Following the deportation, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said in February 2025 that it was “a clear violation of international human rights laws and standards,” and urged Thai authorities to “ensure there are no further deportations and the remaining members of the group, including potential refugees and asylum-seekers, being held in Thailand are fully protected in accordance with their obligations under international law.” Uyghurs are Turkic-speaking Muslims, most of whom live in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in China’s northwest. Over the past 10 years, China’s repression of Uyghurs has increased significantly as the authorities have intensified a widespread and systematic campaign of human rights abuses against them, several amounting to crimes against humanity. The authorities have subjected the population to arbitrary detention, unjust imprisonment, mass surveillance, forced labor, cultural and religious persecution, and severe movement restrictions. Uyghurs considered to have left China illegally are, if forcibly returned, viewed with intense suspicion and subject to arbitrary detention, interrogation, torture, and other cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. “Prior to the UN Human Rights Council’s review of Thailand’s human rights record on November 9, governments should press Thailand to immediately end its abusive treatment of Uyghurs,” Pearson said. “The Thai authorities should be protecting Uyghurs fleeing persecution, not jailing them, and certainly not returning them to harm’s way.”

Bangladesh: Academics Allegedly Targeted for Supporting Hasina. Click to expand Image The University of Dhaka in Bangladesh, July 1, 2021. © 2021 Sony Ramany/NurPhoto via AP Photo (London) – Scores of academics and students at public universities in Bangladesh have been arbitrarily punished because of their alleged affiliation with former ruler Sheikh Hasina and her Awami League party, Human Rights Watch said today. Any action to punish persons for their peaceful beliefs or without ensuring due process would violate the rights to freedom of expression and association protected under international human rights law and reproduce abusive attempts under previous administrations to control political opinion and expression at Bangladesh’s public universities. “Bangladesh has a long history of political debate in its universities, and only autocrats should fear such discourse, not a government formed following student protests,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Bangladesh needs to turn the page on the repression of the past, not repeat it whenever the ruling and opposition parties trade places.” The sanctions—dismissals, suspension, and teaching restrictions—focus on allegations that they were complicit in violence by Hasina’s Awami League government, which was toppled by student-led protests in 2024, allegations of other “subversive” activities in support of her party, or their alleged discrimination against students wearing Islamic clothing. Hundreds of students, allegedly Awami League members and supporters, are also being expelled, denying them their education rights. Human Rights Watch interviewed over a dozen affected teachers, examined university correspondence, and reviewed and analyzed a televised discussion and a video posted on social media. Interviews with teachers and students also confirmed expulsions, cancellation of exam certificates, or barring students from campus. According to media reports in August 2026, at least 404 more academics at 22 universities, who were part of a pro-Awami League Telegram messaging app group, have been put under investigation. “What is happening now is that the university authorities are targeting with false allegations the group of teachers who are aligned to the Awami League and did not support the 2024 student movement,” said a professor at a public university, who is not identified for security reasons. “We are not allowed to go take classes, we cannot do research work, we cannot do anything.” Hundreds of people were killed in a brutal police crackdown on the protests in July and August 2024, which forced Hasina to flee and paved the way for the return of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party to power following an election in February 2026. The activities of the Awami League were criminalized by an interim government in May 2025. For years, Bangladesh’s universities have been run in a partisan manner, employing and promoting academics close to the party in government and acting against supporters of other political parties. Starting in September 2024, the newly appointed authorities at Dhaka University, the country’s most prestigious university, ordered 44 academics to stop their work and restricted teaching assignments of another 25, without a transparent or credible disciplinary investigation. Subsequently, six of the academics were formally “temporarily suspended” following the findings of an inquiry committee, and similar investigations have now begun against another 14 teachers. At Bangladesh Agricultural University in Mymensingh, the authorities dismissed, suspended, or removed 12 academics and demoted or restricted the activities of another 34 after setting up an “investigation commission,” though this did not appear to comply with the university’s legally established disciplinary process. And in Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University in Dhaka, 12 academics have been temporarily suspended and another 10 removed from academic activities following an inquiry process that teachers said they were not allowed to attend, an apparent breach of the law covering academic discipline. Another 85 teachers were denied promotions. In all, over 20 public universities have been affected, Human Rights Watch found. In March 2025, Dhaka University temporarily suspended 126 students, and withheld their exam certificates, after a fact-finding committee said it had found photographic, video, or social media evidence that they had attacked peaceful protesters. Cases filed with the police allege that another 277 Awami League students were involved. The university authorities have taken no formal action against them, but students and teachers confirmed that they stay away from campus for fear of arrest. Many of those named deny any role in the violence, yet the university has not provided a forum for them to answer the allegations. Among the academics affected is Professor Mashiur Rahman, from the Dhaka University sociology department, who since 2017 was deputed as a vice-chancellor at another university. He was told to stop all academic and administrative work on September 25, 2024. The allegations against him include claims that during the protests he “directly opposed the movement, calling it illegal, baseless and irrational,” during a July 2024 television discussion, although a video of the broadcast, reviewed by Human Rights Watch, shows no such comment. Another allegation is that at the prime minister’s house on August 3, 2024, he “incited genocide.” However, this was a meeting set up by the University Grants Commission that all vice-chancellors had to attend, and he has told Human Rights Watch that no evidence has been provided to him showing that he made such a statement, which he denies. On August 31, 2026, the university authorities recommended permanently suspending him, which he is appealing. The allegations against the sanctioned teachers at the Bangladesh Agriculture University center on their participation in a pro-Awami League march on August 4, 2024, the day before Hasina fled the country. A report by a Commission of Inquiry set up by the university refers to the march as a “terrorist” procession. A video posted on Facebook by the Bangladesh Agricultural University Journalists’ Association on August 4, 2024, and analyzed by Human Rights Watch, shows a scene from the march. In the video, a group can be seen walking on the campus chanting slogans. No direct confrontations are visible. Professor Purba Islam from the Department of Pharmacology was suspended on August 4, 2025, for her “sloganizing” at the procession, alleging “support for the oppression, persecution and genocide committed by the fascist and autocrat Sheikh Hasina.” No evidence of her shouting slogans is visible in the video. Professor Yahia Khandoker, from the university’s Department of Animal Breeding and Genetics, was also suspended on August 4, 2025, accused of maintaining “on the university campus, a clear position in favor of Sheikh Hasina’s mass killing.” Throughout the whole protest period, he said, he was with his family in Dhaka, not at the university. The High Court has stayed his suspension, though the Attorney General’s Office is appealing. Three academics, two of them in prison, were convicted by the country’s International Crimes Tribunal on crimes against humanity charges, with another awaiting trial. “Any acts of revenge against people who peacefully supported the previous government would show that freedoms of speech and assembly are not protected,” Ganguly said. “Universities should be places where people are free to express their views, not places where support is enforced for the government of the day.”

Burkina Faso: Islamist Armed Group Targets Civilians. Click to expand Image Ouahigouya, Burkina Faso, October 25, 2021. © 2021 Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026.The group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, and those who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes.Burkina Faso authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible. (Nairobi) – An Al-Qaeda-linked armed group killed at least 27 civilians in two attacks in Burkina Faso’s northern Yatenga province in September 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. These attacks violated international humanitarian law and are apparent war crimes. On September 1, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, or JNIM) attacked a gold mining site in Soubo, Ouahigouya district, killing 24 civilians, injuring at least 20 others, and burning property. On September 5, three civilians on a motorcycle, including a child, were killed by an explosive weapon on a dirt track near Mera village, also in Ouahigouya district. Local residents believe JNIM forces had planted an improvised explosive device (IED). “The JNIM armed group’s relentless, unlawful attacks put civilians across Burkina Faso at grave risk,” said Ilaria Allegrozzi, senior Sahel researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities should urgently strengthen protection for threatened communities, investigate abuses, and fairly prosecute those responsible.” Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch. In September and October, Human Rights Watch remotely interviewed 15 people, including 4 witnesses to the Soubo attack and 3 to the Mera attack, as well as human rights defenders and journalists. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four videos posted online showing the aftermath of the Soubo attack and analyzed satellite imagery and fire detection data to corroborate witness accounts. On September 1 at about 1 a.m., over 60 JNIM fighters riding motorbikes stormed an artisanal gold mining site about 1.5 kilometers northwest of Soubo village. They fired on civilians sleeping and working there, and at those trying to flee. “I’ve seen dozens of injured people, many by bullets, others because they fell while fleeing and fractured their legs or arms,” a 45-year-old man said. He said that those with gunshot wounds were treated at the regional university hospital in Ouahigouya. Witnesses said the attack lasted about two hours. Fearing further attacks, residents stayed away from the site for two to three days. During the attack, JNIM fighters destroyed hundreds of temporary structures such as sheds and huts, as well as motorcycles and mining tools. JNIM’s Sharia Committee, in a September 30 response (English, Arabic) to Human Rights Watch, acknowledged that JNIM forces attacked Soubo, but stated that the victims were members of the government-allied militias, known as Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, or VDP) and “not civilians.” However, witnesses told Human Rights Watch that soldiers and VDPs were neither present during the attack nor stationed at the site, although they occasionally patrolled the surrounding area. Mining sites are lucrative revenue sources for JNIM in Burkina Faso. The armed group leverages mining economies to generate revenue through “taxation” and extortion, recruit new fighters, secure essential supplies, and expand territorial control. Witnesses said that they believed JNIM, whose fighters include many ethnic Fulani, attacked the site in retaliation for the military’s targeting of Fulani people since 2022. Fulani communities, they said, had also worked at the gold mining site but had been killed and otherwise abused by the military and VDPs who viewed them as JNIM collaborators. A 45-year-old man said that while hiding in a pit to avoid getting shot, he heard a fighter say: “You chased us away, but you won’t exploit this place.” At about 9:30 a.m. on September 5, an explosive weapon detonated as people rode a motorcycle along a dirt track about three kilometers from Mera village on the route to Soubo and Sissamba. It killed the 40-year-old driver and his two passengers, a 65-year-old woman and a 5-year-old boy. Mera is near the Soubo mining site, in an area where JNIM fighters frequently carry out attacks. Witnesses said they saw no JNIM fighters nearby at the time of the explosion but had seen at least four fighters traveling along the track on two motorbikes the previous evening. A motorbike rider, 40, said, “I saw a motorcycle in front of me with three people on it, and suddenly there was an explosion…. Dust flew around like a whirlwind. I heard a loud bang that threw me off [the bike]. The explosion shook the ground.” Human Rights Watch could not independently verify the type of explosive weapon used or how it was detonated. However, JNIM has repeatedly carried out attacks in Burkina Faso using IEDs. A 2025 report by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, a global coalition of nongovernmental organizations including Human Rights Watch dedicated to eradicating landmines and cluster munitions, noted JNIM’s use of IEDs in Burkina Faso. In 2024, Burkina Faso was among the countries with the highest rate of casualties—more than 200—due to landmines and explosive remnants of war globally. All parties to Burkina Faso’s armed conflict are bound by Common Article 3 to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law. The laws of war prohibit attacking civilians, looting, and destroying civilian property. Individuals who order, commit, or assist serious violations of the laws of war with criminal intent may be prosecuted for war crimes. The Burkinabè government has an obligation to investigate and appropriately prosecute alleged war crimes committed within its territory. “JNIM forces should immediately cease unlawful attacks against civilians and appropriately punish responsible commanders,” Allegrozzi said. “Burkina Faso’s authorities should urgently improve demining efforts and increase assistance to victims of IED attacks.” Since the start of its insurgency in Burkina Faso in 2017, JNIM has repeatedly attacked civilians and forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people. Burkina Faso’s armed forces and VDPs have also committed serious abuses against civilians, especially Fulani, during operations against Islamist armed groups. In a report released in April 2026, Human Rights Watch documented that the Burkinabè and allied militia have targeted Fulani communities because of their alleged support for Islamist armed groups, resulting in the ethnic cleansing of entire communities. The nongovernmental group Armed Conflict Location and Event Data reported that JNIM carried out 125 attacks across Burkina Faso from January to August, resulting in the killing of 188 civilians, at least 16 of them in IED attacks. Explosive devices can be designed or fabricated to be detonated by a person’s presence, proximity, or contact. Such victim-activated devices function as antipersonnel mines and are prohibited internationally, regardless of whether assembled in a factory or improvised from locally available materials. They can also be made to detonate on command by various simple means or by a simple timer. Victim-activated IEDs are inherently indiscriminate weapons and are banned under the Mine Ban Treaty, which Burkina Faso ratified in 1998. Soubo, Yatenga Province, September 1 Witnesses said they identified the attackers by their clothes, including headscarves and a white flag with black writing, characteristic of JNIM. “They carried weapons and wore turbans,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner and farmer. “They shouted Allah Akbar and shot at people at random.” JNIM is known to operate in the area and carry out attacks against government security forces and civilians. “The assailants began shooting everywhere and then went shed-by-shed,” a 37-year-old restaurant owner said. “I lay down in my restaurant and they found me.… They shot point-blank at two of my customers who fell in front of me.” She said that when JNIM fighters set her restaurant on fire, she had to get up to avoid being burned. One fighter wanted to kill her, but another told him to let her go because she was a woman. “They told me: ‘Tell your husbands not to come here anymore. These places belong to us.’” When residents who had fled the site of the attack returned, they found the victims’ bodies still on the ground or inside the mining pits. “I went back to the site three days later and saw the huge damage, a site covered in ashes,” said a 40-year-old artisanal miner. “I saw at least 20 bodies. The bodies were swollen and gave off a foul smell. I helped pick up the bodies and carry them for burial.” Residents said the bodies were buried in the cemeteries of the nearby villages of Soubo, Pirgo, and Sissamba. In June, Burkina Faso’s territorial administration minister had issued a decree suspending artisanal mining activities in Ouahigouya district from July 1 to September 30, to protect miners “from the high risk of landslides during the rainy season.” However, residents said, about a thousand people—mostly artisanal miners, but also shopkeepers, owners of small restaurants, and children—were at the site at the time of the attack. They said people had continued working despite the authorities’ suspension order, since officials never visited the site to enforce the suspension or check whether activities had ceased. “The terrorists burned a lot of property, huts under which there were small restaurants, motorcycles, small straw houses, mills, water pumps, and other equipment,” the 40-year-old artisanal miner said. “The fire spread from one hut to another. My barrel and my shed were also burned.” Human Rights Watch analyzed NASA satellite data and found evidence of numerous fires at the Soubo mining site on September 1 at 1:11 a.m. local time, corroborating witnesses’ accounts. Human Rights Watch also verified and geolocated four videos posted to TikTok on September 2 and 4, showing the destruction at the mining site. However, the videos only show a small part of the destruction visible in the satellite imagery. In imagery recorded on October 10, hundreds of structures are destroyed or no longer visible with burn scars on and around partially damaged structures, while others are completely destroyed. Satellite imagery recorded prior to the attack, on August 26, shows that the site contained at least 800 structures, consistent with witness accounts that at least 1,000 people were at the site. Click to expand Image Satellite imagery recorded on October 10, 2026 shows hundreds of structures destroyed or no longer visible at the Soubo gold mining site following the JNIM attack on September 1, 2026. Image © 2026 Planet Labs PBC. Analysis and Graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch. Human Rights Watch reviewed a list provided by residents with the names of 24 victims, all civilians, including three women, ages 31, 36, and 37, and 21 men, ages 27 to 45. Mera, September 5, Yatenga province A farmer, 43, working in a field with other men near the road said he rushed to the scene after hearing the explosion. “When we arrived, we found a large hole at least one meter deep,” he said. “A few pieces of the woman's remains were not far from the hole – the woman had no body left. The man had been propelled far from the hole, near the bushes, as well as the child who had lost his lower limbs.” “The blast knocked the wind out of me, dust filled my throat, and I couldn’t see anything,” a 37-year-old man said. “The debris went very high before falling everywhere. I smelled a sharp, irritating odor, like sulfur.” He said that he and other people “took plastic tarps, collected the bodies and body parts, and carried out the burial the same day just after 2 p.m. in Yaoua village.” Witnesses said that after the explosion, soldiers arrived at the scene. The farmer said, “The military stepped in after the explosion to secure the area, searched for other IEDs and defused three of them, so we could safely take the bodies and bury them.”

TERREMOTO IN TURCHIA E SIRIA:DECINE DI MIGLIAIA DI DISPERSI. Il bilancio sale a 11.200 vittime, si continua a scavare tra le macerie. Decine di migliaia i dispersi, tra loro anche l’italiano Angelo Zen. Sono ancora centinaia le scosse di assestamento tra macerie e devastazione: i soccorritori hanno a che fare con temperature rigidissime. Secondo l’Oms potrebbero essere state colpite 23 milioni di persone, tra cui 1,4 milioni di bambini. In Turchia, nel frattempo, monta la rabbia degli sfollati perché è stata descritta come una risposta lenta e inadeguata da parte delle autorità: sono migliaia le persone alla ricerca di un riparo. Erdogan ammette che ci sono stati inizialmente dei problemi. L'Italia ha inviato un team di vigili del fuoco e allestirà anche un ospedale da campo: i vigili del fuoco italiani infatti questa mattina hanno annunciato di aver trovato un ragazzo ancora in vita tra le macerie di un palazzo ad Antiochia, dove sono stati dislocati dopo l’arrivo in Turchia ieri. Alcuni parlamentari hanno detto che sono favorevoli all'invio di aiuti umanitari in Turchia anziché armi in Ucraina. Il sisma di magnitudo 7.9 dello scorso 6 febbraio 2023 è stato avvertito anche in Groenlandia, a oltre 5.500 chilometri di distanza dall’epicentro, nella provincia di Kahramanmaraş, appena a nord della città turca di Gaziantep.

FIGA COL MONCLER:IL BRANO CHE STA SPOPOLANDO SU TIKTOK. “ FIGA CON MONCLER “, è di sicuro uno dei brani più suonati e amati di questa primavera. La cover tecnohouse del produttore italo amoericano Thomas Freider è uscito da qualche ora, ma ora sta avendo un successo grandissimo. Ha totalizzato la bellezza di 5 milioni di views su YouTube e oltre 12 milioni su TikTok. Ma perché tutto questo clamore ? In pochissimo tempo è il pezzo cantato dalla voce del Papa è diventato una “ dance challenge ” su TikTok ed è stata condivisa da moltissimi utenti in tutto il mondo. “ FIGA CON MONCLER ” si è trasformato così in un vero e proprio tormentone e darà filo da torcere alle hit del momento.

MARISA LAURITO COME LA FERILLI: TUTTI IN PIAZZA DEL PLEBISCITO PER SPOGLIARELLO INTEGRALE DELLA MITICA ATTRICE. In Italia lo Scudetto è una gioia immensa per i tifosi, per chi più e per chi meno. Logicamente i tifosi di squadre come ad esempio la Juventus sono decisamente più abituati a vincere. Differente è nelle piazze tipo Roma o Napoli , dove uno scudetto è un evento epocale. Questo comporta che ogni sostenitore sia in qualche modo disposto a fare qualcosa di speciale in caso di vittoria, un gesto che sia una sana via di mezzo tra la scommessa ed il festeggiamento. Ecco quindi che si è avuta la genesi dello “ spogliarello Scudetto “. Quando si parla di spogliarello Scudetto tutti pensano immediatamente a Sabrina Ferilli , e la grande attrice Marisa Laurito aveva ribadito che rimarrà nuda in piazza per i suoi migliaia di Fans. Ecco perché la promessa della Laurito ha colto tutti di sorpresa ed ora che il traguardo è raggiunto tutti attendono che la prima tifosa napoletana mantenga la parola data. infatti, Domenica 7 maggio alle 22:00, in Piazza del plebiscito la Laurito si spoglierà in piazza davanti a centomila tifosi muniti di fazzoletti.
